audits.title: Animal health - aquaculture animals and products, disease prevention and control

recommendations.text: The CA should finalise guidelines for official controls on the aquaculture sector in order to be able to check that the requirements in Articles 4 and 5 of the Directive are implemented in a harmonised way throughout the country.

The CA should coordinate activities and standardise procedures to ensure a harmonised supervision system of official controls in APBs in all Voivods, as required in Articles 4 and 8 of Regulation (EC) No. 882/2004.

The CA should review their registration procedures in order to register, as required by Article 6 of the Directive, all premises that fall within the definition of an APB in Article 3. 1(c) without exceptions.
The CA should review their registry of authorised farms, to include only APBs that fully implement the requirements in Articles 8, 9 and 10 of the Directive.
The CA should endeavour to prepare a CP for exotic diseases as required in chapter V article 47 of the Directive.

The CA should designate a laboratory to carry out diagnostic analyses on crustacean diseases; furthermore they should satisfy themselves that a laboratory is designated to carry out analyses for the exotic diseases listed in Annex IV part II to the Directive.
The NRL should achieve the accreditation process for the methods used in the diagnosis of the diseases listed in Annex III and required in Article 56 of the Directive.
The NRL should review its methodology of analysis for VHS and IHN to take into sideration the requirements of Decision 2001/183/EC.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the National Contingency Plan considers the specific requirements within the scope of this audit, as required by Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

To ensure that procedures are in place to verify the effectiveness of controls, in particular with regard to the holding registration, herd registers, animal movement notifications, as required by Article 8.3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

To ensure that dealers resell or relocate animals within a maximum of 30 days of purchasing animals from the first premises to other premises not within their ownership as foreseen in Article 2.2 (q) of Council Directive 64/432/EEC.
To bring the computerised database in line with Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 1760/2000, in particular in accordance with Articles 14 and 18 of Council Directive 64/432/EEC.
To ensure that the selection of holdings to be inspected is based on a risk analysis in line with Article 2.4 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 1082/2003.

To ensure that the data in the computerised database are correct so as to ensure compliance with Article 14 of Council Directive 64/433/EEC and other Directives in respect of health restrictions and that administrative sanctions laid down in Article 4 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 494/98 are applied when needed.

audits.title: Import/transit control system and border inspection posts

recommendations.text: To ensure that National Legislation in force provides for collection of veterinary fees for the veterinary checks on imported and transited consignments as required in Annex V to Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

To strengthen the procedures and supervision to ensure correct implementation of import/transit requirements by applying enforcement measures and where appropriate also sanctions provided for by EU and national import/transit legislation in accordance with Artt. 54 and 55 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
To complete the implementation of a system for internal or external audits as required by Art. 4 (6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

To strengthen supervision and provide further training and more detailed instructions for BIP staff with respect to veterinary checks, in particular for correct and uniform application of physical checks of live animals to ensure correct and uniform performance of the official controls in accordance with Art. 4 (4) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and in line with Art. 4 of Directives 91/496/EEC.

To strengthen supervision and provide further training and more detailed, corrected and completed instructions for BIP staff with respect to decision on consignments, in particular for reduced physical check regime of imported POAO to ensure correct and uniform performance of the official controls in accordance with Art. 4 (4) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and in line with Decision 96/340/EC.
To ensure adoption of procedures allowing the performance of reinforced checks on 10 consecutive NHC consignments in accordance with Art. 24 (1) of Directive 97/78/EC.

To ensure that notifications are received in advance of physical arrival of the consignment of POAO on the Community territory as required by Art. 2 of Regulation (EC) No 136/2004 and Art. 3 of Directive 97/78/EC and at least one working day before physical arrival of the consignment of live animals on the EU-territory as laid down by Art. 3 of Directive 91/496/EEC jointly with Art. 1 of Regulation (EC) No 282/2004.
To ensure that reduced frequency of physical checks are applied to every third country and each commodity group as foreseen in Art. 1(1) and Annex I of Decision 96/340/EC.
To strengthen supervision and provide further training for BIP staff with respect to certification rules laid down in Annex IV of Directive 2002/99/EC and Directive 96/93/EC.

To provide further training and more detailed and completed instructions for BIP staff with respect to channelling procedures, in particular to identification of intermediate products for channelling and follow up of confirmation on arrival to controlled destination in accordance with Art. 8 (4) of Directive 97/78/EC.

To strengthen supervision and provide further training for BIP staff to ensure that decisions on consignments are done correctly, in particular regarding import and transit requirements for live animals from third countries and correctness of veterinary certificates, in accordance with Artt. 5, 8 and 9 of Directive 91/496/EEC.

To ensure that monitoring plan for sampling the imported consignments is risk based and addressed properly to allow sampling proportional number of consignments as required by Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 136/2004.

To further strengthen supervision of transit of non-EU conforming consignments stored in customs warehouses approved under Art. 12 (4) of Directive 97/78/EC to ensure that registers kept by operators guarantee the traceability of consignments and the reconciliation of the quantities of material entering and leaving the warehouse in accordance with Artt. 11 and 12 of Directive 97/78/EC and Decision 2000/571/EC.

audits.title: Food hygiene, traceability, labelling and bottled water

recommendations.text: Ensure efficient and effective coordination between all CAs involved in official controls on food according to Article 4(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
Ensure the implementation of the contingency plan as required by Article 4.2(f) and 13 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
Ensure that staff performing official controls receive appropriate training in assessment of HACCP procedures as required in Article 6 and Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
Ensure that official controls are carried out with appropriate frequency following the requirements of Article 3(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
Consider harmonising of the verification of the effectivenes of official controls.

Ensure that staff performing official controls receive sufficient information and instructions to enable them to perform their tasks correctly in accordance with Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
Ensure that internal audits are carried out within all CAS and that they meet all requirements of Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
Ensure that the MANCP contains informations about all CAs as required in Article 42(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

Consider applying the flexible approach to the implementation of HACCP principles according the EU guidance document on the implementation of procedures based on the HACCP principles and on the facilitation of the implementation of the HACCP principles in certain food businesses
Ensure that all guides to GHP assessed by CA comply with the requirements of Article 8 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004
Ensure that recognition procedure for NMW fully follows the requirements of Annex I to Directive 2009/54/EC.
Ensure that all CAs are involved in a network of RASFF as required by Article 50 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002.

audits.title: food contact materials and food additives

recommendations.text: Ensure an efficient and effective coordination between all CAs as required by Article 4.3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
Ensure the implementation of the contingency plan as required by Article 4.2(f) and 13 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
Ensure that staff performing official controls receive appropriate training in the area of FA and FCM as required in Article 6 and Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
Consider broadening the scope of analytical tests on FCM (Article 24(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1935/2004 and Article 3(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

Ensure that staff performing official controls of FA and FCM receive sufficient information and instructions to enable them to perform their tasks correctly in accordance with Article 8 (i) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
Ensure that official controls include the examination of written material as required by Article 10.2(e) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
Ensure that internal audits are carried out and that they meet all requirements of Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
Ensure that the MANCP contains all the information required in Article 42(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
Ensure that official inspectors are aware of the requirements of the declaration of compliance prescribed by Annex VIa of Commission Directive 2002/72/EC and ensure their correct implementation.
Ensure that FCM manufacturers implement GMP as required by Commission Regulation (EC) No 2023/2006.
Ensure the implementation of the monitoring system for the consumption of FA as required by Article 27 of Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008.

audits.title: Pesticide residues in food of plant origin

recommendations.text: Ensure the implementation of a contingency plan as required by Article 4 (2) (f) and 13 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
Ensure that auto-control systems in place at FBOs are evaluated for the purposes of the official controls as stipulated in Article 10 (2) (a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
Ensure that the MANCP contains all the information required in Article 42 (2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 for the different sectors in the food safety area.
Ensure that the national control programme for pesticide residues is multi-annual as required by Article 30 (1) of Regulation (EC) No 396/2005.
Ensure that all the necessary details are provided in the written instructions on sampling for pesticide residues in order to ensure that a uniform approach is followed by all the inspectors.

Ensure that decisions are taken on the frequency of physical checks, including sampling for pesticide residues at the points of entry, based on the criteria listed under Article 16 (2) (a) and (b) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

Increase the analytical scope (number of pesticides sought) in most of the official laboratories, so that the PPPs authorized for placing on the market and use in Poland and the pesticides listed in Annex I to Commission Regulation (EC) No 901/2009 are covered.

Ensure that any information relating to MRLs or pesticide residues in and on FNAO considered as a serious direct or indirect risk to human health is immediately notified to the Commission under the RASFF as required by Article 50(2) of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002.

Ensure that in the case of suspicion of non-compliance of FNAO imported from TCs official controls are performed in order to confirm or to eliminate any suspicion or doubt concerning the compliance, as laid down in Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
Ensure that obsolete pesticides in "tombs" are kept under supervision and safely disposed of in order to avoid possible contamination of food, feed and the environment.

audits.title: Plant Health - potatos and the general system of surveillance for harmful organisms

recommendations.text: There are adequate human and financial resources available to enable the minimim level of official checks and samples specified in EU phytosanitary legislation, and in particular Article 4 of Commission Directive 92/90/EC.
Activities for scientific purposes that involve the use of harmful organisms are monitored as required by Article 2(3) of Commission Directive 2008/61/EC.
In the event of a finding of ring rot in seed potatoes, all measures are taken to establish the primary source of infection as required by Article 8 of Council Directive 93/85/EC.

The extent of the demarcation is reassessed in light of any further findings of ring rot in clonally related lots as required by Article 6 of Council Directive 93/85/EC, and in particular in the event that ring rot is found in consecutive years in seed potatoes of the same origin.

Additional measures to encourage the use of certified or ring rot tested seed potatoes are considered to assist in the control of ring rot, as provided for in Article 11 of Council Directive 93/85/EC.

An increase in the frequency of ring tests for Clavibacter michiganensis ssp. sepedonicus is considered in order to ensure that the level of performance of the regional laboratories carrying out analysis for this organism, is satisfactory.

audits.title: organic production and labelling

recommendations.text: Ensure that operators put in place the respective control arrangements as specified in Title IV of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 and in particular that when the control arrangements are first implemented, the operator shall draw up and subsequently maintain a full description of the unit and/or premises and/or activity and that records shall be compiled in the form of a register.

Ensure that where transportation is direct between an operator and another operator who are both subject to the organic control system, the products are accompanied by a document giving the information required under paragraph 1 of Article 31 Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 and that both the expediting and the receiving operators shall keep documentary records of such transport operations available for the control body or control authority of such transport operations as required by paragraph 2 of the same Article.
Ensure that designated laboratories carry out the analysis of samples taken during official controls as required by Article 12 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

Ensure that that official controls are carried out regularly, on a risk basis and with appropriate frequency as required by Article 3(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 including measures to ensure compliance with Article 27(13) of Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. This should include controls at market level and additional measures to ensure traceability of each product at all stages of production, preparation and distribution. 7. 8. Ensure that the certificate of inspection referred to in Article 13 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 1235/2008 is always endorsed as required by Article 19(7)(a) of 9. the same Regulation and that where required, box 16 is filled in. Ensure that imports of organic products in accordance with procedures referred to in Article 19 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 1235/2008 are only authorised if the importer provides sufficient evidence showing that the conditions referred to in Article 33(1)(a) and (b) of Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 are satisfied. Ensure that random (additional) controls of operators are primarily unannounced as required by Article 65(4) Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Ensure that control bodies communicate the results of the controls carried out to the competent authority on a regular basis and whenever the competent authority so requests. If the results of the controls indicate non-compliance or point to the likelihood of non-compliance, the control body shall immediately inform the competent authority as required by Article 27(5)(d) of Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Ensure that the CA verifies the effectiveness of the controls performed by CBs as required by Article 27(9)(b) of Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 and in particular that information is assessed continuously and based on appropriate criteria.

audits.title: evaluate the use of the TRACES system

recommendations.text: ure that the system for verification of the use of TRACES covers different users, so that the related official controls are effective and appropriate, as laid down in Article 4.2 (a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation based on conclusion 62. Associated findings: 56, 57, 59 and 60.

citations.text: There is a system of supervision developed within the import control sector, which includes verification of the correct use of TRACES. This includes both local supervision by the head of each BIP and central supervision via supervisory visits to each B IP by the Borders Office (4 BIPs are visited per year). However, this supervision mainly focuses on correcting individual mistakes done by BIP staff. Supervision did not identify the shortcomings described in this report (e.g. use of collective user accounts, control of re-entry horses, follow-up at controlled bodies and destruction plants).

The Border Office also carries out periodic reviews of TRACES from central level using 11 data warehouse and Clickview since December 2012 to monitor the confirmation of receipt and takes appropriate actions when receipt is not recorded as required in respect of consignments imported under Articles 8 and 15 of Directive 97/78/EC.

The regional coordinator stated that TRACES was used for management of economic operators at LVUs and statistical information. Requirements for the regional coordinators do not foresee the supervision duties on the use of TRACES for INTRA-CERTS and control of animal by-products issued and received by LVUs .

At LVUs there is no system of supervision or other activity to assess the correct use of TRACES, therefore shortcomings identified by this audit and described under findings have not been noticed. There is no routine or pro-active analysis/verification of data within TRACES. Records are checked only in response to problems identified by the competent authority of the Member State of destination.

There is a system to assess the use of TRACES in BIPs by means of supervision. At the LVUs level the system of verification does not sufficiently cover the use of TRACES, therefore it is not ensured that deficiencies are detected and corrective actions are implemented when required. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS Poland has designated a competent authority for use of TRACES in relation to products of animal origin and live animals. Other competent authorities use TRACES for non-animal origin products for training purposes. In general staff at BIPs and LVUs are qualified and experienced in relation to TRACES activities and use TRACES correctly, with the exception of the controls of live animals at abattoirs and animals exported to third countries transiting through other Member States, and the follow-up of specific consignments (e.g. animal by-products for intra-EU trade, consignments re-imported, sent for destruction, quarantine or approved bodies). In some areas the lack of sufficiently detailed documented procedures (instructions) in both BIPs and LVUs reduces the performance of the use of TRACES on these issues, therefore the relevant official controls are either not recorded or recorded incorrectly in TRACES, contrary to the legal requirements. The systematic approach to assess the use of TRACES in BIPs is developed, however the system of verification does not sufficiently cover the use of TRACES at LVUs level, where the verification system does not ensure that deficiencies are detected and corrective actions are implemented when required. 12 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held on 28 February 2014 with representatives from the GVI, the State Sanitary Inspection, the State Plant Health and Seed Inspection Service and the regional veterinary inspectorate of Lublin. At this meeting, the main findings and the preliminary conclusions of the audit were presented by the audit team. The GVI requested clarification in relation to some issues but did not express disagreement with the findings and conclusions presented. 8 RECOMMENDATIONS The competent authority are invited to provide the details on actions taken and planned, aimed at addressing the recommendations set out below, within 25 working days of receipt of this audit report. N°. Recommendation 1. To ensure that the system for verification of the use of TRACES covers different users, so that the related official controls are effective and appropriate, as laid down in Article 4.2 (a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation based on conclusion 62. Associated findings: 56, 57, 59 and 60. 2. To ensure that all required data is entered into TRACES, including relevant official controls at abattoirs and control posts and controls on consignments which require confirmation of receipt at destination, e.g. intra-EU movements of certain animal by- products, sent to approved bodies or destruction consignments, as laid down in Decision 2004/292/EC. Recommendation based on conclusion 14. Associated findings: 7, 12, 28, 38, 39, 40, 44, 45, 46 and 48. citations.text: In one BIP visited where imported live animals were sent to approved bodies, the confirmation from the place of destination was not received and consignments were not followed-up by BIP staff contrary to the requirements of Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 282/2004. Staff were not aware of this requirement and the instructions do not contain information about it.

GVI provided a number of training courses, as required by Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, relating specifically to the use of TRACES or including it as a part of training themes. Staff also obtain on-the-job training and practice. The training courses were provided to regional services, LVUs and BIPs staff. Evaluation of the training material on control of animal by-products showed that training was sufficient and clear, however training was not effective because it had not improved the awareness of staff on the control of animal by-products at the place of destination and TRACES was not correctly used for those purposes.

The competent authority has suitably qualified and experienced staff, facilities and equipment relating to TRACES activities. Different users of TRACES received appropriate training enabling the correct use of TRACES. In some areas where instructions were not sufficiently detailed for both BIPs and LVUs, the relevant official controls are either not recorded or recorded incorrectly in TRACES. 5.3 USE OF TRACES Legal Requirements Decision 2004/292/EC, Commission Decision 2000/571/EC, Regulation (EC) No 136/2004, Regulation (EC) No 282/2004, Regulation (EC) No 599/2004, Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 of the European Parliament and of the Council, Commission Decision 93/444/EC, Directive 97/78/EC, Council Directive 2002/99/EC and Council Directive 90/425/EEC. 4 Findings 5.3.1 Management of users and organisations 5.3.1.1 Competent authority user accounts

Several consignments were sent to customs warehouses located in other Member States, but confirmation of arrival in TRACES was not received from the competent authorities at destination, what is not in line with the requirements of Article 2 of Decision 2000/571/EC. However, the BIP staff contacted the Polish customs authorities, who confirmed that consignments had arrived to the place of destination. The data in TRACES were never confirmed and there is no evidence that the consignment was controlled at the warehouse by the veterinary authorities of destination. The lack of feedback from destination is not notified by the BIP to the GVI, since instructions do not foresee follow-up of non- conforming goods transported to the customs warehouses, free warehouses or free zones. 3 In its response to the draft report the competent authority noted that two customs warehouses for storage of non- conforming products of animal origin currently operating in Poland, however there is the third customs warehouse (under supervision of district veterinary office of Gdynia) which is temporary suspended. 6 5.3.3.2 Transhipment/Transfer from BIP/DPE/DPI to BIP/CP and Transhipment to a non-EU country

For consignments re-imported, sent for destruction, transiting and others which need to be followed-up, the BIP of entry follows-up those consignments by contacting the customs services in writing. Customs provide confirmation in writing that the consignments in question arrived to the place of destination. Therefore such consignments were regarded as followed- up although confirmation was not recorded in TRACES.

One BIP visited received consignments of live animals destined for approved bodies in accordance with the national legislation, after the GVI issued an import licence for certain animals. CVEDAs issued were entered into TRACES, but part 3 (Control) of the CVEDA was never completed by an official veterinarian responsible for supervision of the controlled destination contrary to requirement laid down in Part 3 of Annex 1 of Regulation (EC) No 282/2004. 5.3.6.1.2 At destination

LVUs controlling the economic operator at the place of destination do not ensure that the outcome of control on the arriving consignment is correctly recorded in TRACES (this recording is required by Annex III of Regulation (EC) No 136/2004 and Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 282/2004). This requires additional follow-up efforts from the BIPs staff. The low level of confirmation of receipt at the place of destination (e.g. re-imported, sent for destruction, approved bodies) in Traces indicates that LVUs have a low level of controls to follow-up consignments at the place of destination. 5.3.7 Animal welfare checks

In relation to exports of live animals to third countries transiting through other Member States, it was noted: · that they are accompanied only by the certificate to export to the third country (in Polish and in the third country's language). The relevant instruction "Exportation of live animals and animal products to third countries" does not require an INTRA-CERT to be issued. Certifying officers entered data related to the consignment into TRACES as soon as possible after the consignment had departed but this could take a few days and the animals may have left the EU by then. Therefore, the requirements of Article 2(1) of Decision 93/444/EEC which requires consignments of live animals to be accompanied by an INTRA-CERT when being the subject of trade are not complied with. · the INTRA-CERT did not always contain the list of the individual animal identification numbers, contrary to the requirements of Article 3.1 of Decision 2004/292/EC. In the relevant box, it was cross-referenced to an Annex with this information, but the details were not accessible via TRACES. The relevant instruction was amended as from 14 February 2014 and now requires that the individual identification numbers are included in every certificate.

In relation to consignments of live animals arriving from other Member States, it was noted that: · according to the competent authority, all incoming TRACES notifications are checked to verify that the details they contain are acceptable, however in order to implment Article 5(a) of Directive 90/425/EC on non-discriminatory checks, 5 percent of consignments of live animals are physically controlled at destination often in the case of suspicion. · official controls related to ante-mortem inspections or welfare controls at Control Posts are not routinely recorded in TRACES, contrary to the requirements of Article 3.1 of Decision 2004/292/EC. There are currently no national instructions that require these 9 controls to be recorded in TRACES. LVUs inform the designated veterinarians at abattoirs when notifications via TRACES are received and veterinarians inform the LVU when any problems are detected with the consignments and the nature of the problem. The LVU then enters this information into TRACES. The competent authority stated that it was currently revising instructions for this area and that recording data into TRACES would be taken into consideration.

In relation to the movement of specific animal by-products, it was noted that: · The GVI stated that commercial documents were provided via the INTRA-CERT module of TRACES as required. Neither of the LVUs visited during the audit were responsible for controls on trade that would require issuing documents for the outward movement of such animal by-products to other Member States. · There is a national instruction on the requirements of Article 48.3 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 and it was covered in training courses in recent years. However, the GVI did not have an overview to what extent it was being implemented (i.e. the requirement that incoming consignments of certain animal by-products (Categories 1, 2 and processed animal proteins from Category 3) should be controlled and confirmed as having been received at destination in TRACES). The competent authority, on request of the audit team, checked the TRACES database for two separate CN codes. Over two different periods of time, figures of 8 and 29 percent of confirmation of receipt were obtained, despite thorough adequate training having been provided (finding 12) and verification did not cover use of TRACES at LVUs (finding 60). At the two LVUs visited, it was stated that no incoming consignments of animal by-products had been notified in recent years. 5.3.10 DOCOM module

Instructions on use of DOCOMs does not contain information on the requirement of follow- up of consignments of animal by-products received from other Member States contrary to the requirements of Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009.

recommendations.text: in place arrangements in order to ensure that official controls are carried out sufficiently thoroughly at transporters, traders and plants carrying out intermediate activities in the area of ABP/DP, so that it can be ascertained that the relevant requirements of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 are fulfilled, as required by its Article 4(3).Recommendation based on conclusions 13.Associated findings: 10, 21, 22, 23 and 27.

citations.text: According to the GVI, a relatively high frequency of official controls is planned for certain types of plants, to encourage compliance with the relevant requirements. The CVO instruction does not provide for the possibility to reduce the frequency of inspections to be carried out in plants with a strong record of compliance with the relevant requirements. The audit team noted that in some cases, the time spent on individual inspections is reduced in order that the required number of inspections can be carried out, leading to some tasks being completed in a superficial manner or not being completed. For example, in one transporter and two traders visited, the inspection reports indicated less than one minute had been spent on each question in the relevant check-list for ABP/DP controls. Although the check-lists provide for checks on incoming and outgoing materials, these had not been carried out sufficiently thoroughly to identify issues noted by the audit team; in an intermediate plant visited, this concerned receiving and stocking more ABP than the actual storing capacity, and in a transporter of fats, the dispatching of less ABP than had actually been received from a slaughterhouse (see paragraphs 21 and 22). In a DVI visited, an official stated that it was not possible to confirm the arrival of consignments of ABP/DP in TRACES owing to the workload.

The competent authorities have the necessary elements, including co-operation, supervision and documented procedures, to maintain and implement a mostly effective system of official controls as required by Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. Official controls are planned and carried out at a relatively high frequency. Nevertheless, in some cases, in particular in transporters, traders and plants carrying out intermediate activities, these are carried out and recorded rather superficially, which results in non-compliances being overlooked. 5.2 OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON TRACEABILITY REQUIREMENTS ALONG THE CHAIN Legal requirements Articles 4(3), 21, 22, 41, 43, 45(1), 46, 48 and 53 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009; Article 7 of Regulation (EC) No 999/2001; Articles 17(1), 32 and Chapter II of Annex VIII of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011; Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004; Articles 1, 2 and 3 of Commission Decision 2004/292/EC and; Article 8 of Directive 97/78/EC. Findings and observations 5.2.1 Imports, exports and intra-EU trade

In an intermediate plant visited dealing with former foodstuffs (different cuts and parts from slaughtered animals) the audit team noted that the operator was unable to demonstrate to which customers a certain batch of incoming ABP was distributed because apart from the archived commercial documents, no register of incoming and outgoing batches of ABP was kept. In the said plant, stock balance checks were almost impossible. The audit team compared the in-coming and the out-going quantities and found that in certain periods of the year the operator appeared to have more incoming material than could be stored on site. The operator explained that indeed that happens and in those cases they make use of other storage plants but was unable to adequately show that this had happened because no commercial documents were issued for this transfer. Official controls overlooked this issue.

National rules foresee dedicated transport for food or ABP/DP. However, in a transporter visited, the audit team noted that it could not be demonstrated that these requirements were fulfilled and that fats considered as food or ABP were actually kept separately, especially during reloading (the operator could not provide any evidence where reloading took place). This increases the risk that ABP could be diverted to the food chain. These findings were overlooked by official controls. In addition, the audit team noted that the official controls in 7 this establishment were particularly short (less than one hour), which would make a thorough covering of all points on the check-list impossible.

According to a trader of fats visited, his company was the only client of a transport company for the transport of fats. The audit team noted that the number of cistern vehicles owned by the specific transport company and registered as ABP vehicles was very high in comparison to the quantities of fats transported for the trader. In light of the national requirement for dedicated ABP vehicles, no plausible explanation could be provided about the usage of all ABP cistern vehicles which appear to be idle all year round. The audit team noted that official controls did not investigate this issue. It was also noted that official controls were particularly short (between half an hour and an hour) to cover thoroughly all points mentioned in the check-list.

In a trader visited, incoming loads of fish meal were accompanied by commercial documents which did not contain any information about the batch numbers of the product concerned. This was overlooked by the official controls.

citations.text: The CCA is not complying with the requirements of Article 21 of the Regulation to: ensure that training courses are available for personnel involved in killing and related operations (Article 21(1)(a)); deliver certificates of competence attesting the passing of an independent final examination (Article 21(1)(b)); approve training programmes of the courses (Article 21(1)(c)). The CCA explained that the legal basis to implement these requirements is in a draft national law which is ready to be adopted except for one controversial issue. This law also bans the slaughter of animals without prior stunning and this ban has been challenged by stakeholders. The issue was brought to the Constitutional Court which suspended the application of certain provisions of the Animal Welfare Act that were directly related to the prohibition on the slaughter of animals without stunning. As a consequence the publication of the draft law implementing the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009 was suspended. 5.1.2 Scientific support, guides to good practice and provision of certificates of competence Legal requirements Articles 13, 20, 21 and 29(2) of Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009. Findings

The CCA informed the audit team that: it had not identified scientific support for the purposes of Article 20 of the Regulation; at the time of the audit it had not been contacted by stakeholder organisations to assess guides to good practice to facilitate the implementation of the Regulation; although the system for training and provision of certificates of competence, as required by Article 21(1) of the Regulation, is not yet in place new personnel involved in the slaughter of animals and related operations are required to undergo three months practical training in the slaughterhouse of employment. A certificate of training is issued by the local CA at the end of this training. Conclusions on framework for controls

The ruling of the Constitutional Court of Poland against the prohibition of ritual slaughter has delayed the CCA's compliance with the requirements of the Regulation regarding guides to good practice, scientific support for both the CAs and the BOs, and a system for the training, examination for and provision of certificates of competence. citations.text: The CCA had very recently issued detailed instructions for OVs working in poultry slaughterhouses to monitor animal welfare indicators in broilers as required by Point 2 of Annex III of Directive 2007/43/EC. These instructions include the evaluation of samples of chicken's feet for footpad dermatitis and a relevant scoring system with two trigger levels of action depending on the severity of the welfare conditions of the birds: A trigger level for average welfare conditions, in which the OV at the slaughterhouse reports the findings to the supervising DVO. This information is kept at the supervising DVO and only communicated to the DVO of the farm of origin if a second notification is made. A trigger level of poor welfare conditions, in which the OV at the slaughterhouse reports the findings to the supervising DVO. The DVO in turn communicates the findings to the DVO of the farm of origin for necessary action.

A cumulative daily mortality rate of more than 5% triggers a notification of poor welfare conditions. This value is significantly higher than the maximum permitted CDMR in poultry flocks being kept at stocking densities between 39 and 42 kg/m², as indicated in Point 1(c) of Annex V of Directive 2007/43/EC.

The system that has started being implemented for the monitoring of welfare indicators of broilers at slaughterhouses takes into account the main animal based indicators but there is a risk of having only limited impact on the welfare conditions in farms. This is due to the high trigger values for the CDMR and the lack of availability of this data at the CAs where this matters, namely the DVO of the farm of origin and the CCA. 5.5 ACTIONS TAKEN IN CASE OF NON-COMPLIANCE Legal requirements Articles 22 and 23 of Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009. citations.text: The CCA had very recently issued detailed instructions for OVs working in poultry slaughterhouses to monitor animal welfare indicators in broilers as required by Point 2 of Annex III of Directive 2007/43/EC. These instructions include the evaluation of samples of chicken's feet for footpad dermatitis and a relevant scoring system with two trigger levels of action depending on the severity of the welfare conditions of the birds: A trigger level for average welfare conditions, in which the OV at the slaughterhouse reports the findings to the supervising DVO. This information is kept at the supervising DVO and only communicated to the DVO of the farm of origin if a second notification is made. A trigger level of poor welfare conditions, in which the OV at the slaughterhouse reports the findings to the supervising DVO. The DVO in turn communicates the findings to the DVO of the farm of origin for necessary action.

The data collected in the slaughterhouses on the welfare indicators of broilers is kept at the slaughterhouse unless this requires action according to the trigger system. Conclusions on monitoring of broiler welfare at the slaughterhouse and follow up

The system that has started being implemented for the monitoring of welfare indicators of broilers at slaughterhouses takes into account the main animal based indicators but there is a risk of having only limited impact on the welfare conditions in farms. This is due to the high trigger values for the CDMR and the lack of availability of this data at the CAs where this matters, namely the DVO of the farm of origin and the CCA. 5.5 ACTIONS TAKEN IN CASE OF NON-COMPLIANCE Legal requirements Articles 22 and 23 of Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009. Findings

When analysing these reports it is not possible to identify repeat offenders, trends in non-compliances in slaughterhouses of specific characteristics (throughput, species slaughtered, stunning method, etc.). Furthermore, these reports are not accompanied by any data analysis that could have made by the reporting DVO.

Similarly to the reports sent by the DVOs to the RVOs, these are not accompanied by any data analysis that may have been carried out by the reporting RVO. Furthermore, the format adopted by the CCA for the collection of data, including the data categories selected by the CCA, does not allow the CCA to carry out an effective analysis of the results of official controls (e.g. trends in non-compliances detected and repeat offenders). This notwithstanding that Section 9.2.2 of the Annex to Commission Decision 2008/654/EC provides guidance on the analysis of non- compliances for the submission of consistent annual reports to the Commission as required by Article 44 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Conclusions on evaluation and review of official controls

Regional and district CAs are effectively carrying out the evaluation of official controls on compliance with the Regulation. The CCA has put in place a system to collect results of official controls for the purpose of further analysis and review. The process of data collection aggregates data in two phases and as a consequence, some information is lost in the process. From the aggregate data reaching the CCA, it is not possible to effectively analyse certain aspects of compliance e.g. trends in non-compliances or recurring issues. This undermines the CCA's ability to achieve the objectives laid down in point 2(b) and 9.2 of the Annex to Commission Decision 2008/654/EC (to outline progress and analyse non-compliances). 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS There is a high level of BO compliance with the requirements of the Regulation which has been facilitated by the early actions undertaken by the CA since 2011 and the effective official controls being carried out by the local and regional CAs. Controls are similarly effective in detecting, and acting upon, cases of unfit animals arriving at slaughterhouses. Although the system for the training, examination and provision of certificates of competence is not in place, the system put in place for previous national training requirements ensures that persons slaughtering animals possess basic competences. Regional and district CAs are effectively carrying out the evaluation of official controls on the requirements of the Regulation. The CCA's system for the verification of the effectiveness of official controls utilises results of controls carried out for the purpose of further analysis and review. The information in these reports provides some degree of overview but not a full and clear picture of what is happening on the ground. This does not allow the CCA to carry out an effective analysis of the results of official controls for the purposes of identifying key issues and areas for improvement. The system that is to be implemented for the monitoring of welfare indicators of broilers at slaughterhouses takes into account the main animal based indicators but there is a risk of having limited impact on the welfare conditions in farms. 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held on 13 March 2015 with representatives of the CAs, at which the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit were presented by the audit team. 8 RECOMMENDATIONS The Competent Authorities are invited to provide, within 25 working days of receipt of the report, an action plan containing details of the actions taken and planned, including deadlines for their completion, aimed at addressing the recommendation set out below: No. Recommendation 1. audits.title: Pesticide residue controls in organic production

recommendations.text: Ensure further implementation of the provisions for sampling unauthorised pesticides in organic production, in particular regarding (a) weight of the laboratory sample in line with the national Regulations, (b) follow-up of suspected irregularities in line with the national Guidelines and Article 91 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Recommendation based on conclusions No 11 and 36 Associated findings No 10 and 34

citations.text: Both CBs visited had included in their Manual of Procedure a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for inspectors on the risk assessment for prioritising samples for pesticide residue analyses. There were also detailed sampling instructions. CB1 requires a laboratory sample of 500 g only, which is less than the 1-2 kg required for fresh fruits and vegetables in the national Regulations. The SOP of CB2 correctly implemented the national sampling provisions, but two laboratory files for samples of leaves indicated a weight of 32 and 107 grams, respectively, which is less than the 200 grams required for leaves in the national Regulations, and which may not be sufficient for a representative sample. Pesticide residues were detected in these two cases, and enforcement actions considered by the CB. Conclusions on sampling for detecting unauthorised pesticides at Organic Operators

The recent national guidance on pesticide residue control in Organic production provides for a process of harmonising pesticide residue controls within Poland. Both control bodies complied with the requirement of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 for testing 5 % of the operators. Clear sampling procedures have been specified in national legislation. They were implemented by the CBs visited, except for the minimum weight of the laboratory sample. This can influence the representativeness of the samples and the validity of any enforcement decision. 5.3 LABORATORY PERFORMANCE Legal Requirements Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 on delegation of specific tasks related to official controls; Article 12 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 on official laboratories; 5 Article 33 of the Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 on national reference laboratories. Standards and Guidelines Guidance Document (SANCO/12571/2013). Findings

A file for pesticide detection in 2014 was examined by the audit team at CB1. The producer had been informed of the decertification of her field based on a pesticide residue detection of 0.03 mg/kg of the pesticide pendimethalin. There was no evidence of consultation of the producer concerned, contrary to Article 91(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Neither follow-up inspection nor re-sampling was performed. In 2014, a total of 146 samples of organic products had been taken and in two cases only there were pesticides detected. In a further eleven cases, the producer admitted the use of unauthorised pesticides without samples being taken. Conclusions on measures in cases of pesticide residue detections

The national Guidelines will help harmonising investigation procedures across CBs. Files for pesticide residue detections in 2014 show the different approaches taken by CBs at the time. This demonstrates the need for further harmonisation through the new Guidance, in order to achieve consistent investigation procedures compliant with Regulation (EC) No 889/2008.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the delegation of tasks and documented procedures include clear instructions for the laboratory analysis, in line with Articles 5(2)(a) and 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation based on conclusion No 23 Associated finding No 13

citations.text: The MIAFQI Guidelines (see point 7) specifies that the scope of laboratory analyses should not focus on the price, but on the likelihood to find pesticides. The analyses should also take into account the type of product, the risk of infringement and plant protection measures in conventional farming. The Guidance does not explicitly specify which pesticides should be checked, and the sensitivity of methods as expressed by the Limits of Quantification (LOQs) to be applied by the laboratory. Article 5(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires that the CA may delegate specific tasks to a particular control body only if there is an accurate description of the tasks to be carried out and of the conditions under which it may carry them out. Article 8(1) of the same Regulation requires that CAs carry out official controls in accordance with documented procedures.

The laboratories and an NRL have been adequately designated in line with Article 12 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. There were no official criteria for the CBs on the laboratory checks to be carried out, contrary to Articles 5(2)(a) and 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Consequently, the performance of the analysis is compromised. This affects the range of pesticides checked and the quality control procedure applied.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the results reported by designated laboratories are supported by adequate quality control procedures, in line with the DG SANCO Quality Control Procedures (SANCO/12571/2013). Recommendation based on conclusion No 25 Associated findings No 20 and 22

citations.text: The two laboratories are accredited to ISO 17025 with flexible scope in pesticides and commodities by the Polish Accreditation Body (PCA), although a full validation of the methods was only performed in apple. The two laboratories apply the criteria of the EU Quality Control Procedures (SANCO/12571/2013), providing adequate traceability of the sample, matrix matched calibration, adequate identification criteria and quality control activities. Recovery checks were evaluated routinely, but in the private laboratory not all analytes covered by the scope of the MRM were checked regularly and an inadequate calibration process by a single point calibration was observed. Uncertainty values were not applied consistently. The laboratory in Skierniewice follows a specific bottom up approach for estimating uncertainty, as recommended by PCA. In the private laboratory the uncertainty values used are not sufficiently supported by results from quality control and proficiency tests.

The SANCO Quality Control Procedures for pesticide residue analysis are not considered by PCA for the accreditation of the laboratories to ISO 17025. These procedures are regularly revised by DG SANTE and the EU Reference Laboratories (EURLs) for pesticide residues, taking into account the latest scientific information on pesticide residue analysis. Conclusions on laboratory performance

The Accreditation Body did not consider the science-based SANCO Quality Control Procedures for the accreditation of laboratories to ISO 17025. Consequently, the private laboratory visited did not sufficiently apply these procedures. Especially where the laboratories do not participate in the EU proficiency tests, it is not ensured that the reported results are supported by relevant quality control procedures which can undermine the reliability of test results. 7 5.4 MEASURES IN CASES OF PESTICIDE RESIDUE DETECTIONS Legal Requirements Article 54 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 on action in case of non-compliance; Article 55(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 MSs on sanctions; Article 30 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 on measures in case of infringements and irregularities; Article 91 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 on measures in case of suspicion of infringements and irregularities; Article 92(d) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 on catalogue of measures in case of irregularities and infringements; Article 92 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 on exchange of information between control authorities, control bodies and competent authorities. Recommendation based on conclusion 77 Associated finding Nos 69 and 74 The CA should ensure that the food chain information document provided in Section III of

citations.text: The audit team was informed by the CA that, under the SNCPs for all poultry populations, a flock is only considered positive when a relevant Salmonella serotype has been isolated either during official sampling or when positive own-check sample has been confirmed by official sampling and analysed by the official laboratory.

When reviewing the information provided by the CCA the audit team noted that in breeders of Gallus gallus, laying hens and broilers, positive FBO samples are reported as negative flocks if the routine official confirmation is negative. In breeders of turkeys and fattening turkeys, flocks are reported as positive when the own-check result alone is positive. 11 The CCA informed the audit team that the prevalence in 2014 in breeding flocks of Gallus gallus was recorded as 1.54 % (25 positive adult flocks out of 1,627 flocks tested). Seventeen flocks tested positive for relevant Salmonella serotype in the FBO own-check sampling and nine of these seventeen flocks proved negative in confirmatory sampling and were reported as negative flocks. The prevalence in breeders of Gallus gallus would be 2.09 % if all nine own-check positive flocks were included. The CCA informed the audit team that the prevalence in 2014 in laying hen flocks was recorded as 1.90 % (45 positive adult flocks out of 2,364 flocks tested). Fifteen flocks tested positive for relevant Salmonella serotype in the FBO own-check sampling and ten of these fifteen flocks proved negative in confirmatory sampling and were reported as negative flocks. The prevalence in laying hens would be 2.33 % if all ten own-check positive flocks were included. The CCA informed the audit team that the prevalence in 2014 in broiler flocks was recorded as 0.15 % (54 positive adult flocks out of 35,662 flocks tested). Sixty-eight flocks tested positive for relevant Salmonella serotype in the FBO own-check sampling and 45 of these 68 flocks proved negative in confirmatory sampling and were reported as negative flocks. The prevalence in broilers would be 0.28 % if all 45 own-check positive flocks were included. Conclusion on general issues on SNCPs

The routine confirmatory sampling and the reporting policy applied in Poland has an impact on the calculated prevalence of Salmonella compared to other Member States. In particular regarding flocks of breeding Gallus gallus, laying hens and broilers, given that routine confirmatory sampling is applied and that flocks are deemed positive only after official confirmation of positive own-checks. 5.4 SNCP FOR BREEDING HENS Legal requirements Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 2160/2003. Article 1 of Regulation (EU) No 200/2010. 12 Findings

responses.response: Reply from GVI: All the flocks considered as positive are included in the reports as positive ones. In case of negative result of confirmatory sampling, according to the programmes, a flock is treated (and reported) as a negative one. The programmes, which provide confirmatory sampling, were approved by the Commission. If required change of national law ­ the Act on animal health protection animal diseases eradication ­ will be implemented official confirmatory sampling will be removed from the programmes for 2017 and the following years.
