audits.title: Animal Welfare - Dairy Farms

recommendations.text: The organisation of the GVI is described in detail in the report DG SANCO 2014-7013 of the "Country Profile" of Poland, including the control systems of relevance for animal 5 Commission guidelines for the prudent use of antimicrobials in veterinary medicine (OJ C 299, 11.9.2015, p.7) http://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?qid=1450453756494&uri=CELEX:52015XC0911%2801%29 4 welfare at farm, and which is accessible at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/fvo/country_profiles_en.cfm
There is no specific national policy on welfare of dairy cattle; the GVI covers it within the national farm animal welfare checks for cattle and calves (see also paragraphs 9 to 13).

The Agency for Restructuring and Modernisation of Agriculture (ARMA) is responsible for cross compliance inspections and the respective direct payments and/or deductions, which include animal welfare requirements (Regulation (EC) No 1782/2003). The animal welfare part of those inspections is performed by the GVI (see also paragraphs number 14 and 19).

The Department of Rural Development of the Ministry of Agriculture indicated that under Rural Development Funds, for 2014-2020 there are two types of grants available for dairy farmers that contribute to the welfare of cattle on dairy farms: one for modernising agricultural holdings, namely livestock buildings, available from November 2016 to farms of at least 300 hectares; another for restructuring small farms, expected to be available from the first quarter of 2017.

The Polish Federation of Cattle Breeders and Dairy Farmers developed a selection index (Index PF - Production and Functionality) to identify the desirable animals (applied to the Holstein breed) to be used for breeding. The current index includes the following overall parameters and percentage weights: productivity 40% (milk yield of fat + 2x yield of protein), conformation 25% (parameters related to rump, chest, udder, legs and feet), fertility 15%, somatic cell count 10% and longevity 10%. Longevity was the most recent change, in 2014, to the selection index and it was added by reducing the weight of the productivity parameter from 50% to 40%. In addition to the use of the selection index these Federation of breeders: provides advisory services for dairy cattle breeding, milk production evaluation, and nutrition. Approximately 21 000 dairy cattle farms -with 36% of the dairy cattle in Poland- are registered for the breeding and milk production evaluation service; publishes a breeders magazine, brochures on some subjects of relevance for dairy cattle welfare as well as the book "Cow Signals: A practical guide for dairy farm management".

Other actors include dairy processors, cooperatives, and associations, as well as the Polish Chamber of Milk which congregates many of those processors and, also producers' associations. Different cooperatives and processors, or processors associations, take different approaches concerning the support provided to dairy farmers: all buyers of raw milk perform regular testing of herd milk quality and composition (e.g. total plate count, somatic cell count, protein and fat content); another type of support frequently available is via the provision of farm advisory services (similar to the Federation of Cattle Breeders and Dairy Farmers but without 5 the same emphasis on breeding selection), training, and preferential loans to modernise facilities and equipment.

The Warsaw University of Life Sciences, in cooperation with the National Veterinary Institute and a dairy cooperative, carried out a research project entitled "Healthy Cow", aiming at improving economic efficiency of dairy farms through counseling and training on genetic improvement, health, welfare and nutrition of dairy cows, production technology and the economics of dairy farming. The project included data gathered between 2008 and 2015 from up to 69 participating farms and approximately 7 000 cows. This data showed a very significant increase in milk yield per cow. It showed also a high culling rate (33%/year) and that only ~10% of the cows had been provided with feed correctly formulated, and/or placed under proper environmental conditions and management to allow such a high milk yield without causing some level of malnourishment; The project developed a dairy farm production model that will be made freely available for implementation by other dairy farmers. The University believes that the model is valid for approximately 90% of the Polish dairy farms. 5.2 ASSURANCES FROM COMPETENT AUTHORITY ACTIVITIES ON FARMERS' COMPLIANCE WITH LEGAL REQUIREMENTS Legal requirements Directive 98/58/EC. Commission Decision 2006/778/EC. Articles 3, 4, 6, 7, 17 and Appendix B of the Council of Europe Recommendation Concerning Cattle. Paragraphs 6 and 15 of Annex I to Directive 2008/119/EC. Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

National legislation on animal welfare is found under the Animal Protection Act of 21 August 1997. In particular, legislation regulating the welfare of cattle of dairy farms is found in: the Regulation of the Minister for Agriculture and Rural Development of 28 June 2010 concerning the minimum conditions for keeping livestock species other than those for which protection standards have been laid down in European Union legislation; the Regulation of the Minister for Agriculture and Rural Development of 15 February 2010 on requirements and procedures applicable to the rearing of farm animal species for which protection standards have been laid down in European Union legislation. 6

Documented procedures are available for planning and carrying out official controls on animal welfare in dairy farms, as required by Art. 8 of Reg. 882/2004. These procedures are included in the Chief Veterinary Officer's instruction (GIW pr. 02010-1/2015 of February 2015) which covers official controls on the welfare at farm of all animal species.

This instruction includes the relevant points from Directives 98/58 and 2008/119, and the Recommendation ( e.g. it was updated in February 2015 to include the requirement for the provision of sufficient quantities of iron in feed (Point 11 of Annex I of Dir. 2008/119)- for welfare of calves). It includes sections for the welfare of calves and the welfare of (adult) cattle, without distinctions between production types (beef or dairy), but does adequately refer to differences related to particular housing methods (tethering, loose stalls, grazing, etc.).

The instruction provides an exhaustive description on the minimum requirements of resource-based measurements (stall dimensions and surface area depending on the weight and category of the animal, environmental parameters, etc.) and relevant enforcement actions to take depending on the type of non-compliance detected; It also refers to animal-based indicators that should be taken into account (hoof condition and lameness, nutritional status of the animal, condition of the udder and the skin) when describing what controls should be carried out regarding the health status of the animals but has no indications on how inspectors should assess (or of possible reference guidance to use for assessing) herd lameness and body condition (e.g. what should be the body condition of an adequately nourished dairy cow at the different stages in its production cycle).

There are dedicated checklists annexed to the instruction, including checklists for general farm animal welfare requirements (Dir. 98/58), for calf welfare requirements (Dir. 2008/119) and for additional welfare requirements for cattle (based on national requirements mainly on stall dimensions).

In line with Art. 6 of Directive 98/58, the instruction requires each Poviat (District) Veterinary Inspectorate (PVI) to carry out controls on 5% of cattle farms annually. The instruction indicates: 50% of farms should be selected using risk-assessment criteria, e.g results of previous inspections, non-compliances (including where milk collection has been suspended due to raw milk non-compliances), size of the herd (larger herds may have higher non-compliances due to stocking density and management difficulties), sudden changes in herd size, change of ownership, and (increased) number of fallen animals; other 50% of farms should be selected randomly.

Planning and organisation of official animal welfare controls is in line with the requirements of Art. 3(1) of Reg. 882/2004. In the PVIs visited, the "other 50% of farms" were initially selected using also risk criteria to create an extended list (e.g. with all farms not inspected in recent years for welfare controls, farms with less than 10 cows as more of them are not included in any advisory service or receiving the single farm payment) and then choosing randomly amongst these the specific farms to be visited. 7 The audit team was informed that in addition to these checks, additional welfare controls are carried out when a PVI is made aware of possible non-compliances (from inspections on farm for other purposes, notifications from dairy establishments of somatic cell counts exceeding the legal limit, complaints) and to farms that apply for grants to modernise their facilities.

The GVI carries out all animal welfare controls including those reported under ARMA. The PVIs visited indicated that ARMA provides each PVI with a list of all cattle farms present in their district. This list also indicates which farms are enrolled in the single farm payment scheme. When selecting which farms will be the subject to animal welfare controls under Dir. 98/58, the controls have to include a minimum percentage of the farms enrolled in the scheme. Any welfare non-compliances detected in farms enrolled in the scheme are reported to ARMA.

The audit team visited two farms. PVI inspectors explained on site how they performed their animal welfare checks and what information they gathered about the farm prior to coming to inspect it: The explanations covered relevant points with the main emphasis and time spent being on resource-based parameters related to minimum stall dimensions, environmental parameters, record keeping, facilities, hygiene and equipment requirements; Equipment was available to measure environmental parameters and stall dimensions as required by Article 4(2)(d) of Reg. 882/2004; Audit team queries regarding the evaluation of animals to decide on their welfare status resulted in replies referring to presence of wounds or injuries, aspect of the cows' udder, cleanliness and hoof condition; Both farms kept cows tethered in stalls with abundant straw bedding. Stall dimensions were compliant with minimum national requirements. Most cows were longer than the stalls, but the audit team noted that animals did not present significant lesions on their hind legs that would indicate unsuitable accommodation. One of the farms kept part of the cows (the milking ones) in a building with a loose house system with access to stalls with abundant straw bedding. These stalls were longer than the stalls for the tethered animals.

The GVI collects the results of PVIs' welfare inspections through the Voivodship (Regional) Veterinary Inspectorates, for the purposes of Dec. 2006/778. PVIs carried out 25 563 general animal welfare inspections of cattle farms (dairy and beef) in 2013 and 24 883 in 2014. For both years, 83% of the farms were reported in full compliance. Regarding conditions for rearing calves, 20 063 inspections were performed in 2013 and 19 316 in 2014. For both years, 83% of farms were in full compliance.

The most frequent non-compliances reported in 2013 and 2014 for both cattle and calves concerned 'Buildings and accommodation' (including insufficient stall dimensions), record keeping and the provision of feed, water and other substances. The PVIs visited indicated that from their analysis the main reasons for these non-compliances were old 8 farm structures that needed renovation, excessive number of animals for the available space due to calving season or increased herd size, and increased inspectors' attention on quality of record keeping due to the addition of this criterion for cross-compliance controls as from 2013.

Data provided by ARMA indicated that 274 dairy farms receiving single farm payments had animal welfare non-compliances in 2014. The most frequent non-compliances concerned access to water (29% of farms with non-compliances) and medicinal and mortality records (20% of farms with non-compliances). Conclusions on assurances from competent authority activities on farmer's compliance with legal requirements

The level of checks together with the detailed instructions for controllers and risk- based planning ensure compliance of farms with structural requirements linked to cattle welfare. The systems is less robust for ensuring that other factors which might impact animal welfare (e.g. lameness, nutritional status) are controlled systematically and in a harmonised manner. 5.3 INDICATORS OF ANIMAL WELFARE Legal requirements Directive 98/58/EC. Articles 3, 4, 6, 7, 17 and Appendix B of the Council of Europe Recommendation Concerning Cattle. Paragraphs 6 and 15 of Annex I to Directive 2008/119/EC. Findings

The main animal welfare indicators identified, and how they are used, are listed in Table 1 below: Table 1 Indicators WHO uses them? HOW are they being What are the used? TRENDS? Related to GVI Official controls National level data MASTITIS Genetic selection not immediately Federation of Cattle Penalties available Somatic cell count Breeders and Dairy Farmers Dairy processors 9 Related to GVI Condition of hooves National level data LAMENESS not available Federation of Cattle Conformation of legs Breeders and Dairy and hooves Farmers Related to Federation of Cattle Genetic selection National level data REPRODUCTIVE Breeders and Dairy (indirectly through not available Farmers their impact on diseases/issues fertility) Federation of Cattle Related to Breeders and Dairy Not yet in use METABOLIC Farmers Warsaw University Research diseases of Life Sciences

Milk testing for somatic cell count (an indicator of mastitis) is the almost universally used (all farms that place milk in the market) animal based welfare indicator. Sometimes, signs of metabolic diseases such as acidosis and ketosis are also used. Somatic cell count is performed by dairy processors to ensure compliance with raw milk criteria legal requirements. The limit value is the maximum legally allowed (400 000/ml) and dairy processors will usually impose a payment deduction if the limit is exceeded and, if the rolling geometric average exceeds the limit, they suspend milk collection. The Federation of Cattle Breeders and Dairy Farmers is planning to add parameters related to acidosis and ketosis into its milk testing. The Warsaw University of Life Sciences also took these into account within the "Healthy Cow" project.

The mentioned Federation of Cattle Breeders created a selection index that includes animal based indicators such as milk yield and composition, somatic cell count, conformation, fertility, and longevity, and verifies such indicators through milk testing and on-site advisory services to the farms subscribing to that programme. Approximately 36% of the dairy cattle in Poland belong to farms subscribed to this programme.

For the remaining cattle population, dairy farmers carry out daily checks for injuries and the general health status of their animals but indicators such as lameness and/or body condition scores, longevity, reproductive diseases and disease in calves are not yet used systematically as possible indicators of animal welfare issues. Conclusions on indicators of animal welfare

Other than somatic cell count, the use of animal based welfare indicators, which can 10 help identify and prevent animal welfare issues from developing, is still not widespread or systematic in Poland. 6 OVERALL C

audits.title: Animal health - identification and registration systems for bovines, small ruminants and porcines

recommendations.text: The Competent Authority should ensure that pigs can be traced back to the holding from which they came as required by Article 5(2) of Directive 2008/71/EC (i.e. they are marked with either an ear tag or tattoo making it possible to determine the holding from which they came and enabling reference to be made to any accompanying document which must mention such ear tag or tattoo). Recommendation based on conclusion No.32 Associated findings Nos.16, 18, 19, 20

citations.text: The Polish Act of 2 April 2004 on the identification and registration of animals requires pigs born in Poland to be identified with an ear tag or tattoo bearing the 12 digit holding number of birth. If pigs move to another holding, there is no requirement for them to be marked with the 12 digit holding number of the second holding when they leave. This is not in accordance with the requirements of Article 5(2) of Directive 2008/71/EC.

In one pig slaughterhouse visited, carcases observed were identified in a number of ways including : single illegible plastic ear tags, single fully legible ear tags, fully legible 12 digit tattoo of Polish holding number, single fully legible ear tag from another Member State but no tattoo/ear tag with a Polish holding number (even though it arrived at the slaughterhouse from a Polish farm) additionally carcasses were seen with no eartag or tattoo.

Regulation (EC) No. 853/2004, Annex III, chapter IV (3) requires the food business operator (FBO) to ensure animals sent for slaughter are identified so their origin can be traced. In the case of carcases with no ear tag or tattoo, this had not been detected by the operator at ante-mortem examination or by the OV during their verification.

In the slaughterhouse visited, FBO operated an internal traceability system whereby all pig carcases were identified with a FBO batch code which related to the supplier. One batch code reviewed by the audit team demonstrated that pigs presented by one supplier had been sourced from 11 other holdings. The operator was in possession of holding numbers for these 11 suppliers but it was not possible, with the information available in the abattoir, to determine the holding where each pig had been consigned from; for this, as a minimum, each holding register for the 11 holdings would have to be examined.

In case of disease outbreak, the existing weaknesses in pig identification would lead to an increased number of herds being restricted and investigated in order to determine the route and source of infection. Consequently, this would result in increased demands on official services and likely delay in implementing control measures. The necessary backward tracing using holding registers would not be possible where pigs had no identification or illegible identification.

recommendations.text: The Competent Authority should ensure that bovine animals sent from its territory to another Member State have remained in a single holding of origin for a period of 30 days prior to loading or since birth, as required by Article 6(1) of Directive 64/432/EEC and that this is certified in line with the principles in Directive 96/93/EC. Recommendation based on conclusion No. 53 Associated findings Nos. 43 and 44

citations.text: In the assembly centre visited, the audit team selected and reviewed a sample of certificates from the Trade Control and Expert System (TRACES) and supporting documents for consignments of bovines certified for intra-EU trade and noted the following: one calf had pre-certification from its birth herd and a passport showing it left its birth herd at 21 days of age and arrived at the assembly centre three days later. The passport confirmed the calf had been registered in three holdings before arriving at the assembly centre. records for a second calf showed it arrived at the assembly centre, at 23 days of age, having been registered in three other holdings before arriving at the assembly centre.

The audit team reviewed approximately five intra-trade certificates selected from TRACES and issued from an assembly centre in a different region of Poland and cross checked animal movements in the ARMA database. One calf left its holding of birth at 21 days of age, spent three days at a second holding before moving to an assembly centre and being certified for intra-EU trade the following day. This, along with point (43) above, is not in compliance with the requirements of Article 6 to Council Directive 64/432/EEC. In the final meeting, the competent authority provided a copy of a letter dated 25 January 2016 and addressed to all regional veterinary inspectorates. This letter stated that all animals moving to an assembly centre must move there directly from a farm where they have spent at least the previous 30 days or since birth if less than 30 days of age.

There is a weak system of certification of live bovine for intra-union trade from assembly centres. As all relevant available information is not reviewed by certifying officers prior to issuing veterinary certification, the system does not provide the necessary guarantees and illegible animals (i.e. animals that did not stay 30 days prior to loading or since birth in holding of origin) are certified and traded, which increases the risk of spreading diseases through the EU. 5.3 REVIEW / CONTINUOUS IMPROVEMENT Compliance with minimum legal requirements requires significant investments but doesn't guarantee efficient and effective functionalities for the various services provided. In order to bring the systems up to a level where users get real benefits and return for investment, more 6 In their response to the draft report the Competent Authority noted that the registered office of dealers without premises has a special identifier in the Central Database. This means that even if a movement of animals to such a location is registered in the Central Database, it is apparent that the animals have not been physically moved to that entity. 13 than minimum compliance is needed. Review and continuous improvement are the mechanisms, which ensure that users receive a good quality of service, and the system continues to deliver efficiently and effectively what is expected from it. Four elements of monitoring and review were assessed: Monitoring of control results for: o Food business operator's compliance levels, types of non-compliance and trends; o Verifying effectiveness of controls and further development; Analysis of existing data for various purposes; and Internal and external audits or other evaluations. Legal requirements Monitoring of control results: Commission Decision 2008/654/EC provides guidance on the annual report for the single integrated multiannual control plan. Point 9.2.2 of the Annex to this Decision suggests that control data should be analysed, patterns and trends identified and root causes for non-compliance described, as appropriate. Article 4.2 of Regulation (EC) 882/2004 has a generic requirement: "The Competent Authorities shall ensure the effectiveness and appropriateness official controls on live animals..." Article 8.3 of the same Regulation requires Competent Authorities to "have procedures in place to verify the effectiveness of official controls that they carry out..." Monitoring of control results is one way of addressing the latter requirement ­ other means do exist but those fall outside the scope of this audit. There is no explicit legal requirement in the specific identification and registration systems legislation to monitor, review and improve the systems. Equally, analysis of existing data for various purposes is not a legal requirement ­ this audit attempted to harvest good/best practice in this area, if possible. Internal and external audits or other evaluations: Article 4.6 of Regulation (EC) 882/2004 requires that Competent Authorities "...carry out internal audits or have external audits carried out, and shall take appropriate measures in the light of their results..." Findings Monitoring of trends and patterns in non-compliance

recommendations.text: The Competent Authority should increase the quality of their identification and registration data of bovine, ovine and caprine animals by increasing the check rates when a significant degree of non-compliance is identified- as required by Article 2(2) of Regulation (EC) No 1082/2003 and Article 2 of Regulation (EC) No 1505/2006. Recommendation based on conclusion No. 31 Associated finding No. 26

citations.text: Data provided by GVI for 2012 - 2014 demonstrated high levels of non-compliance in bovine and ovine holdings inspected. 7 Percentage of holdings where non-compliance found during inspection: Bovine 2012 2013 2014 Ovine 22.5% 39.9% 37.7% 14.5% 27.8% 19.6% GVI confirmed they had not considered increasing the minimum rate of checks in subsequent years where a significant degree of non-compliance exists as required by Article 2(2) of Regulation (EC) No 1082/2003 and Article 2 of Regulation (EC) No 1505/2006.

GVI and ARMA are directing significant resources to implementation of official controls on identification and registration of animals and the verification of data quality in the database. Timeliness of data reporting is improving but despite efforts, weaknesses remain with data quality and actions taken don't appear to be significantly improving data quality.

recommendations.text: The Competent Authority should ensure that the database contains the geographic co- ordinates or equivalent geographic indication of the holding as required by Section D(1)(b) of the Annex to Regulation 21/2004 (sheep and goats) and Article 1(d) of Decision 2000/678/EEC (pigs). Recommendation based on conclusion No. 33 Associated findings No. 12 17

citations.text: The database does not contain the geographic co-ordinates or equivalent geographic indication of the holding as required by Section D(1)(b) of the Annex to Regulation 21/2004 ( sheep and goats) and Article 1(d) of Decision 2000/678/EEC (pigs).

The ARMA database does not include a geographical indication of the holding nor data on ASF restrictions. Holdings could include non-contiguous parcels of land. Thus, the process for tracing back animals is burdensome and time-consuming (e.g. to ascertain whether pigs come from holdings in restricted areas due to ASF, officials would need to cross check manually data from the land register and EU legislation listing restricted districts). 5.2 USER INTERFACES User interfaces provide the various user-groups with relevant information from the database. The needs of users vary depending on the user-group and the use-case-scenario. For the purposes of this audit, three use-case-scenarios were used to evaluate the services provided by the databases: disease outbreaks, eradication programmes and certification for intra-Union trade (as described in the objectives of this audit). Legal requirements: The suitability of user interfaces in achieving animal health traceability was evaluated using the following criteria: Access to relevant data and functionalities; Fitness for purpose; and Usability. 4 In their response to the draft report the Competent Authority noted that the template register for bovine animals, sheep, goats and swine is published in the Regulation of the Minister for Agriculture and Rural Development of 29 July 2005 concerning the register of bovine animals, swine, sheep and goats (Journal of Laws 2005/151, item 1268, as amended). 9 Access: Article 3 of Regulation (EC) 1760/2000 (for bovines) and of Regulation (EC) 21/2004 (for small ruminants) both require that: "The Member States and the Commission shall take the measures necessary to ensure access to these data for all parties concerned, including consumer organisations having an interest which are recognised by the Member State, provided that the data confidentiality and protection prescribed by national law are ensured." While a database is also required for porcine holdings, there is no specific requirement for providing access to all parties concerned. Fitness for purpose: there are two very basic legislative requirements on the functionalities of the databases ­ both of these are under point C (3) to Article 14 of Council Directive 64/432/EEC. It says: "The database must be able to supply the following particulars at any time: the identification number of all animals of the bovine species present on a holding, or in the case of groups of animals of the porcine species, the registration number of the holding of origin or herd of origin and the number of the health certificate where applicable; and a list of all changes of holding for each animal of the bovine species starting from the holding of birth, or the holding of importation in the case of animals imported from third countries; and for groups of pigs the registration number of the last holding or last herd and for imported animals from third countries the holding of importation." Usability: legislation does not prescribe criteria to evaluate usability. It is up to the Member States to decide the level of support and efficiency provided by the databases for each user group. Findings Stakeholders' access to data

audits.title: National Audit Systems

recommendations.text: To ensure that the internal audits are subject to independent scrutiny as required by Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation based on conclusion 14. Associated findings: 12 and 13.

citations.text: Neither GVI-CO nor GSI-DFNS have any arrangements in place to perform independent scrutiny of the audit process contrary to the requirement of Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 7

The competent authorities discussed some examples of external assessments that cover the audit functions within the context of administrative review and/or ISO assessments. However, the audit activities form a minor component of these assessments and focus rather on examining the administrative arrangements of the covered departments than the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Conclusions on independent scrutiny

The competent authorities have not put in place arrangements to ensure the independent scrutiny of the audit process which means that they cannot avail of external inputs for promoting continuous improvement of the audit process to ensure that the audit process is capable of producing objective results and meeting its obligations under Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5.2.3 Auditor competence Legal requirements and other audit criteria Articles 2(6) and 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 do not lay down specific requirements regarding the competence of auditors. Article 6 of the same Regulation requires that staff performing official controls "receive, for their area of competence, appropriate training enabling them to undertake their duties competently" and "keep up-to-date in their area of competence and receive regular additional training as necessary" Section 6.6 of the Annex to Decision 2006/677 provides guidance on auditor competence: "Auditor competence and selection criteria should be defined under the following headings: -- generic knowledge and skills -- audit principles, procedures and techniques; management/organisational skills, -- specific technical knowledge and skills, -- personal attributes, -- education, -- work experience, -- auditor training and experience. It is essential to put a mechanism in place to ensure auditors are consistent and their competencies are maintained. Competencies required by audit teams will vary depending on the area they are auditing within the control or supervision systems. As regards the technical knowledge and skills required by auditors, the training requirements for staff performing official controls (Chapter 1 of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 882/2004) should also be considered." 8 Findings

recommendations.text: To strengthen the risk based approach in the development of the audit programme in order to ensure that the internal audits meet the objectives of Recommendation based on conclusions: 30 and 31. Associated findings: 23, 24 and 26.

citations.text: Neither authority has documented procedures for the preparation of the audit programmes and neither could demonstrate that audit plans result from a risk prioritisation. GVI-CO develops a five year Veterinary Inspection audit programme on the basis of which the annual Veterinary Inspection Audit Programmes are prepared. The Chief Veterinary Inspector approves the audit programme. The VVI do their own selection of the PVI to be audited, based on the audit topics determined centrally by the GVI-CO. The areas to be audited include minced meat and meat preparations, poultry meat, dairy production, animal health, eggs and egg products, African swine fever related matters, supervision of approved establishments, controls on fishery products, feed production, veterinary medicine products and pharmaceuticals. The audit team 10 noted that the areas to be covered are not updated, the priorities remain unchanged over the years and the programme will continue until all are covered. The five-year programme was planned as follows: central level audits cover all VVIs and BVIs as regards the thematic areas indicated in the annual programmes and 20% of the PVIs are selected for a voivodship level audit.

The SSI internal audit programme covers a five-year cycle. The current programme covers the period 2015 ­ 2019. GSI-DFNS initiates and co-ordinates the preparation of the programme. GSI-DFNS requests each VSES to prepare their programmes which must be risk-based and: a) reflect all areas relevant for VSES activity, b) cover activity of BSES (if exists on the VSES territory), and c) contain priority topics determined by GSI-DFNS. GSI-DFNS collects individual audit plans proposed by all VSESs and compiles them in a collective multiannual internal audit programme. The Chief Sanitary Inspector approves the audit programme. Each VSES can update the plan, on an annual basis, if additional areas of interest and/or risks are identified. The audit team noted that for 2015 the local audit programmes proposed by VSES varied in their form. Some referred clearly to areas foreseen for audit while some others referred to legislation without being specific about the topics to be covered. GSI-DFNS representative stated that, in March 2016, GSI-DFNS distributed to VSES the NAS document on risk-based selection and requested VSESs to use the document as guide when preparing individual audit programmes. A GSI-DFNS representative stated that before 2016 VSES had prepared their plans with no guide, instruction or written procedure. In the majority of cases, auditors familiar with ISO standards, thus familiar with the risk-based concept, were involved in the preparation of the local audit programmes.

The audit team noted that neither of the audit systems covers the central level offices related to official controls in the scope of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Both competent authorities (CAs) stated that they are not authorised to implement audits at central level departments and that such activities are covered by internal audits in the 11 context of ISO certification and by occasional controls performed by the Supreme Chamber of Control (NIK) (see finding 13).

The CAs have developed and implemented processes for establishing annual and multiannual audit programmes. The processes are not adequately documented and had not considered all relevant areas to be audited in the last five years. The methodology applied for risk based prioritisation of audit planning is still under ongoing development with the aim of addressing this shortcoming.

The audit programmes do not cover the central level of the competent authorities' hierarchies and this means that the audit systems cannot ensure that the objectives of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 are fully met. 5.2.5 Implementation of the audit process Legal requirements and other audit criteria Article 2(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 states that "Audit" "means a systematic and independent examination to determine whether activities and related results comply with planned arrangements and whether these arrangements are implemented effectively and are suitable to achieve objectives." In section 5.1 of the Annex to Decision 2006/677/EC further guidance is provided to Member States on the `Systematic Approach', including: "A systematic approach should be applied to the planning, conduct, follow-up and management of audits. To that end, the audit process should: -- be supported by documented audit procedures and records to ensure consistency between auditors and to demonstrate that a systematic approach is followed, 12 -- include procedures for generating audit findings, including the identification of evidence of compliance and noncompliance, as appropriate, and for preparing, approving and distributing audit reports, -- include procedures to review audit conclusions, in order to identify system-wide strengths and weaknesses in the control system, disseminate best practice and ensure the monitoring of corrective and preventive actions, -- be monitored and reviewed to ensure the audit programme's objectives have been met and to identify opportunities for improvement." Section 6.1 of the Annex to Decision 2006/677 provides guidance on implementation of the Audit Process: "To comply with the requirements of Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, the audit system should cover the following three points set out in Article 2(6): (a) Verification of compliance with planned arrangements in order to provide assurances that official controls are carried out as intended and that any instructions or guidelines given to staff carrying out the controls are followed. This may largely be addressed by document review, but will also require on-site verification. The audit team will require good generic audit knowledge and skills to address this audit objective. (b) Verification of the effective implementation of planned arrangements. In order to assess effectiveness, that is the extent to which planned results are achieved, on-site operational implementation must be included. This should include an assessment of the quality and consistency of the controls and should involve on-site audit activities. The audit team will require the relevant technical expertise in order to address this audit objective. (c) The audit system should also seek to assess whether the planned arrangements are suitable to achieve the objectives of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, and in particular the single integrated multi-annual national control plan. This should include assessing the suitability of official controls, with regard, for example, to their frequency and the methods applied, having regard to the structure of the production chain(s) and to production practices and volume. The audit team should have substantial knowledge and understanding of system auditing, together with relevant technical input to address this audit objective. In order to determine whether the planned arrangements are suitable to achieve the objectives set out in (c) above, the following should be considered: Audit criteria should include strategic objectives stemming from Regulations (EC) No 178/2002 and (EC) No 882/2004 (including the single integrated multi-annual national control plan) and national legislation. The primary focus of audits should be the control arrangements relating to the critical points for control in the production chain(s). recommendations.text: To ensure that documentary checks for products of non-animal origin are carried out in line with Articles 5 and 9(3) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 884/2014 and to take adequate action when non-conformities are found, in compliance with Article 54 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation based on conclusions: 35 and 42 Associated findings: 33 and 39

citations.text: The audit team checked a total of 33 files related to import of products of non-animal origin and noted that the documentary checks had been performed correctly using all available information with the following four exceptions: 1 In its response to the draft report, the competent authority stated that during the checks, it informed the operators which, under current EU legislation, were supposed to pre-notify consignments at the required time. The operators informed the competent authority that in some cases they were not able to prepare the common entry documents (CED) in advance because the requisite documents whose numbers they needed to enter in box I.10 of the CED were not available. It was not until the operators had received the full set of documents that they were able to fill out the CED as required. 7 In one airport DPE one consignment of hazelnuts falling under provisions of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 884/2014 had been imported without the number of the health certificate issued by the non-EU country having been entered in box I.10 of part I of the CED. In one port DPE one consignment of liquid spices falling under provisions of Commission Implementing Decision 2011/884/EU had been imported although the analytical report the date of issue was not specified. In one port DPE several consignments of nuts falling under provisions of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 884/2014 had been imported without having reference to the health certificate number and lot number in the analytical report issued by the non-EU country official laboratory. In one port DPE several consignments of peanuts from Argentina had been correctly rejected by the DPE staff as the consignments had been presented for the controls with an expired health certificate. This is in line with the provisions of the Article 9(3) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 884/2014. However, following of an appeal of the importer, the VSES decided to sample these consignments and to accept new health certificates issued by the competent authority of the non-EU country of origin after the arrival of consignments at the DPE and finally to allow importation into EU. This is contrary to the provisions of Article 9(3) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 884/20142.

There are adequate mechanisms in place to ensure that consignments are presented for official controls and with few exceptions (in DPEs), the implementation of documentary checks was carried out correctly in the BIPs and DPEs visited, being performed using all available information.

However, in some cases of imported food of non-animal origin the competent authority did not take the appropriate actions, which is contrary to the requirements of Article 54 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 (see finding 33).

On the whole, actions taken when non-compliant goods are detected during documentary check, are appropriate and, with few exceptions, are in line with Union rules. 5.4 THE USE OF TRADE CONTROL AND EXPERT SYSTEM Legal requirements Article 3(2) of Commission Decision 2004/292/EC 9 Findings

audits.title: Animal health - rabies

recommendations.text: Ensure that in all relevant regions, the official controls and verifications on the vaccine distribution are sufficient to verify that vaccine distribution is carried out as described in the approved rabies eradication programme, inter alia that bait location data are always checked against actual flight lines. Point (6)(a) and (6)(c)(i) of the Annex to Commission Decision 2008/341/EC. Recommendation based on conclusion 31. Associated finding 27.

citations.text: Electronic files containing actual flight routes and bait drop locations were received and verified by official from the Regional Veterinary Inspectorates within 24 hours of the flight. Not all checks were carried out in accordance with the instructions from the CCA and the Commission services. In one region, a flight expert had been employed for this task and he carried out these controls in the airfield directly after each flight. This expert swiftly demonstrated how flight-lines and bait drops were checked and compared, using data for the most recent flights. In the second region, at the end of each distribution day the operators prepared a file with all data for the official veterinarian who delivered the data to the Regional Veterinary Inspectorate. In this region, the inspector was notified when the files were uploaded into the system and checked the data within 24 hours of the flights. However, when demonstrating how this was done it was evident that only the bait drop locations and visual densities were checked and these were compared to printouts of the planned routes, not to actual flight data. However, this was not a technical problem since the flight lines and bait drop locations could be superimposed and visualised using the software in the regional office, when requested by the audit team. Once printouts of the actual flights were obtained there were no indications that the bait drop locations deviated from the flight lines and the flight lines bore all signs of being actual recordings. The CCA was not aware of the practice in the second region as this had not been evident in the reports submitted from this region to the CCA after each ORV campaign.

Despite clear instructions from the central competent authority one of the regions subject to intensified ORV campaigns did not carry out sufficient daily controls comparing actual flight lines to recorded bait drop locations. This indicates that the central competent authority may have failed to explain the importance of these checks, and has not verified that the checks are carried out as instructed. 5.3 MONITORING, AWARENESS AND SURVEILLANCE The principles and techniques for detection of rabies and monitoring the effectiveness of rabies vaccination in foxes are described in the overview report "Rabies eradication in the EU" (DG(SANTE)/2016-8980). Briefly, vaccine baits contain tetracycline as a marker substance. When a fox tastes the vaccine bait, the tetracycline leaves a permanent trace in teeth and bone. Hunted foxes are tested for tetracycline to check if the vaccine bait distribution has reached the target population. In order to become vaccinated against rabies (develop protective antibodies), the fox needs to bite into the vaccine capsule in the bait and swallow the vaccine. If many foxes have been in contact with baits (i.e. show traces of tetracycline) but have no antibodies this could indicate a problem with the quality of the vaccine. The age of each fox is also determined to verify the effectiveness of the most recent vaccination campaign. Legal requirements Point (6)(c)(i) of the Annex to Commission Decision 2008/341/EC. Findings 5.3.1 Monitoring of bait uptake and population immunity

recommendations.text: To ensure that the expert group provides assistance in all areas covered by the sub-indents of Article 15.2(a) of Directive 2002/60/EC and in particular, in the verification of effectiveness of all control measures, as required by the last subinde based on conclusion No. 112. Associated finding No. 107.

citations.text: In general, the ASF expert group exercises the functions set out by the ASF control Directive. In particular, the expert groups did assist the competent authorities in defining infected areas as required by the EU legislation and in defining additional control measures to combat ASF disease. The members of expert groups receive regular updates on the evolvement of ASF epidemiological situation. However, the ASF group had not yet received the results of some official controls (e.g. on compliance with biosecurity measures for hunting and on pig holdings) in a manner that would allow them to fully evaluate the effectiveness of those additional measures, although this is required by Article 15(2)(a) fourth indent of Directive 2002/60/EC.

The system of internal audits, supervision and analysis contributes to the harmonisation of official checks and to the detection of weaknesses in the implementation of disease control measures. There is a limited quantitative analysis of the results of official controls by both central competent authority and ASF expert group which limits the capacity to ascertain the effectiveness of the implemented activities. This analysis at central level is particularly weak in assessing the effectiveness of biosecurity measures implemented by hunters and, to a lesser extent, by pig holdings. This hinders the central authority's ability to identify potential gaps and to fine-tune its measures. 5.7 FOLLOW-UP OF PREVIOUS AUDITS

recommendations.text: To ensure the standards defined in Articles 3, 4 and 8 of Commission Implementing Decision 2014/709/EU for sampling procedures are applied when the relevant derogation is used for movements of live animals. Recommendation based on conclusion No. 53. Associated finding No. 13.

citations.text: The movement documents reviewed by the audit team demonstrated compliance with movement restrictions. However, the official veterinarian in one district visited who was in charge of health certification in this district did not apply the criteria for selection of pigs to be sampled as foreseen in the plan for eradication of ASF (Article 3 (2) of Decision 2014/709/EU). When pigs were moving from the infected area, the veterinarian performed pre-movement ASF testing, selecting pigs randomly instead of considering whether there had been a recent occurrence of sick animals. This is the same finding noted in the 2014 Commission report (DG(SANCO) 2014-7294).

The strengthened controls on the movements of live pigs reduce the risk of disease spread between holdings. Pre-movement testing is inadequately targeted, and thus provides less guarantees than it could in reducing the spread of diseases due to the movement of pigs from the infected area. 5.2 EARLY DETECTION AND SURVEILLANCE Legal requirements Articles 4, 14, 15, and 18 of Directive 2002/60/EC, Commission Decision 2003/422/EC; articles 4 to 10 and 12 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004; the approved national programme (based on ASF strategy for Eastern Part of the EU (SANTE/7113/2015-Rev 4) 5.2.1 Surveillance in wild boar

citations.text: Commission audit reports (DG(SANCO) 2014-7294 and DG(SANTE) 2016-8776 describe the identification and registration system for pigs in Poland, highlighting the 4 following: there were two pig registers/databases in the country, with different systems for entry and control of information and managed by different authorities ­ a pig database required by EU legislation and maintained by Agency for Restructuring and Modernising Agriculture (ARMA) and the registers required by national legislation kept by individual District Veterinary Offices (DVOs). Both of them had limitations in their use as a disease management tool. Since then this situation has not changed as was evidenced during this audit (for more see paragraphs 14, 40 and 102). DVOs still use their own database for the planning of inspections on farms, as they consider data in the ARMA database outdated.

The Polish authorities had already scheduled the development of the new system called e-IRZ to address the limitation of the ARMA database and a tender for this system has been prepared. The new system should include functionalities to fulfil the new requirements for identification and registration introduced in 2016, enhance support to the veterinary services, improve the efficiency of electronic data exchange between the authorities involved, and provide for implementation of two-way communication with the livestock owners. The timeframe to have e-IRZ ready is a year after the tender is awarded.
Farms still keep two holding registers - required by the legislation, which creates an additional burden for pig keepers, and leads to a double registration system. Movement restrictions

The existence of two pig databases complicates the proper planning and implementation of official controls. The amendment of functionalities of the ARMA database should address the majority of the problems, but it will take more than one year to implement.

recommendations.text: To ensure that practical arrangements required by Commission implementing Decision (EC) No 2014/709 have been put in place for the collection and transport of ABPs from Part III in order to reduce the risk of the spread of disease through potentially contaminated products. Recommendation based on conclusion No. 93. Associated finding No. 92.

citations.text: Article 7 of the Decision 2014/709/EU (related to the derogation from the prohibition on the dispatch of consignments of animal by-products from porcine animals from the areas listed in Parts III and IV of the Annex) has been transposed in the national legislation. One DVO visited and in charge of some areas listed in Part III of the Decision No 2014/709/EU acknowledged that the measures and controls included in Article 7 have not been implemented (e.g. registration of vehicles used for the transport of animal by- products, satellite navigation system on those trucks, etc). At the final meeting the central competent authority presented new instructions for both DVOs and business operators aimed at ensuring the adequate implementation of these requirements. Conclusions on ABPs

The absence of practical arrangements for the collection and transport of animal by- products from Part III pose a risk for the spread of the disease through potentially contaminated products. 5.5 TRACEABILITY OF MEAT AND MEAT PRODUCTS Legal requirements Commission implementing Decision 2014/709/EU; Directive 2002/99/EC; Annex II, section III of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004; Articles 4(6) and 5 Regulation (EC) No 854/2004. 5.5.1 Traceability of wild boar meat

recommendations.text: To ensure that all measures under the ASF approved programme, including the feed ban are subjected to official controls in order to ensure their effective implementation. Approved programme for ASF. Recommendation based on conclusion No. 50. Associated finding No. 31.

citations.text: The Polish hunting association and State Forest informed their members on the decision taken at the ASF expert group to ban the feeding of wild boar in the WAMTA and requested them to keep appropriate records on baiting, for future inspections carried out by the DVO. To date, there have been no checks to verify the implementation of the ban which is not in line with the ASF approved programme.

The authorities successfully implemented measures regarding management and handling of wild boar in ASF restricted areas (Parts I, II and III). The absence of checks on the implementation of the feed ban for wild boars constitutes a weak point in ensuring correct management. The decrease in wild boar density together with the biosecurity measures applied contributed to the slowing down of the advance of the disease in this region. 11

recommendations.text: To ensure that all feral pigs found dead, killed on the road, or shot in restricted areas, are serologically tested for ASF, as stated in ASF approved programme. SANTE/7113/2015-Rev 4 ­ ASF Strategy for Eastern Part of the EU. Recommendation based on conclusion No. 78. Associated finding No. 65. 23

citations.text: Antibodies have been tested only in 6,876 wild boars which represent 68.80% of hunting bags which is not line with the national ASF eradication programme and ASF Strategy for Eastern Part of the EU (SANTE/7113/2015-Rev 4) that require testing of all shot wild boars in ASF restricted areas for antibodies against ASF virus. The partial testing hinders from drawing conclusion on the apparent increase of seropositivity rate between 2015 and 2016. The central CA is aware of this last weakness and as remedial action updated (at the end of 2016) procedures for sampling of wild boar. 5.2.2 Surveillance in pig holdings

The effective and well implemented passive surveillance in wild boar provides assurances that new cases of ASF will be detected at an early stage. The competent authority has access to updated data on the epidemiological situation and geographical spread of the infection. The system benefits from good cooperation between hunters and competent authorities and the active role of the ASF expert group. However, the insufficient serological tests performed reduce the amount of epidemiological information available to follow the evolution of the disease in the region.

recommendations.text: To ensure that following a ring rot outbreak, the measures in place will be enforced for eradicating Clavibacter michiganensis ssp. sepedonicus and prevent re-occurrence of ring rot contamination. In particular: a. that official or officially supervised laboratory testing will be carried out in order to confirm or refute the suspected occurrence, in line with Article 4.1 of Directive 93/85/EEC; b. that demarcated areas and the extent of contamination and probable contamination will be adequately designated in line with Article 5.1b of Directive 93/85/EEC; c. that tubers designated to be contaminated will be destroyed or otherwise disposed of, provided that it is established that there is no identifiable risk of the organism surviving or spreading in line with Article 7.1 and Annex IV.1 of Directive 93/85/EEC; d. that within the demarcated zone the cleaning and disinfection measures shall be implemented immediately following the designated contamination in line with Annex IV. 4.2 of Directive 93/85/EEC; e. that the re-introduction of potato crop in a place of production affected by ring rot will be carried out in line with Annex IV. 4.1 of Directive 93/85/EEC. Recommendation based on Conclusion 53, Associated findings 44 and 45

citations.text: However, the audit team also noted that the action taken by VIPHSI to enforce and prevent re-occurrence of ring rot is often not effective and in particular: In a place of production following a ring rot finding, no further testing of other potato lots to fully determine their plant health status and the extent of contamination was carried out. Other potato lots having clonal links with contaminated material were only assumed being probably contaminated without testing; In the same place of production this resulted in pronouncing two fields, the contaminated and a neighbouring one operated by the same machinery, as contaminated whilst all other fields of the same place of production were declared probably contaminated, technically allowing for continuing potato cropping already during the next growing period.

Compliance with movement prohibition, cropping restrictions imposed for the next growing period and safe handling / disposal of contaminated and probably contaminated material is not effectively monitored even for registered potato producers. The audit team noted that: Based on commitments undertaken by the farmers, a usual practice for contaminated or probably contaminated material is storage for long periods in the farm for personal consumption or animal feed; The fate of this material is not adequately followed up by the regional competent authorities; it usually results in potatoes remaining in the place of production and in decontamination measures applied too late in the season; In one case certified or tested seed was not used during the next growing period for ware potato production, although this constituted a clear legal requirement set by VIPHSI. No further effective action was taken to enforce and prevent re- occurrence of ring rot in this place of production. 17 Ralstonia solanacearum in places of production of Rosa

recommendations.text: To ensure that the minimum number of isolates is subject to antimicrobial susceptibility testing as required by point 2.3.2 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU. In particular, that all available Salmonella isolates are subject to antimicrobial susceptibility testing, when the minimum required number of isolates is not achieved. Recommendation based on conclusion No 23. Associated findings No 14, 16 and 18.

citations.text: With regard to the fulfilment of the requirements for the minimum number of samples and isolates and caecal samples to be tested and reported for the mandatory categories, the situation was as follows: Salmonella: The minimum 170 isolates were achieved and exceeded only in 2016 for those isolates derived from samples taken at laying hen farms under the SNCP. 4 According to personnel from the NRL, there are different reasons to explain why the number of isolates was not reached in the other 2 years for either of the 2 groups of required Salmonella isolates (see point 15). E. coli: For 2014, 2015 and 2016, the minimum isolates were achieved and for the relevant combination of bacterial species and type of samples. C. jejuni: The minimum 170 isolates were achieved for broilers and turkeys in 2014 and 2016. ESBL-, or AmpC- or carbapenemases- producing E. coli: In 2015, 299 caecal samples at slaughterhouses were collected from pigs, as well as from pork and beef meat from retail outlets. In 2016, the required 300 caecal samples were achieved for broiler and turkey slaughterhouses as well as from broiler meat from retail outlets. 5.2.1.2.2 Representativeness of sampling Salmonella isolates from samples collected at poultry primary production

Contrary to the requirements of point 2.3.2 of part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU, less than 170 of the isolates from the SNCP were subject to AST in 2014 and, except for laying hens, in 2016. According to data provided by the Veterinary Inspectorate, during these 2 years a number of available isolates for each category of animals (broilers, turkeys and laying hens) were not reported. This is because: The NRL does not know the total number of available isolates. Although in a given year the Veterinary Inspectorate gathers information on the total number of isolates obtained in the regional veterinary laboratories participating in the SNCP, this information is not complied as such and sent to the NRL. The system used by farmers to identify a flock is not considered to be fully reliable. As a consequence and to avoid sampling more than once from the same flock, it has been decided that if in doubt, only one isolate from the whole farm is subjected to AST. However, the audit team saw examples from turkey caecal samples where several isolates were obtained from the same epidemiological units, subject to AST and reported (see point 20). Some of the isolates received were lacking the necessary epidemiological information required for reporting to EFSA. Salmonella isolates from carcass samples collected at slaughter

According to data provided by the Veterinary Inspectorate, the number of isolates available from the samples taken was much higher than the actual number of isolates subject to AST and reported. The reasons for not subjecting to AST and reporting the remaining isolates were as follows: It was difficult to ascertain the flock or herd of origin (as applicable) because this information was not clearly included in the form that accompanied the samples to regional veterinary laboratories. In the case of samples taken from broiler and turkey carcasses, and due to the sampling methodology, not all isolates obtained could be used from one positive sample to Salmonella. This is because they could easily come from birds from the same epidemiological unit (flock). In accordance with national rules applicable to the financing of laboratory testing, only the isolates obtained in regional veterinary laboratories can be subject to AST. Recommendation based on conclusion No 23 Associated findings No 11, 20, 21 and 22. 11

citations.text: The Veterinary Inspectorate informed the audit team that these instructions were signed and distributed around March or April, only after the Grant Decision (which details the EU funds that would become available for the co-financing of the plan) is published. As a consequence, both the sampling at slaughterhouses and at retail outlets did not start before April in any of the years that the plan has been running (see points 20 and 21). This does not comply with the requirements set out in Part A, point 2.3 of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU, which requires, among other things, that samples are evenly distributed over each month of the year.

In contrast to the requirements laid down in point 2.3 of Decision 2013/652/EU, the collection of samples at the slaughterhouses was not representative due to the following: The caecal samples gathered were not evenly distributed over each month of the year. Aside from the late start, (see point 10) the audit team noted that in the slaughterhouses visited, the total number of allocated samples were taken in 2 months (2014) and in 4 months (2016) in 1 of them, and in 6 months in the other 2 6 (2016). Personnel from the Veterinary Inspectorate declared that this early finish was mainly due to the total number of samples needed in Poland being achieved before December. Unlike the selection of slaughtering batches to be sampled, a lack of randomisation in the collection of samples was noted. The work instructions drafted by the CVO for the years 2014-2017 stated that samples should preferably be taken on Mondays, Tuesdays or Wednesdays. This is to allow the laboratories to complete their processing within the 5 working days of the week. In the slaughterhouses visited, samples were mainly taken on Mondays and Tuesdays and, in some cases, only on one of these 2 days. Officials from each slaughterhouse visited declared that they organised their sampling to avoid repeating epidemiological units. However, the audit team noted that in two of the slaughterhouses visited this repeated sampling had occurred. This was particularly the case in the turkey slaughterhouse, where the high number of samples to be taken each month in the only day allocated for that (due to the vehicle available to transport the samples to the laboratory being available only once per month) made it very difficult for the inspector not to sample repeated epidemiological units 2. Isolates from meat samples collected at retail

For the same reasons stated in point 10, retail samples were not taken over the entire year, which does not comply with point 2.3 of Decision 2013/652/EU. In addition, and contrary to what is recommended in EFSA technical specifications 3, in each sampling year, samples were not allocated proportionally to the population of the relevant administrative divisions. Instead, each of these was allocated the exact same number of samples.

The audit team noted from the documentation seen that the right type of meat and from the right type of outlets was collected. However, the Sanitary Inspectorate decided that only unpacked meat could be sampled. As a result, only butcher shops (including the butchery department in the supermarkets) selling unpacked fresh meat were sampled, which created problems to identify the batch of the meat. The audit team noted that in almost half of the sampling forms checked, the batch identification had not been included. This was not detected in the NRL, which accepted all the samples sent from the region visited. In the examples seen, sampling was carried out mostly on Tuesdays, as Mondays were systematically excluded to avoid problems with the expiry date of the meat collected. recommendations.text: To ensure that the monitoring analyses carried out at laboratory level are performed in line with points 3, 4 and 5 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU, in order to comply with Article 4 of the said Decisio based on conclusion No 32. Associated finding No 31.

citations.text: The different laboratory procedures were available on-the-spot and largely followed the relevant international standards. The audit team noted however a number of deviations from these standards (ISO 20776-1:2006, Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute or the EURL for AMR) which, in the absence of validation, is contrary to the requirements of point 4 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU. These concerned the following issues: The use of reference strains and colony counts on inoculum suspensions for MIC determination for E. coli were performed with a different frequency to that indicated in the relevant standard. This alternative frequency was not validated. Incubation time and temperatures combinations differed from the applicable standards for Campylobacter MIC determination. This alterative arrangement has not been validated. The procedures for the media validation for the selective growth of ESBL-, or AmpC producing E. coli were not fully in line with the EURL protocol as required. Although the reference strains were regularly used to validate the media after its preparation, the self-life validation was not documented. The procedures for the detection of presumptive E. coli producing ESBL and AmpC enzymes were not fully in line with the EURL protocol. The sub- cultivation step in MacConkey agar with cefotaxime was not systematically performed. The audit team noted that a number of unusual combinations of MIC (atypical phenotypes) reoccurred, often in different years 4. These combinations were not detected by the NRL and therefore no action was taken to ensure that the results obtained did not reflect a deviation from the relevant standard operating procedures. Conclusions on official laboratories

The NRL performs largely satisfactorily. However, the reliability of the results reported to EFSA is affected by the use of some non-validated laboratory practices that are not aligned to the relevant international standards, and by the overlooking of atypical phenotypes. 4 Examples of the combinations found are as follows: a) resistance to ciprofloxacin and susceptibility to nalidixic acid for Campylobacter in 2014 and 2016, b) resistance to erythromycin in Campylobacter in 2014 and 2016, c) resistance to colistin in Salmonella and/or E. coli in 2014, 2015 and 2016, d) resistance to azithromycin in 2015 and 2016 and e) resistance to tigecycline in E. coli 2016. 9 5.3 ASSESSMENT AND REPORTING OF AMR Requirements Article 9 and Annex IV of Directive 2003/99/EC and Article 5 and the Annex of Decision 2013/652/EU. recommendations.text: To ensure that reporting complies with the specifications established by the European Food Safety Association's reporting manual and data dictionary, as set out in point 2 of Part B of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU. Recommendation based on conclusion No 35. Associated finding No 34.

citations.text: Although most of the information reported to EFSA generally follows the requirements set out in the reporting manual and data dictionary, the audit team identified a number of frequently reoccurring gaps regarding reporting practices, which is not in line with point 2, Part B of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU: Atypical phenotypes, as described in EFSA's business rules, are not routinely retested before reporting them to ensure that the MIC values obtained are correct. Salmonella isolates obtained in poultry slaughterhouses, other than those from neck skin samples, are reported under the programme code AMR MON. Most of the information required by the text forms was provided in 2015 and 2016. However, the descriptions under a) stratification procedures per animal population and food category, b) randomisation procedures per animal population and food category and c) description of sampling designs sent in 2015 and 2016 did not fulfil the relevant requirements. Although measures were in place to exclude repeated epidemiological units from being subject to AST, isolates obtained from the same epidemiological units were eventually reported. HACCP and own controls was wrongly used as a code to describe the sampler in Salmonella isolates from the SNCP in 2014 and 2016. Conclusions on assessment and reporting of AMR

Although the basic guidelines described in EFSA's reporting manual and data dictionary are followed when reporting data, a number of reoccurring mistakes hampers the ability of the competent authority to provide harmonised and comparable data on AMR. 6 GOOD PRACTICES AND DEVELOPING AREAS Findings
