recommendations.text: The CA should indicate: what were the root causes for the visited laboratory to be unable to provide timely Salmonella serotyping results at the end of 2016; what changes will be made to the system in place to ensure that laboratories approved for testing within the Salmonella national control programmes can provide timely testing results (providing legal support for the control measures required by Art. 5, 3.(c) of Regulation (EC) No 2160/2003) even in crisis periods.

Recommendation based on conclusion: 55. Associated finding: 33. The CA should ensure that, in breeding hen flocks the sampling protocol used in confirmatory sampling, and prior to lifting of trade restrictions, is fully in line with point 2.2.2.2 (b) of Annex to Regulation (EU) No 200/2010 for non-confirmed source of infectio based on conclusion: 56. Associated findings: 37 and 38.

citations.text: During the 2016 outbreak this laboratory needed additional days (up to 3 weeks) from the detection of Salmonella to provide the results on serotyping. This was caused by different factors including the very high number of additional samples to be serotyped at this crisis period and to exhausting the stock of reagents. In both laying hen holdings visited affected by the 2016 outbreak and with samples tested at this laboratory, the measures restricting marketing of eggs from these holdings as class A eggs (for direct human consumption) had been implemented at the time of Salmonella detection (without waiting for serotyping) therefore preventing additional risk for consumers. 5.2.3 SNCP for breeding flocks of Gallus gallus Legal requirements Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 2160/2003. Article 1 of Regulation (EC) No 200/2010. Findings

The fact that during the 2016 Salmonella outbreak some serotyping test results were issued with delays of up to 3 weeks, indicates that the system in place did not satisfactorily deal with high demand on its capacities in crisis times, in particular to assure timely testing. The measures implemented still prevented additional risk to consumers, nevertheless, without the serotyping result, the competent authorities could have faced legal difficulties in imposing the necessary marketing restrictions.

audits.title: Animal welfare Transport

recommendations.text: To ensure that documented procedures are sufficiently clear so that all DVOs are consistent in their controls, as required by Article 4(4) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, in assessing travelling and resting times in proposed journey plans until the final place of destination in the non-EU country, as required by Article 14(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Recommendation based on conclusions 15, 22 and 24. Associated finding: 6 and 19.

citations.text: Some points in the animal welfare instructions are unclear, such as: The instruction to check that journeys are planned until "final place of destination". Two of the districts visited were correctly evaluating journey plans until the final place of destination in the non-EU country. In the other district visited journey plans to non-EU countries did not include the non-EU leg of the journey and the exit point but were still incorrectly stamped as satisfactory by that district; When supervising transporters, the instructions indicate "compare SNS data with completed journey logs". This is a verification of coherence between different registers which is useful but does not address the main intent of verifying if SNS data and completed journey logs show that effective journey times were realistic and complied with EU requirements, as required by Article 15(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005.

Poland has detailed documented procedures for official controls on animal welfare at all stages of transport and on animal health certification, even though with a few shortcomings. Some instructions for those procedures are also not sufficiently clear and thus differently understood by the different districts resulting in a non-harmonised approach in carrying out official controls.

Regarding the organiser's plans to rest the animals during the journey and provide them with feed and water (Article 14 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005): 7 Journey plans seen by the audit team generally used the same regular routes for specific destinations. This facilitates the evaluation of the journey plans considering, in particular, that the OV only receives such plans at the moment of loading, contrary to Point 3(b)(ii) of Annex II of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005; The GVI indicated that their interpretation since entry into force of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 is that the journey plan has to be until the final place of destination in the non-EU country, as confirmed in 2015 in a judgement by the European Court of Justice1. This was however not implemented at one of the DVOs visited, as the audit team noted that stamped journey plans for exports to a non-EU country did not include the exit point from the EU and the non-EU leg of the journey until final destination; Planned travelling times in the other two districts were in compliance with EU requirements.

Although the central competent authority indicated that the journey plan must be until the final place of destination in the non-EU country and that this has been always their interpretation, this was not clear to all DVOs and therefore there is a risk that travelling times are sometimes exceeded once past the EU border.

There is a system in place to assess planned and actual resting and travelling times before and after the journey. Assurances given by this system are nevertheless weakened by the failure to ensure that all journey plans cover the full journey until the final place of destination in the non-EU country and by the lack of evidence that the prescribed retrospective checks have been carried out.

recommendations.text: To ensure that, as required by Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, documented procedures: Correctly reflect the requirement of Article 15(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 that the competent authority shall verify that the journey complies with this Regulation and in particular that travel times and rest periods have complied with the limits set out in Chapter V of Annex I; Include instructions so that organisers submit properly completed signed copies of Section 1 of the journey log at least two working days before the intended date of departure of the consignment, as required by Point 3(b)(ii) of Annex II of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005; Include instructions to verify, when journey plans include the use of livestock vessels, that the selected livestock vessel is approved, as required by Article 7(2) of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Recommendation based on conclusions 15, 23 and 24. Associated finding: 5, 6 and 18.

citations.text: A few shortcomings in the animal welfare instructions were noted: The instructions do not require journey plans to be submitted to the districts at least within two working days before the intended date of departure. This is required by Point 3(b)(ii) of Annex II of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 (see paragraph 18); When carrying out controls during transport the instructions do not require the OV to check the suitability of drinking devices for the categories of animals being transported. This is nevertheless included in the relevant checklist annexed to the guidelines; When a long journey includes the use of livestock vessels the guidelines do not instruct the OVs to request a copy of the vessel's approval certificate to verify that it is approved to carry live animals, contrary to the requirement of Article 14(1)(a)(i) of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. There is therefore the risk that the journey of live animals transported through a port would not operate smoothly due to poor planning and lengthen the journey contrary to the requirements of Article 3(a) of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005.

Some points in the animal welfare instructions are unclear, such as: The instruction to check that journeys are planned until "final place of destination". Two of the districts visited were correctly evaluating journey plans until the final place of destination in the non-EU country. In the other district visited journey plans to non-EU countries did not include the non-EU leg of the journey and the exit point but were still incorrectly stamped as satisfactory by that district; When supervising transporters, the instructions indicate "compare SNS data with completed journey logs". This is a verification of coherence between different registers which is useful but does not address the main intent of verifying if SNS data and completed journey logs show that effective journey times were realistic and complied with EU requirements, as required by Article 15(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005.

Poland has detailed documented procedures for official controls on animal welfare at all stages of transport and on animal health certification, even though with a few shortcomings. Some instructions for those procedures are also not sufficiently clear and thus differently understood by the different districts resulting in a non-harmonised approach in carrying out official controls.

Organisers notify the DVO well in advance of the intention to transport animals over long distances. This notification: Indicates the date and place of departure, the place of destination, the number of animals to be transported, the transporter and the vehicle number plate; Does not include a properly completed signed copy of Section 1 of the journey log, contrary to the requirements of Point 3(b)(ii) of Annex II of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. The OVs therefore cannot check in advance if the planned journey is realistic and complies with the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005, in particular with travelling and resting times.

Under the current system of official controls, the journey plan can only be evaluated at the moment of loading. This is not in line with EU requirements and places the OV under unnecessary pressure as this is the only stage at which all the necessary welfare checks are carried out prior to departure.

There is a system in place to assess planned and actual resting and travelling times before and after the journey. Assurances given by this system are nevertheless weakened by the failure to ensure that all journey plans cover the full journey until the final place of destination in the non-EU country and by the lack of evidence that the prescribed retrospective checks have been carried out.

recommendations.text: To ensure that certificates of approval of vehicles for long distance journeys distinguish between adult and unweaned animals to be transported, as required by Chapter IV Annex III of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Recommendation based on conclusion 17. Associated finding: 12.

citations.text: Certificates of approval of vehicles for long journeys do not distinguish between adult and unweaned animals, contrary to Chapter IV Annex III of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. This implies that unweaned animals may be transported on vehicles that are inadequate for this category of animals with the biggest risk being the inability to access liquids due to unsuitable drinking devices (Point 2.2 of Chapter VI, Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005).

Certificates of approval of vehicles for long distance journeys do not distinguish between adult and unweaned animals. As a result unweaned animals may not have access to liquid and be if necessary fed during long distance journeys. This shortcoming may negatively impact journeys starting from another Member State, if in that Member State the suitability of the vehicles is not also systematically verified at the moment of loading. 5.3 RESTING Legal requirements Articles 14, 15, 19, 25 and 26 and Chapter V, Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Articles 1 and 2 of Commission Decision 2013/188/EU. Findings

recommendations.text: To ensure that the regional level correctly checks the districts' compliance with the required minimum percentage of retrospective checks, ensuring the efficient and effective coordination required by Article 4(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, so that data collected for the analysis required by Article 2(1)(e) of Commission Decision 2013/188/EU is accurate and reliable. Recommendation based on conclusion 25. Associated finding: 20 and 21.

citations.text: Regarding retrospective checks to verify the travelling and resting times to provide water, feed and rest to the animals (Articles 15(1) and 15(4) of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005): According to the animal welfare instructions each DVO has to carry out retrospective checks on 20% of journeys departing from and arriving at the district. Returned journey logs were available for all exports examined by the audit team. The audit team saw evidence of retrospective checks carried out on those journeys for which notifications of non-compliances had been received. However, there was no evidence of retrospective checks done on returned journey logs for which there was no notification of non-compliance. One DVO visited did not require the planning to include the final place of destination when it was a non-EU country. Here, the audit team detected that several returned journey logs for unweaned calves going to a non-EU country showed that during the non-EU leg the journeys had exceeded the maximum times set out in Chapter V Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005.

The regional CAs collect summary reports from their DVOs on the number of checks carried out during transport: These summary reports are collated and forwarded to the GVI to analyse the main non-compliances, as required by Decision 2013/188/EU; One of the DVOs visited reported having done retrospective checks on 100% of consignments in 2016 and 2017; The other two DVOs visited reported that they had not carried out retrospective checks in 2016 and 2017. The corresponding supervising regional CAs had not 1 Judgement of the European Court of Justice (Fifth Chamber) of 23 April 2015 ­ Case C424/13. 8 detected that the DVOs had not respected the 20% minimum. One of the regional CAs investigated this during audit and confirmed that retrospective checks had not been carried out by the DVO in 2016 whereas 10 checks had been carried out in 2017. This lack of detection can undermine the validity of the data collected by the GVI. Conclusions on resting

The regions' ineffective verification of the reports submitted on the number of checks during transport can undermine the validity of the data collected and negatively affect the analysis of data that the GVI is required to perform. 5.4 UNEXPECTED DELAYS AT THE BORDER Legal requirements Article 11 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Articles 3, 4, and 5 of Directive 96/93/EC. Findings

recommendations.text: To ensure that organisers provide the certifying officer with correct information on the ages of animals to be transported in order to reduce the risk that animals are detained in possibly inadequate conditions and/or for extended periods at a border crossing to the detriment of their welfare, as required by Articles 3(a) and 5(3)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Recommendation based on conclusion 34. Associated finding: 29.

citations.text: Calves were being transported from one of the districts visited to a non-EU country (other than Turkey). According to the documented dates of birth calves younger than ten days of age (as young as four days) were being transported for journeys longer than 100km. This is contrary to point 2(e) of Chapter I of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 1/2005: The OV explained that he always checks if the navel is completely healed, as envisaged by 2(d) of Chapter I of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 and that this has always been the case. The OV also explained that these animals were actually older than ten days. That being the case, the animals were transported with documentation holding incorrect age information thus increasing the likelihood of delays during the journey, namely at the EU borders. The CA indicated that most probably the farmers introduced wrong dates of birth when registering the animals and that they had not been notified of any delays at the EU's borders because of this issue. The OV did not record that he had carried out the above mentioned verification of the navel as one of the means of confirming the fitness (as required in Annex I, Chapter I, (1) of Regulation (EC) no 1/2005) and the age of the animals, prior to issuing the export health certificate.

Assurances given by official controls when issuing animal health certificates for exports were satisfactory. However, if the organisers provide incorrect accompanying age documentation and that documentation is forwarded without any official remark there is the risk of animals being detained in a stationary truck at the EU borders.

recommendations.text: To ensure that transporters carrying out live animal exports have contingency plans to meet the animals' needs for bedding, feed and water in the eventuality of unexpected long delays at the borders where this risk is high as required by Article 3(a) and 11(1)(b)(iv) of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Recommendation based on conclusion 36. Associated finding: 33.

citations.text: Concerning contingency plans (Article 11(1)(b)(iv) of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005): The animal welfare instructions concerning the authorisation of Polish transporters list details that must be included in contingency plans. These include: names and phone numbers of persons responsible for taking decisions, description of strategies for the change of means of transport, procedures to be followed in the event of unexpected stops and in case assistance is needed to care for the animals. The contingency plan of the transporter visited was of good quality and included procedures to follow, both for the driver and for the person responsible at the transporter's headquarters. Contingency plans however do not include information on how to deal with unexpected long delays at EU borders where there is a high risk of unexpected delays (e.g. Turkey), in particular on how to obtain and provide bedding, feed and water to see to the animals' needs at this location. Arrangements to meet the animals' needs in the case of unexpected long delays at the border are therefore not in place contrary to Article 3(a) of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. 11 Conclusions on unexpected delays at the border

Transporter's contingency plans, as required by Regulation (EC) No 1/2005, do not include measures to provide bedding, feed and water to the animals in the eventuality of unexpected long delays at those EU borders where this risk is high, such as Turkey. There are therefore inadequate assurances that the needs of animals can be met if blocked at the border on board Polish vehicles and that these animals are not caused unnecessary suffering. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The system in place has produced good results with live animal exports to non-EU countries operating with a tiny number of non-compliances. However, Poland did no exports to Turkey which is the EU land border with more frequent live animal transport delays. The national policy to carry out inspections of 100% of consignments at the moment of loading enables the competent authority to verify a much wider number of requirements in addition to the animals' fitness for transport. The official verification, at the moment of loading, on the adequacy of the vehicles, bedding, handling, space allowances and ventilation contribute to prevent causing unnecessary pain, suffering or injury to animals during long distance transport by road. This is considered a good practice. Nevertheless, the shortcomings detected in the system of official controls (with regard to Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 and/or to the national procedures) related to: Organisers not being required to submit the journey plans within two working days before the time of departure; Procedures in place not preventing all districts from approving journeys that did not include the final place of destination in the non-EU country; The lack of evidence that the districts performed the prescribed retrospective checks on journeys logs, and the fact that this went undetected by the regional level; Animals being sent for export with correct health certificates but sometimes accompanied with documentation known to be incorrect; are, as main consequences, placing an unnecessary burden on official veterinarians at the time of departure (who are under time pressure to verify the correctness of the journey plan 12 additionally to performing all the checks at loading), and weakening the assurances of the system on preventing unnecessary pain, suffering or injury to animals particularly during the non-EU part of their journeys. Polish transporters involved in export consignments from other Member States to Turkey have significantly reduced their reported percentage of consignments with non-compliances between 2016 and 2017 (11.2% to 2%). However their contingency plans, even if correctly descriptive on what to do in case of emergency, do not include measures to provide bedding, feed and water to the animals in the eventuality of unexpected long delays at those EU borders where this risk is high, such as Turkey. There are therefore inadequate assurances that Polish transporters carrying out live animal exports can see to animals' needs if blocked at these borders and that the animals are not caused unnecessary suffering. 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held on 2 March 2018 with representatives of the competent authorities, at which the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit were presented by the audit team. 8 RECOMMENDATIONS The competent authorities are invited to provide, within 25 working days of receipt of the report, an action plan containing details of the actions taken and planned, including deadlines for their completion, aimed at addressing the recommendations set out below: No. Recommendation 1. audits.title: Ready-to-eat food

recommendations.text: The CCAs should ensure that staff performing official controls at all levels undertake their duties competently and in a consistent manner in compliance with the provisions of Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. In particular, GSI should: provide the control staff involved in official controls of RTE foods establishments with training on the documented control procedures to verify the FBO's compliance with Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 especially with the provisions on RTE food; revise their documented control procedures in relation to risk assessments to determine inspection frequencies of establishme based on conclusion Nos 35, 92 and 93. Associated findings Nos 28, 57, 58, 74, 77 and 78.

citations.text: Although in each establishment visited, PSES inspectors provided the audit team with evidence (i.e. training certificates) on their participation in training sessions relevant to official controls of RTE food, these were not effective as the audit team noted some 8 weaknesses in their knowledge regarding the relevant requirements. For example: in one establishment visited, the audit team noted that when carrying out verification on the FBO's own-check sampling programme for microbiological analyses, the PSES inspector was not familiar with the existing CCA Order on this subject (see paragraph 64). The inspector attributed the lack of knowledge of the CCA Order to the absence of adequate training; in other establishments visited PSES inspectors had lack of knowledge on certain provisions of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 (number of sample units to be taken and how to evaluate FBOs' shelf-life studies) and on the CCA guidelines on environmental sampling and testing for Listeria monocytogenes (see paragraphs 74, 77 and 78).

A training system, also covering issues related to the RTE food sector, aimed at ensuring that official staff can execute their tasks effectively is in place. However, the system could not ensure in some cases that official controls are carried out in a consistent manner; in particular, weaknesses were noted in the knowledge of SSI staff on the procedures and guidance for official controls to verify the FBOs' compliance with Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005.

The audit team noted disagreement between GSI and VSES/PSES officials regarding the interpretation of the CCA procedure to be followed. GSI informed the audit team that frequency of inspections should be determined based on the result of the risk assessment (as described above). However, the VSES visited informed the audit team that when calculating the frequency of visits PSES inspectors should take into account further risk elements (e.g. volume of production, if the establishment is one of the major producers in the district, etc.).

The cases reviewed by the audit team showed an adjustment of inspection frequency by the PSES inspectors, resulting in a higher frequency of planned visits than based solely on risk assessment. However, in the absence of clear CCA procedures on determining the frequency of inspection, this result is not guaranteed in the future. Nevertheless, GSI informed the audit team of their commitment to review the risk assessment procedure in the light of the findings and conclusions of this audit (see Chapter 7). 5.4.1.2 Procedures for official controls VI

In one of the establishments visited (under the control of SSI) that produced certain RTE products able to support the growth of Listeria monocytogenes, the food safety criterion of point 1.2, Chapter 1, Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 was applied, with the limit to be 100 cfu/g during the shelf-life of products. The audit team noted however, that the CA inspector accepted the use of this limit without the FBO's adequate demonstration that the product will not exceed the limit 100 cfu/g throughout the shelf- life, which is in breach of footnote 5 of point 1.2, Chapter 1, Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 (see paragraph 96).

The audit team noted in one establishment visited under SSI supervision that the FBO took one sample from RTE products instead of the required five for microbiological 16 analysis without being able to demonstrate to the CA by historical documentation that it has effective HACCP-based procedures (which is in breach of Article 5(3) of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005).

Moreover, in two establishments visited under SSI supervision, the FBOs regularly took swab samples from processing areas and equipment and analysed them for Listeria monocytogenes. However, all these samples were taken after cleaning and disinfection. This is neither in line with SSI guidelines on this issue nor with the guidelines of the EU Reference Laboratory (EURL) (Guidance on sampling the food processing area and equipment for the detection of Listeria monocytogenes) which recommends (in order to increase the probability of detecting a persistent strain) that the sampling should be carried out during processing. Sampling only after cleaning and disinfection makes the detection of the pathogen difficult and can lead to a false sense of security. These practices had not been noted during official controls as the CA inspectors were not familiar with the provisions of the above mentioned SSI guidelines. 5.4.1.4 Official sampling and laboratory analysis

The CAs put in place a system of risk based official controls over production of RTE foods, supported by comprehensive documented procedures and guidance. Although these procedures do not fully take into account the specific risks related to RTE food (in particular those identified by the CAs as high risk RTE), the impact is mitigated by the frequent and efficient controls in place. Some inconsistencies in the implementation of GSI procedures for risk assessments to determine inspection frequencies were noted.

Official controls and enforcement actions over RTE foods were satisfactory. However, shortcomings in the official controls to verify FBOs' compliance with Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 were noted in particular for GSI.

audits.title: African Swine Fever

recommendations.text: To improve the accuracy and quality of the tools for the traceability of pigs, in order for them to be effective tools for animal health controls. (Article 3 of Directive 2008/71/EC, Article 18 of Directive 64/432/EEC, Article 15/2(b) of Directive 2002/60/EC). Recommendation based on conclusion No. 44. Associated findings No. 1, 2, 3, 8 & 17.

citations.text: The identification system for pigs and the Agency for Restructuring and Modernisation of Agriculture (ARMA) database are described in reports from previous Commission audits related to this area, i.e. DG(SANTE)/2017-6114-MR, DG(SANTE)/2016-6114- MR and DG(SANTE)/2014-7294-MR.

In response to Recommendation No 3 from report DG(SANTE)/2017-6114-MR, i.e., "To improve the accuracy and quality of the tools for the traceability of pigs, in order for them to be effective tools for animal health controls", Poland proposed a public procurement procedure for the design and development of a new database, i.e. "e-IRZ Plus". ARMA informed the audit team that a tender process had been opened in 2017 and then cancelled. A decision was taken during 2018 to modify the existing database and create "IRZ Plus". This modification improved electronic data exchange with livestock owners. However, it did not improve the functionality for adding animal health information and official veterinarians still have limited direct access to statistical data on the database, both of which would support planning and implementation of official disease control programmes. The audit team was told that "IRZ Plus" could still become a reality in the future if funding was to become available. The system currently maintained by ARMA was never designed as a system to contain information on animal health (its main task is to cover the whereabouts and movements of animals -- Article 3(2) of the Law of 2 April 2004 on the animal identification and registration system). The DEPiRZ (Producer Register and Animal Registration System Department) issues various statistics required by the GVI. In addition, the Agency made available the application platform and the `IW SIRZ' browser, which are tools allowing an overview and analysis of data from the IRZ database. 4

As described in previous reports, the GVI maintains its own separate database ("Vetlink") which includes animal health information and is used to support District Veterinary Offices (DVOs) to manage disease control programmes including ASF. There is limited access to data on Vetlink from areas outside the region in which holdings are located. The GVI have plans to expand the capabilities of the system.

The high number of visits to holdings in the ASF affected area has provided an up-to- date picture of pig numbers on holdings. This has allowed a cross check with the information on the central database and the removal of many holdings that no longer 5 keep pigs which has also contributed considerably to the reduced numbers of pig holdings. (A similar exercise has not taken place in the ASF free area and therefore the accuracy of pig holding information in the database would be lower.)

DVOs produce annual reports on how many such visits are carried out and the main non-compliances detected. They do not confirm the extent to which the target of twice annual visits was achieved, e.g. percentage of holdings visited twice. The reports do not include data on the number of holdings that should have been inspected and the reasons why inspections did not take place as planned. The competent authority did say that many holdings on the list may not have pigs when contacted to arrange a visit but records viewed by the audit team in DVOs did not include this information.

The existence of two pig databases complicates the proper planning and implementation of official controls. The fact that the pig holding data is not accurate in the ARMA database for the ASF free area of the country will slow down the application of control measures should the disease spread to it.

recommendations.text: To ensure that all measures under the ASF approved programme, including the feed ban are subjected to official controls in order to ensure their effective implementation. (Approved programme for ASF). Recommendation based on conclusion No. 48. Associated findings No. 32 and 33.

citations.text: In response to Recommendation No 5 from DG(SANTE)/2017-6114-MR, i.e., "To ensure that all measures under the ASF approved programme, including the feed ban are subjected to official controls in order to ensure their effective implementation.", Poland proposed that the Polish Hunting Association (PHA) would supervise the activities of hunting clubs including compliance with the biosecurity rules. The PHA would provide the GVI with reports on those checks and a summary of those reports were to be submitted to the ASF expert group for evaluation.

According to the competent authority, the PHA checked the implementation of the biosecurity rules by hunters in 371 hunting clubs during the 2017/2018 hunting season. The PHA forwarded reports to the GVI but in the absence of a national template, the 9 reports varied greatly and the information they contained could not be compared or assessed by the ASF expert group. The audit team was informed that a proposal for a national template for reporting inspections on hunting grounds/carcase collection points is being discussed between the PHA and the GVI with June 2019 as the current target for agreement and subsequent use.

The absence of a national template for reporting on the implementation of biosecurity measures at hunting grounds made the system ineffective, as the ASF expert group cannot compare the information and use it to provide further advice.

recommendations.text: To ensure that practical arrangements required by Commission Implementing Decision (EC) No 2014/709 have been put in place for the collection and transport of ABPs from Part III in order to reduce the risk of the spread of disease through potentially contaminated products. Recommendation based on conclusion No. 49. Associated finding No. 40.

citations.text: A system has been implemented for the dispatch from Part III of ABPs from porcine animals based on the requirements of Article 7 of Decision 2014/709/EU. The GVI confirmed that they do not require that compartments in lorries are sealed by an Official 11 veterinarian nor have they designated disinfection points at the exit from Part III, which are requirements in Article 7(c) and (e) respectively.

The likelihood of the disease spreading through movement of ABPs of domestic and 12 wild boar is low due to the controls over these products, although the system presents weaknesses due to the absence of official sealing and of designated disinfection points for the lorries. 5.2 MEASURES IN CASE OF SUSPICION/CONFIRMATION OF ASF IN DOMESTIC PIGS Legal requirements Articles 4-5 and 8-11 of Directive 2002/60/EC Decision 2003/422/EC Findings

recommendations.text: To ensure that when pigs move from Part III to a slaughterhouse that they move directly as required by Article 4.3 of Commission Implementing Decision 2014/709/EU and do not pass through "collection points". Recommendation based on conclusion No. 43. Associated finding No. 25.

citations.text: The audit team visited two slaughterhouses, both in Part II, which received pigs from different areas, including Part III. The movement documents examined by the audit team were in compliance with the relevant requirements of Decision 2014/709/EU with the exception of Article 4.3 which requires that "the pigs are transported for immediate slaughter directly, without stopping or unloading, to a slaughterhouse...". Many of the consignments had passed through "collection points" which is specifically allowed under current national law. According to the competent authority, pigs from smaller holdings would be taken to "collection points" by their owner and reloaded onto larger lorries and then taken to the slaughterhouse.

The system in place to implement the requirements and derogations to dispatch live pigs and pig meat/products from the ASF restricted area generally works as intended. There is a provision in national law allowing live pigs from Part III to move to slaughter via "collection points" instead of directly to the slaughterhouse. This intermediate stop of animals from infected area increases the risk of spreading the disease within the country.

recommendations.text: To ensure that only fresh meat from wild boar that complies with the requirements of Article 15 of Commission Implementing Decision 2014/709/EU are dispatched from the areas listed in the Annex of that Decisio based on conclusion No. 46. Associated finding No. 30.

citations.text: The audit visited a game collection centre in Part I where wild boar carcases from Part I are stored after they receive a negative result for ASF (was previously stored in a "carcase collection centre" ­ see finding 31). The centre was also used to store wild boar carcases from the free area and the carcases from Part I and the free area were destined for a game processing establishment in the free area. Based on discussions with the operator of the game collection centre, only about 5-10% of hunted wild boar carcasses were sent to game processing establishments with the rest being consumed locally. Although the risks are minimal, Article 15.1(b) of Decision 2014/709/EU does not allow wild boar carcases from a free area to enter Part I and then return to the free area as no derogation exists in the Decision unlike for example carcases from wild boar shot in Part I which can leave Part I if tested with negative result for ASF.

There are no wild boar farmed and hence no trade. The system in place generally ensures that wild boar meat can only leave restricted regions if it complies with all the requirements. However, there are instances where wild boar carcases go out to the free area and then return back again, increasing the risk of introducing the disease.

audits.title: Feed additives, their ingredients and traceability

recommendations.text: To ensure that inspections are carried out without prior warning as required by Article 3(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation based on conclusion: 33. Associated findings: 20.

citations.text: The audit team noted that the Instruction of the CVO No GIWhig-500-4/08 on the methodology of official controls advises prior notice to be given for "comprehensive controls". In two FeBOs visited, the inspector (same for the both operators) stated that prior notice had been given to the FeBOs on the controls to be carried out by the DVI. The official explained that this had been given to ensure the availability of the necessary staff and access to relevant documentation. The audit team pointed out that while such an approach can be justified in rare cases (remote locations, irregular working hours, etc.), providing FeBOs with prior notice is not in line with the requirements laid down in Article 3(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

The system of planning of inspections is based on appropriate risk-related factors and thus ensures that the official controls are carried out regularly, on a risk-basis, with an appropriate frequency and, as such are suitable to verify operators' traceability and correctness of labelling. However, the effectiveness of inspections is weakened by several elements including the giving of notice to establishments prior to inspections, and inadequate assessment of operators' HACCP-plans. 5.2.2 Sampling 5.2.2.1 PLANNING OF OFFICIAL SAMPLING

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls are capable of verifying that feed business operators meet the requirements on hazard analysis and critical control points (HACCP) in accordance with Articles 6 and 7 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, and that the effectiveness of such controls is guaranteed, as required by Article 4(2(a)) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation based on conclusion: 33. Associated findings: 21, 22, 23, 24 and 25.

citations.text: In every establishment visited, the audit team checked the DVIs' feed inspectors' assessment of the operators' HACCP-plans. In one case, the inspector's assessment was (7) Available at https://www.wetgiw.gov.pl/nadzor-weterynaryjny/listy-kontrolne-spiwet---sektor-paszowy 5 sufficient. However, in 10 of the 11 establishments visited, the audit team noted shortcomings in relation to the adequacy of the hazard identification for some ingredients and processing aids used for the production of feed additives (predominantly contaminants of chemical origin, e.g., heavy metals, dioxins/polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), etc., but also the necessity to verify the authorisation of the microbial strain(s) used for production of certain feed additives where fermentation process had been applied). The failure of the operators to identify relevant hazards, as required by Article 6(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, was neither spotted by the inspectors met during the audit nor had been identified in any of the previous inspection reports reviewed by the audit team.

The audit team noted that the operators' quality assurance systems seen rarely contained unambiguous provisions on ensuring that the raw materials and ingredients are sourced from registered or approved FeBOs. This contradicts the requirements laid down by Article 5(6) of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. This was neither spotted by the inspectors met during the audit nor had been identified in any of the previous inspection reports.

The audit team noted that the CVO has developed detailed guidance on the assessment of homogeneity of compound feed. The purpose of the document is to determine rules for assessing homogeneity of compound feed based on the degree of mixing of the key ingredient(s). While most of the inspectors met demonstrated good knowledge of verification of establishments' controls on this aspect, the audit team encountered instances when the inspectors did not possess adequate knowledge on the assessment criteria for homogeneity. Consequently, the inspectors could not adequately verify that the requirements laid down in part 3(b) of the section "Facilities and equipment" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005 were respected by the FeBOs.

The audit team noted that there was no dedicated guidance on the assessment of carry- over. At all operators visited, where the risk for carry-over was relevant, the inspectors interviewed were struggling with the assessment of the operators' control for the carry- over, specifically of coccidiostats to non-target feed. For example, two operators used markers which were irrelevant to assess carry-over of coccidiostats ­ this was not spotted by the inspectors interviewed. As a result, the inspectors could not adequately verify that the requirements laid down in part 2(b) of the section "Facilities and equipment" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005 were respected by the FeBOs.

The audit team noted that many inspectors interviewed experienced difficulties in verifying that establishments' controls on scales and metering devices (in form of a check of documented and traceable procedures for testing/calibration and its completeness/adequacy) were appropriate. Thus, the requirements laid down by part 3(a) of the section "Facilities and equipment" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005 could not be properly verified by the inspectors. 6 5.2.1.3 TRACEABILITY

The system of planning of inspections is based on appropriate risk-related factors and thus ensures that the official controls are carried out regularly, on a risk-basis, with an appropriate frequency and, as such are suitable to verify operators' traceability and correctness of labelling. However, the effectiveness of inspections is weakened by several elements including the giving of notice to establishments prior to inspections, and inadequate assessment of operators' HACCP-plans. 5.2.2 Sampling 5.2.2.1 PLANNING OF OFFICIAL SAMPLING

recommendations.text: To ensure that staff carrying out official sampling, and interpreting the pertinent analytical results, follow the requirements laid down by Article 1 and Annex I and II to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. Recommendation based on conclusion: 45 and 46. Associated findings: 41, 42 and 43. 13

citations.text: In every establishment visited, the feed inspectors met were interviewed in relation to the sampling provisions laid down by Article 1 of, and Annex I to, Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. The feed inspectors interviewed could in general demonstrate good knowledge and implementation of the respective requirements. In many of the cases the inspectors used the mobile application (see finding 40). However, in several cases the inspectors interviewed experienced difficulties in establishing the distribution pattern of chemical contaminants and displayed weak knowledge of the concept of 'sampled portion', which resulted in (i) erroneous identification of the number of incremental samples to be taken, and (ii) inappropriate preparation of final samples from the aggregate samples for the control of substances where non-uniform distribution of the analyte/substance is presumed. In the latter case, some inspectors interviewed erroneously suggested simple manual mixing would ensure appropriate homogenisation (8) Available at https://www.wetgiw.gov.pl/nadzor-weterynaryjny/badania-kontrolne-monitoring-pasz 9 rather than using special equipment (e.g., mechanical or automatic dividers) which is required by part 9(4) of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. For substances with a non-uniform distribution, simple manual mixing alone cannot ensure complete homogenisation of the aggregate sample. The audit team noted that mechanical dividers were available in all of the districts visited.

The audit team noted that most of the sampling protocols seen contained all of the mandatory parameters required by part 10 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. However, in one district visited, an old template, not containing the mandatory field for the size of the sampled portion, was in use.

The official laboratories send the analytical reports to the DVIs where the district feed inspectors interpret the results obtained. Certain guidance on the topic is available in Chapter VI of the NFCP. However, the guidance does not consistently explain the role of analytical measurement uncertainty, recovery rate and moisture content in the interpretation of the test results. Consequently, the interpretation does not take account of all of the relevant criteria as required by part 6 of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009 (this situation was confirmed during the interviews with the district feed inspectors met). The audit team saw several analytical reports and could conclude that the data required by part C(5) and C(6) of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009 were not always provided.

The system in place for planning of official sampling is effective and risk-based. However, the effectiveness of the sampling is weakened by the fact that the representativeness of the sampling, and thus the samples' legal and analytical validity, is not consistently ensured, especially for controls on substances with a non-uniform distribution.

The interpretation of the analytical results does not take into account all required parameters thus weakening the legal validity of the decisions made by the competent authorities. 5.2.3 Actions taken on non-compliances

recommendations.text: To ensure that when official controls identify non-compliance, comprehensive actions are taken to ensure that the operator completely remedies the situation as required by Article 54 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation based on conclusion: 53. Associated findings: 50 and 51.

citations.text: The audit team examined three RASFF notifications (one originated from Poland and two which were sent to Poland due to the distribution of the affected products) and the actions taken by the relevant competent authorities (mainly by the DVIs). In general, the actions taken to ensure rectification of the non-compliances were sufficient and timely and in agreement with the requirements laid down in Article 54 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. However, in one case the audit team noted that the retained sample was analysed as a commercial sample sent by the operator thus creating the possibility for questioning the legal validity of the decision made by the DVI.

In every establishment visited, the audit team studied non-compliances from previous inspections (if any had been identified). Examples included deficient labelling, HACCP- related deficiencies, etc. The audit team noted that in several cases the inspection reports and communication with the FeBOs did not unambiguously specify any timeframe for the FeBO to remedy the deficiency(ies). In all of the non-compliances scrutinised, no evidence was observed that the operators had been requested to identify the reason(s) for the deficiency(ies) and take adequate actions to amend their quality systems to eliminate the risk of repetition. The follow-ups seen were not necessarily comprehensive and complete (in one case with an expired product, it was not verified that the product had been adequately disposed of by the operator; in another case, a deficiency with traceability was allegedly mentioned orally but was not documented and never followed up (see finding 28). The situation observed is not fully in line with the requirements laid down by Article 54 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

A lack of comprehensiveness and completeness of actions taken on non-compliances weakens the effectiveness of the overall control system. 5.2.4 Establishments producing/trading non-authorised (in the EU) feed additives but are exporting or re-exporting them from the EU to a third country

citations.text: The audit team was informed by the DVOs in the districts visited that all AVs are paid from the state budget and that no direct payments from FBOs occur. However, their remuneration is based on the number of animals inspected or on the amount of meat introduced to the cutting plant they supervise. If the activity of the establishment where they perform their duties is stopped for any reason, they are not paid for the period concerned. Therefore, this payment system undermines the AVs' independence in those situations where the required enforcement measures to be taken on the spot would imply or include e.g. stopping of the slaughter operation (see paragraphs 77 and 92).

The CCA informed the audit team that the total number of AVs involved in official controls of meat establishments (including slaughterhouses) was 3,318 in 2018. The audit team noted that this number remained constant between 2016 and 2018 (3,320 in 2016 and 3,279 in 2017). However, during the same period the number of permanent official veterinarians decreased by 141, most of them (90) in the districts, from 2,172 (1,638 in the districts) in 2016 to 2,031(1,548 in the districts) in 2018.

In particular, in 2018, in all 305 districts, there were 396 full time employed official veterinarians in charge of food safety. In each district visited, the audit team noted that there are vacant posts (in some cases for years) which cannot be filled in the absence of applicants, due to non-competitive salaries. In at least two districts visited, only one Food Safety official was available, while there were two posts assigned for the performance of the planned activities.

Despite the shortage of permanent staff declared in all of the districts that were visited, the audit team was informed and saw evidence that the DVIs were able to achieve the number and scope of controls for the establishments visited. Nevertheless, this did not always result in reaching the quality of controls necessary to verify compliance of the FBOs concerned (see Chapter 5.4.2.1). 5.2.4 Training
Decreasing number of official staff, their low salaries, as well as the production related remuneration for AVs impact on the enforcement of the relevant EU legislation.

In one of these (in addition to the deficiencies related to post-mortem inspection - see paragraph 92) the CA did not identify the existing structural problems in the slaughterhouse and the cutting plant (rooms were not large enough for the hygienic performance of the activities carried out (see paragraph 55). The DVI official performing a control, in the presence of the audit team, was able to detect relevant non- compliances but not to make a conclusion concerning the overall situation in the establishment.

In the other establishment, the audit team noted several non-compliances which had not been previously noted by any level of CA controls (i.e. by the permanently present AV, the DVI or the RVI) before the visit of the audit team, or which, in any event, had not been corrected. For example, the audit team noted: inefficient cleaning and unsatisfactory flow for dirty crates, poor hygienic practices with regard to cleaning of equipment and premises, the structural elements of the old part of the establishment were worn out, with rusty support elements, damaged wall to floor junctions, surfaces of walls, floors and equipment were not clean and not easy to clean and disinfect, an extensive leakage of water from the ceiling above exposed products. Although this issue had already been noted during the DVI control carried out 10 days before the visit of the audit team, no corrective action was taken.

Moreover, in the evisceration room, the audit team noted the absence of adequate ventilation causing huge condensation above exposed products with high risk of cross- contamination. Although the AVs are obliged to verify the pre-operational and operational conditions, the slaughter operation was authorised to start and was not stopped until the visit of the audit team (see also paragraph 24).

Official controls for verification of FBOs' compliance with the relevant EU requirements (including: hygiene, HACCP, own-check sampling, animal welfare, traceability, labelling, food additives, identification marking, etc.) in PM/PMP establishments are in place and in general can provide guarantees that the establishments meet those requirements. However, there were two exceptions, where establishments presented serious structural and hygiene requirements which had not been detected by any level of the CA controls.

Ante-mortem and post-mortem inspections are, in general, carried out in compliance with the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004, with the exception of significant failure in performing post-mortem inspection in one establishment visited.

The audit team reviewed several cases of RASFF notifications and food incidents related to PM/PMP which did not reach RASFF (in most cases due to Salmonella spp.) and noted that the CA procedures were followed: an adequate investigation was carried out at establishment level and corrective actions were taken by the FBOs. Although CA actions were prompt and comprehensive, in most cases, they were not effective regarding prevention of reintroduction of the hazards (Salmonella). 25 Conclusions on RASSF

The system for follow-up of RASFF notifications and for food incidents, implemented in Poland, provides guarantees that adequate actions are taken by the CAs in case these notifications/incidents are linked to PM/PMP, particularly concerning their follow-up and measures adopted regarding the products involved. However, these actions are not effective in preventing the re-introduction of Salmonella in the poultry meat processing chain which is evidenced by the continuously high number of RASFF notifications linked to this commodity. 5.7 FOLLOW-UP OF PREVIOUS AUDIT RECOMMENDATIONS The table below summarises the follow-up of the relevant recommendation made in the previous DG Health and Food Safety audit report: Audit report DG(SANTE)/2014-7160 MR Final No Previous recommendation Assessment 1. Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 (i.e. the placing of their Recommendation 1 of this products on the market only when an identification report. mark is applied in accordance with Annex II, Section I, of this Regulation). 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The official controls over production of PM/PMP are organised on a risk basis and implemented using comprehensive documented procedures and guidance, and covering relevant aspects of the legislation. Official controls for verification of FBOs' compliance with the relevant EU requirements in poultry establishments are in place and in general, can provide guarantees that the establishments meet those requirements. However, deficiencies concerning mostly structural and hygiene requirements, not detected by any level of CA controls, or in any event, not corrected, in particular in two establishments out of eight visited, were noted by the audit team. Staffing and remuneration issues, the low salaries for the official staff, as well as the production related remuneration for AVs, undermine the correct functioning of the official 26 control system in Poland and impact on the enforcement of the relevant EU legislation. Due to the high and increasing number of RASFF notifications in Poland linked to Salmonella in PM/PMP, special official sampling procedures are in place at slaughterhouse level, in order to verify the reliability of FBOs' own-check sampling, which currently gives much lower rates of detection. Although the system for follow-up of RASFF notifications and for food incidents, implemented in Poland, provides guarantees that adequate actions are taken by the CAs particularly concerning their follow-up and measures adopted regarding the products involved, these actions are not effective in preventing the re-introduction of Salmonella in the poultry meat processing chain. The CA has implemented national measures that apply to low throughput establishments which allow the use of a round national identification mark intended only for the national market. As these measures are not in line with the EU legislation, a recommendation was already made in the audit report DG(SANTE)2014-7160 (PM/PMP) requesting the CA to correct the situation in this regard. Nonetheless, no corrective action has been taken or planned by the CCA to address this recommendation. recommendations.text: Ensure coordination and cooperation between and within the CAs, as required by Article 4(5) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, specifically: coordination between CSI and ARMA to give access to official databases of primary producers; coordination between CSI, VSES and PSES in order to optimise resources and to help inspectors at district level to gain experience; to implement a system in order to have efficient use of the available information collected. Recommendation based on conclusions: 24, 25, 61, 83, 85 and 86. Associated findings: 17, 19, 28, 31, 59, 72, 74, 75, 77 and 78.

citations.text: The CSI informed the audit team that due to shortages in resources the official control frequencies for primary production could not be fully implemented. CSI stated, that this was caused by the increasing workload (e.g. increase of registered primary producers) without increasing the number of staff. This was already stated in 2016 during the last audit.

The database system implemented at central level of SSI collects general information and does not support the collection and in place to manage the registration of primary producers, the approval of processing/freezing establishments or for the does not support the collection of inspection and sampling results for FNAO primary producers, ready-to- eat and freezing establishments. This limits the availability of information that could be (3) Commission notice on guidance document on addressing microbiological risks in fresh fruits and vegetables at primary production through good hygiene 6 used for future planning of inspection and supervision purposes. The CSI stated, that some of the VSES and PSES have individual IT based systems to collect detailed data. The audit team noted at the PSES visited that excel sheets developed by the local inspectors were used. Other CAs involved in controls in the scope of the audit

However, the capability to implement an effective system for official controls is limited by the lack of adequate tools to gather process and analyse information on registration, approval and inspection results for primary producers, ready-to-eat producers and freezers this undermines efficient planning and targeting of controls in particular for primary producers. This is of particular relevance given that staff numbers had not increased in parallel to the increased work load in recent years.

In addition, the limited cooperation between SSI and ARMA results in a further limitation of relevant information being available for the purposes of planning and implementing effective controls, and is in contrary to the requirements of Article 4(5) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5.2.2 Registration / Approval of Food Establishments Legal requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/204, Article 2 of Regulation (EU) No 210/2013 and Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings Registration of food establishments Primary producers

The CSI is aware that not all primary producers are registered. CSI stated that they do not know the number of un-registered primary producers. This is the same situation as encountered by the audit teams in 2013 and 2016.

At one PSES visited, an establishment processing and freezing vegetables and soft fruit was involved in several RASFF notifications, the last one in 2018 regarding the presence of norovirus in a consignment of frozen red currants. 23 primary producers of this district had been identified as suppliers for this consignment. None of these suppliers was registered at the time of the RASFF notification. The audit team noted after document cross-checks that the freezer/processor's supplier list for 2019 still contained unregistered primary producers of soft fruit. One of these produced on more than four hectares, which is considered a medium to big producer in this district. Although it was known to inspectors that un-registered producers were involved in a RASFF notification in 2018 the processor could persist in this practice in 2019, unnoticed by the PSES. PSES informed the audit team that controls at these primary producers were scheduled for 2019.

At the VSES visited, most of the processors are categorised low risk, some medium and none high risk. At central level exact figures were not available level because of the lack of a central database. 12

There is an official control system in place covering the production chain of FNAO. In principle the controls are risk based. However, regarding primary producers, the risk assessment system is less efficient because of the lack of key parameters at registration (e.g. crop surface, production volumes) and does not allow the system to direct the limited resources to the riskiest primary producers. regarding processing establishments the audit team concluded that the risk scoring system for processors does not reflect sufficiently the potential risks in particular regarding the weighing factor for more risky crops and their intended use of it (e.g. ready-to-eat), contrary to the requirements of Article 3(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. This weakens the effectiveness of the official control system.

Currently there are 283 FNAO freezing processors approved in Poland. 512 inspections were carried out in 2018. The SSI could not provide the audit team with an overview of the risk categories assigned to the processors, the number of non-compliances and their nature, mainly due to the absence of a central database for risk categorisation and inspection results.

Three inspections were carried out by the PSSE in April and May 2019 to verify the implementation of traceability and corrective measures in the framework of a RASFF notification (norovirus in red currants). The single non-conformity noted by the PSES was the fact that the operator had failed to inform the PSES immediately about the incident and was fined with 300 PLN for that. The audit team noted further: no non-compliances had been documented since 2016; no dedicated storage for cleaned crates was assigned; openings to the outside under the entrance doors in the preparation room, not identified previously; the general state of the reception room was dirty and not easy to clean and disinfect. Wooden pallets used to transport fruit crates were damaged/in decay, equipment and floor were dirty; in a clean room with finished produce (after freezing) water from the ceiling was dripping in a steady flow in the vicinity where open produce was packaged (frozen paprika cubes and frozen strawberries); massive ice had formed in all three cold stores visited with drip marks on cartons, and the presence of open cartons; environmental sampling to detect Listeria monocytogenes by the operator was not carried out according the ISO norm and was not suitable to detect Listeria (no sponges used, wrong medium).

PSES staff stated that: the water drip had never occurred before; (6) paragraph 71 of the draft report was deleted on request of the Polish competent authority. 15 the ice forming situation in the cold stores was considered as unavoidable and therefore acceptable; that they had insufficient specific knowledge about Listeria monocytogenes swabbing, and had not received relevant training for it.

PSES staff had identified non conformities in former inspections but they were not relevant to the deficiencies seen by the audit team. The last control in the establishment was undertaken shortly before the audit. The audit team noted: heavy condensation from the ceiling in a reception room near open produce in crates (red and black currants); some ice forming in the cold stores and open cartons; carton boxes were prepared to be filled with plastic bags and stacked in such a way that the bottom of the boxes could contaminate the clean bags inside (before the produce was filled in); environmental swabs for Listeria are outsourced to a laboratory, the description of the sampling by the operator suggested that the correct method was used. Third freezing establishment

No non-compliances had been documented since 2016. The audit team noted that: there were no adequate facilities nor a procedure for cleaning and storage of external containers. Containers were sorted in the yard surrounded by trees inhabited with numerous birds. The operator stated that cleaning of containers was the responsibility of the supplier; the processing room was in good condition but not entirely pest proof and a bird was seen flying inside; environmental swabs for Listeria monocytogenes were outsourced to a laboratory, the description of the sampling by the operator suggested that an incorrect method was used; the packaging for final consumers were labelled with a cooking advice; In this establishment very thorough measures were taken by the SSI including sampling of products and swabs for Listeria taken in 2018 due to the RASFF.

During official controls national checklists and instructions were used at all levels of SSI. This allows, in principle, for a uniform way of official control. However, without comprehensive background knowledge inspectors can easily overlook aspects relevant for prevention of microbiological risks at primary production and processing of FNAO.
Official controls of processors showed that non-compliances were rarely detected. During the inspections carried out by the PSES observed by the audit team, important shortcomings were noticed.

Because most inspectors control only a very limited number of FNAO freezer establishments, a lack of theoretical and practical knowledge was observed (e.g. no knowledge about Listeria monocytogenes swabs and certain basic hygiene requirements). This further weakens the effectiveness of official controls in the field of FNAO.

audits.title: Production chain of smoked fishery products

recommendations.text: The competent authority should strengthen the implementation of the arrangements in place to ensure the effectiveness of official controls covering the production chain of fishery products. Recommendation based on conclusions No 21 and 86. Associated findings No 16, 17, 81 and 83.

citations.text: In terms of procedures to verify the implementation of control tasks, the GVI indicated that its audit office carries out supervision over the regional and district levels (thematic controls), throughout a documentary assessment, which may include an on-the-spot assessment. These controls can be planned or non-planned, the former based on a risk analysis and the latter carried out to address specific emergent issues. GVI stated that no thematic controls have been recently carried out to the regions and districts involved in the current audit. In addition, the GVI also stated that it has in place other mechanisms with a view of co-ordination and supervision, which include regular meetings between the different Officers and exchange of correspondence by conventional and electronic mail.

The audit office of GVI carries out internal audits to the services performing official control tasks. These audits are carried out annually and cover particular topics and services. The audit office intends to cover all relevant topics within a five-year period. The last internal audit that covered fishery products matters, including smoked fishery products, was carried-out in 2015.

The authority has in place certain supervision mechanisms as well as internal audits. However, in relation to the controls of smoked fishery products, the implementation of these mechanisms had not been used in recent years and as such, potential deficiencies of the control system were not identified.

The audit team noted that for each individual establishment involved in the iRASFF notifications, the competent authority increased its awareness of the deficiencies that could justify the contamination of the products with L. monocytogenes but it took time 18 for the competent authority to progress in terms of identification and correction of deficiencies. The initial iRASFF notifications dated from 2017 and the training to official staff was provided in 2019 (see paragraph 12) which is coincident with increased detection of non-compliant results during the official sampling (see paragraph 69). Also at the beginning of 2019 the guidance document indicated in paragraph 35 was updated (in particular its annex 5). However, as indicated in paragraphs 61 to 63 official staff is not always able to correctly assess shelf life studies.

Despite of all the progress done in the control of the concerned establishments, the audit team did not find evidence that this progress was adequately captured and disseminated within the relevant levels of the VI. This would enhance the ability of official control staff to identify similar issues in establishments, other than the ones implicated in the iRASSF notifications, in advance, and if possible prevent the occurrence of the same type of outbreaks. Conclusions on measures in case of non-compliance and follow up of iRASFF notifications

At national level, the authority provided training on official sampling and improved the guidance documents, but the audit team did not find evidence that the improvements observed in the official controls carried out in particular establishments would be disseminated throughout the relevant levels of VI across Poland. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The official control system in place for smoked fishery products cover the production chain, it is implemented as planned and in accordance with the applicable procedures. It provides a largely satisfactory basis for the competent authority to verify compliance of several European Union food hygiene requirements. Nonetheless, the audit also identified gaps/shortcomings in relation to the ability of the controls to detect relevant deficiencies, most notably the storage of frozen products 19 (prolongation of the stiffening) and the assessment of the shelf life studies (for which existing guidance was not taken into account). These factors impact on the overall effectiveness of controls in this area in terms of its ability to verify compliance and to ensure the implementation of appropriate corrective measures which, in turn, would also contribute to prevention of future incidents. The competent authority investigated the iRASFF notifications on Listeria monocytogenes in smoked fishery products, including the ones linked with the multi-country outbreaks. This work contributed to certain improvements of the control system, in particular, staff training, official sampling and testing for the microbiological criteria. Further improvements can be achieved with whole genome sequencing expected to start at the end of this year. However, in the case of the non-compliances detected in the concerned establishments, the corrective action was limited to those FBOs involved and there is no evidence that the acquired knowledge was used to improve the overall control system. 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held on 6 November 2020 with representatives of the competent authority. At this meeting, the audit team presented the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit. During this meeting, the competent authority acknowledged the findings and preliminary conclusions presented by the audit team and provided a commitment to look into the issues identified. 20 8 RECOMMENDATIONS No. Recommendation 1. 2. The competent authority should strengthen the implementation of the 3. arrangements in place to ensure the effectiveness of official controls covering the production chain of fishery products. 4. Recommendation based on conclusions No 21 and 86. Associated findings No 16, 17, 81 and 83. 5. The competent authority should ensure that procedures for approval of establishments, in particular in relation to the intermediate deadlines in the case of conditional approval, comply with the requirements of Article 148(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. These factors impact on the overall effectiveness of controls in this area in terms of its ability to verify compliance and to ensure the implementation of appropriate corrective measures which, in turn, would also contribute to prevention of future incidents. The competent authority investigated the iRASFF notifications on Listeria monocytogenes in smoked fishery products, including the ones linked with the multi-country outbreaks. This work contributed to certain improvements of the control system, in particular, staff training, official sampling and testing for the microbiological criteria. Legal basis: Article 2(3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2130. Recommendation based on conclusion: 78 Associated findings: 75 and 76

citations.text: The audit team noted that the documentary checks had not identified certain minor errors in a small number of entry documents. The errors in the documents were not sufficient to affect the validity of the decision to allow importation of the animals or goods concerned. In light of that finding, the Chief Veterinary Officer issued an instruction to BVIs on 18 December 2020, to take measures to minimise errors and inconsistencies in the entry documents and accompanying documents. The VI also confirmed that Section 5 of the BIP Manual concerning documentary checks would be revised and that the issue would be included in future training programmes for border inspectors, in line with Article 12(3) of the OCR.

The audit team also noted that the net weight declared in the CVED accompanying a consignment of frozen prawns, included the weight of the ice-glaze, although the 16 accompanying health certificate indicated the net weight without the ice-glaze, which in this case amounted to a difference of 3,584 kg. The VI informed the audit team that in- line with internal guidance, it was acceptable for the declared weight to be inclusive of glaze, and therefore the CVED was not rejected. The audit team noted that such guidance is not consistent with the clarification previously provided by DG Health and Food Safety to Member States, that in order to ensure consistency between Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 of the European Parliament and of the Council and the information on the food label, `the net weight indicated on the health certificate and CVEDs for glazed food must ... be exclusive of the glaze'. The VI stated that the interpretations of the European Commission and of Poland differed in this case, and that had been communicated in writing to the Commission by the Chief Veterinary Officer. The audit team noted however that documentary checks of glazed food, carried out in-line with the internal guidance, do not ensure that the information in the entry document corresponds to the information provided in the official certificates, official attestations and other documents accompanying the consignment, in-line withArticle 2(3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2130. citations.text: The audit team noted that no storage facilities are available at the rail location at BCP Dorohusk/Dorohusku. The competent authorities confirmed that storage in the means of transport in which the goods were brought to the BCP is permitted under their control 18 instead, in line with Article 3(13) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014, and that in their view, there is no need for storage areas or rooms.

The audit team noted that while such storage is permitted, Article 3(13) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014 does not derogate from the requirement for BCPs to have fixed storage areas or rooms, appropriate to the categories of goods for which the post has been designated, in line with Articles 3(1)(c), 3(2) and 6(2) of that Regulation. Conclusions on minimum requirements for border control posts

The absence of appropriate storage rooms or areas at one rail BCP is not in line with EU legislation and may have an adverse impact on the official controls and the hygienic handling of products for which that BCP has been designated. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION There is a comprehensive system of official controls for animals and goods entering the EU through BCPs in Poland. Those controls were carried out by well-trained officials, supported by detailed guidance, and were generally implemented in line with documented procedures, planned arrangements, and relevant Union legislation. However specific shortcomings were identified in the implementation of certain documentary and physical checks and in the facilities for performing those controls at one designated rail BCP. The competent authorities had initiated corrective actions at the time of the audit aimed at addressing a number of those shortcomings. 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held on 20 January 2021 by video-conference with the representatives of the central authorities in Poland, during which the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit were presented by the audit team. The competent authorities provided details of a number of actions planned/undertaken at that meeting, which are included in the report findings. 8 RECOMMENDATIONS The competent authorities are invited to provide details of the actions taken and planned, including deadlines for their completion ('action plan'), aimed at addressing the recommendations set out below, within 25 working days of receipt of this audit report. 19 No. Recommendations 1.
