citations.text: The audit team noted that the instructions do not detail the requirements on supervision of PVPs and do not provide the necessary safeguard measures on the avoidance of conflict of interest and assurance of impartiality as required by Articles 5 and 30 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. In the DVIs, chosen as examples by the audit team, it was noted that: a. The PVPs had signed a declaration of the absence of conflict of interest. The declarations lacked the above-mentioned additional provisions. The DVOs interviewed had not recognised some circumstances that could be regarded as causing a conflict of interest (e.g. delegating official tasks to PVPs who have professional relations with the establishments in question, who work as practitioners in the farms supplying milk to those 10 establishments, or who have been delegated to collect raw milk samples from holdings which are their clients). b. The DVOs supervision of the delegated veterinarians was limited and there was no formal system in place to ensure that supervision. The DVOs carried out less than one documented supervision visit annually in order to assess their performance of PVPs (i.e. audits or inspections of the delegated officials as required in Article 30 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625).

The PVPs are not invited to participate in the training activities organised by the CCA for official veterinarians (OVs). They can, however, participate in training activities organised at regional and district level. Conclusions on competent authorities

citations.text: According to the CCA, during the periodic controls, the general hygiene requirements for holdings are documented on the basis of checklists drawn up at local level. The audit team saw some examples of inspections reports in which these requirements were covered. The CCA also provided general data on the non-conformities detected annually at national level. However, no such checklists were used by the DVIs assessed by the audit team.

The results of raw milk sampling and testing from the dairy companies and MCCs were not available on the dairy holdings and were not included in the documentation assessed by the official inspectors during their controls. The audit team was informed that farmers usually only receive the results as text messages to their mobile phones.

In relation to the controls on milk traceability, there is not a formal requirement for the farmer to keep data on the fate of raw milk that is not in 14 compliance with the raw milk criteria and therefore cannot be placed in the market (e.g. due to residues of antibiotics). In the case examined by the audit team it was stated by the DVI interviewed that a farmer's oral declaration, on the actions taken in relation to non-compliant milk, is sufficient.

The lack of harmonised checklists impair the uniformity and consistency of controls and reporting thereof. 5.5. citations.text: The audit team noted that specific verification controls on the critical controls points (CCPs) are carried out by the official inspectors. However, not all relevant aspects were consistently covered during these controls. In particular: a. In relation to the verification of the FBOs' monitoring of pasteurisation, the inspectors interviewed had insufficient knowledge of the technical details that need to be checked regarding heat treatments. For example, the inspectors interviewed could not explain the function of the pasteurisation chart, the parameters displayed and monitored (temperature and milk flow) and the specifications and operation of flow diversion valves. Furthermore, they were not aware of the technical details regarding drying of milk powder. b. The official controls on the adequacy of the CCPs and their controls by the FBOs was not always sufficient (e.g. the absence of any other CCP, such as the monitoring of the effectivity of drying, in addition to monitoring of the effectivity of pasteurisation in milk/whey powder production, was not considered an issue by the official inspector; the use of alkaline phosphatase testing was considered as the monitoring (and not the verification) step of pasteurisation). 5.6.2.3 Microbiological criteria for foodstuffs Legal requirements Articles 3 and 4, and Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. citations.text: The guidelines do not cover coagulase positive Staphylococci and not all regions have a policy to test such samples in line with the provisions of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. One RVO mentioned that in 2019 they realised that samples that exceed the 100,000 colony forming units (cfu)/g limit for coagulase positive Staphylococci were not tested for enterotoxins as the regional laboratory did not have that testing capacity. The CA of that region has since put in place a system by which non-compliant samples are tested in one of the two laboratories in the country that have this capacity. The CCA stated that they intend to also extend this system to other regions.

The official tests for process hygiene criteria in dairy products in 2018-2019 detected: a. Coagulase positive Staphylococci in 33 batches out of 1,146 sampled and tested (the CAs did not have the actual testing values in order to assess if some of these 33 batches had exceed the 100,000 cfu/g limit and would have required enterotoxin testing as specified in Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005); b. Escherichia coli in 22 batches out of 757 sampled and tested; c. Enterobacteriacae in 18 batches out of 566 tested.

The audit team assessed the actions taken in the case of two RASFF notifications (Salmonella and Listeria contaminations). It was noted that the above-mentioned guidelines have been, in general, followed. with the exception of official sampling linked to the presence of unsatisfactory hygienic conditions during the production process (see paragraph 112).

The CAs have not established a minimum frequency for official sampling and testing of alkaline phosphatase to verify the efficacy of heat-treatment (pasteurisation). Samples may be taken by DVOs on the basis of risk-analysis. However, no official sampling and testing took place in recent years. The CAs interviewed stated that they had not verified if the method used by the FBO had been validated against the ISO method as required in the EU legislation (they only check if the FBO follows the producer's instructions). The system does not allow the CAs to detect related shortcomings in FBOs' testing for this parameter7. 5.7.2 Official laboratories Findings

Customs carry out plant health related controls on goods which form part of passenger luggage at all border crossings under Article 53(d)(ii) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Customs stated that checks in relation to plants for planting and seeds in personal luggage that are accompanied by a phytosanitary certificate must be carried out at the BCP as they are not exempt from controls at the BCP as specified under Regulation (EU) 2019/2122. The items are treated as commercial consignments whereby the private individual must register with the VIPHSIS, TRACES (NT) and make a customs declaration. These requirements are outlined in the memorandum of understanding (MOU) with customs and national legislation.

Non-compliant goods which form part of passenger luggage are reported to the VIPHSIS via Head of Customs and Fiscal Office in collated form at the end of the year. However, Customs stated that these interceptions are not reported in TRACES interceptions in line with the requirements of Article 40(4) and 41(4) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. The CA informed the audit team that since 14 December 2019 there were 4,651 confiscated/non-compliant items recorded with a total weight of 46 tonnes.

The VIPHSIS in co-operation with Customs carry out regular checks for prohibited and non-declared items at various levels within the framework of procedures for import controls as per the MOU with Customs.

Customs also carry out checks of prohibited and non-declared items at the postal service, courier imports and in personal luggage at the airports, and other points of entry. All findings of these items are notified to the respective VIPHSIS.

Poland implements IMSOC, however interceptions of non-compliant passenger luggage are not reported contrary to the EU requirements. As none of these interceptions are notified on TRACES this data cannot be taken into account by MS when planning their controls.

recommendations.text: Ensure that formulation details of PPPs are provided to the designated official laboratory conducting formulation analysis of PPPs promptly to help ensure that analysis is conducted in a timely manner as required by Article 37 (4) (d) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation based on conclusion No 92 Associated finding No 81

citations.text: In 2020, the laboratory processed samples in an average of 34 days from receipt of the sample to reporting the results. The laboratory explained that analysis can take considerably longer (up to six months) in a small number (circa. 5%) of cases. This occurs in cases where the laboratory requests the formulation details from MARD and there are delays in receiving this information. This information is necessary for the laboratory to conduct the most appropriate analysis and to determine if the analytical result demonstrates compliance. On average, MARD provided this information in 28 days in 2020, but in a quarter of all cases, it took 37 days or longer, which is significant in the context of the average turnaround time of 34 days. These administrative delays during 2020 acted as an impediment to the laboratory delivering analysis results in a timely manner as required by Article 37 (4) (d) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. MARD explained that there were particular challenges in this area in 2020, as this information is confidential, and was difficult to access for staff working from home due to restrictions related to Covid-19.

The administrative delays in providing formulation details to the formulation laboratory during 2020 delayed the timely delivery of analytical results, and weakened the overall effectiveness of the control programme.

citations.text: The audit team looked at more detailed data on monitoring. Those show important variations between the regions regarding the percentage of the target they were achieving. One region (Masovian) was constantly not reaching the targets. This indicates a persistent issue with sampling, in particular in one district that had reported a lower density of foxes. 10

The fact that some districts do not collect and analyse the necessary number of samples and the geographical bias (i.e. samples taken only from some hunting grounds), can reduce the representativeness and reliability of the results obtained from their analysis and the validity of the conclusions drawn up at regional and district level on the levels of immunity reached.

The values of sero-positivity in young foxes demonstrates that, in some regions, oral vaccination campaigns have not successfully reached the young fox population. There is an important variation between authorities regarding the use of hunting data. This likely means that the difference between districts regarding the quality of their planning and monitoring is increasing, with those using hunting data to fine-tune the actions planned in the eradication programme achieving better results.

The insufficient monitoring of vaccination effectiveness in some areas of the country weakens the authority's capability to detect promptly potential issues in the rabies eradication, in particular in oral vaccination of wild carnivores.

recommendations.text: Ensure that when the presence of Clavibacter sepedonicus is suspected based on a positive result of the first detection test, official measures are carried out as required by Article 4 (2) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1194. The recommendation is based on conclusion Nos 14 and 24. Associated finding Nos 9, 10, 21 and 23.

citations.text: For the first detection test, the laboratories mostly use the immunofluorescence (IF) test. Where the result is positive, the second detection test is by conventional PCR for seed potatoes, for other potatoes it is mostly the fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH) test. The laboratories inform the VIPHSIS about positive results and the suspected presence of C. sepedonicus in the form of a test report, which is issued when all detection tests are finished. The laboratories do not inform immediately the VIPHSIS when the first detection test result is positive, even though, based on Annex I. point 1.1 of Regulation (EU) 2022/1194, the presence of C. sepedonicus is suspected where a positive result is obtained in the first detection test.

The MIPHSIS provided detailed information on the diagnostic and administrative steps of 48 samples connected to 43 places of production where C. sepedonicus was recently detected. This is equal to approximately 10% of the places of production where C. sepedonicus was detected in 2022. The laboratories issued the test report more than one week later, after the positive result of the first detection test for more than 25% of these samples. In some cases, this period was longer than two weeks. At the end of the identification test, the test result on the confirmed presence of C. sepedonicus was issued over one week later for 20% of these samples. The delayed information prevents the VIPHSIS from performing official activities in a timely manner (see also findings 21 and 25). The NRL explained the delays were due to the large number of samples, economic and personnel issues.

The laboratories do not inform the VIPHSIS about the positive result of the first detection tests and there are delays with the issuance of the test results. There are cases when the presence of C. sepedonicus is confirmed based on two detection tests other than molecular ones. The delayed information prevents the VIPHSIS from performing timely follow-up measures, which can contribute to the spread of C. sepedonicus. 5.2 SURVEYS OUTSIDE THE DEMARCATED AREAS Legal requirements Article 19 and 22 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2022/1194. Findings

The laboratories do not inform the VIPHSIS about the suspected presence of C. sepedonicus at the time of the positive result of the first detection test (see also finding 9). This way, the VIPHSIS do not implement official measures when the presence of C. sepedonicus is suspected, contrary to Article 4 (2) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1194. There are cases when the results of the tests reach the VIPHSIS with a considerable delay (see also finding 10). Consequently, this delays the start of the required official measures by VIPHSIS. Since the movement of ware potatoes is not limited after sampling (see also finding 17), infected or potentially infected lots may be sold within Poland.

The VIPHSIS trace the origin of the suspected presence of the pest in line with official guidelines. · Tracing is mandatory in case of; every level of seed potato production, when ware potatoes were produced from seed potatoes certified as Union grade A or higher, and, in specified cases when ware potatoes were produced from seed potatoes certified as Union grade B. · To reduce the burden on the VIPHSIS, the inspectors may assume that the origin of the infection is the place of production when potatoes were produced from tubers originated in the same place of production. · For ware potatoes produced from certified seed potato lots of Union grade B, the VIPHSIS may assume that the origin of the infection is the place of production, and do not trace the potential origin, when the following conditions are met: i. the planted seed potato lots were not the subject of any tracing activities, ii. samples were not tested from that place of production during the previous three years, or iii. the place of production is already under quarantine measures because of an earlier detection of C. sepedonicus. 8 However, these certified seed potatoes originated outside of that place of production and other producers might also have planted seed potato from the same lot. Consequently, potential further outbreaks of C. sepedonicus are not detected. Although the MIPHSIS stated that the exemptions are implemented to rationalise the work and cost of the operations, this procedure does not comply with Article 4 (2)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1194. Conclusions on the measures in case of suspicion of the presence

The VIPHSIS often start to implement the required official measures with considerable delays when the presence of C. sepedonicus is suspected and in certain cases they do not trace the origin of this suspected presence. recommendations.text: Ensure that when the presence of Clavibacter sepedonicus is confirmed, the competent authority establish a demarcated area without delay, as required by Article 5 (2) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1194. citations.text: The MIPHSIS provided detailed information on the diagnostic and administrative steps of 48 samples connected to 43 places of production where C. sepedonicus was recently detected. This is equal to approximately 10% of the places of production where C. sepedonicus was detected in 2022. The laboratories issued the test report more than one week later, after the positive result of the first detection test for more than 25% of these samples. In some cases, this period was longer than two weeks. At the end of the identification test, the test result on the confirmed presence of C. sepedonicus was issued over one week later for 20% of these samples. The delayed information prevents the VIPHSIS from performing official activities in a timely manner (see also findings 21 and 25). The NRL explained the delays were due to the large number of samples, economic and personnel issues.

The laboratories do not inform the VIPHSIS about the positive result of the first detection tests and there are delays with the issuance of the test results. There are cases when the presence of C. sepedonicus is confirmed based on two detection tests other than molecular ones. The delayed information prevents the VIPHSIS from performing timely follow-up measures, which can contribute to the spread of C. sepedonicus. 5.2 SURVEYS OUTSIDE THE DEMARCATED AREAS Legal requirements Article 19 and 22 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2022/1194. Findings

Where the presence of C. sepedonicus is confirmed, Article 5(2) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1194 requires that the CA shall establish a DA without delay. In the case of the assessed samples (see also finding 10), more than 15% of the test reports were issued over one week after the test was finished. Contrary to the above-mentioned requirement, the VIPHSIS established more than 50% of the DAs with a considerable delay, more than one month after the presence of C. sepedonicus was confirmed. The NPPO explained the delays were due to administrative and organisational issues.1

citations.text: Interviewed officials indicated that, pending dispatch to the laboratory, the samples could be stored in refrigerators, freezers or at ambient temperature (e.g., honey). The audit team noted that, in the national sampling instruction, there were no guidelines on the suitable storage and transport conditions for any sample/analyte/matrix combination leading to the observation that practices adopted in the three regions visited were somewhat different (e.g., a similar analyte/matrix sample could be stored chilled in one region but frozen in another). The absence in the NRCP of clear instructions on the suitable storage and transport conditions does not ensure full compliance with pertinent legal requirements (15). Furthermore, the absence of temperature measurements/checks by both the samplers (at dispatch) and the laboratory (upon receipt) of the samples, combined with the absence of information on analyte stability in matrix in all but one of the validation files scrutinised in the laboratories (see findings 31 and 35), raises the question whether this approach sufficiently ensures the compliance of the NRCP samples with the relevant legal requirements (16).

Whilst the NRCP is generally implemented promptly and in full accordance with planned arrangements and in line with EU rules, some shortcomings, i.e., absence of clear provisions on the suitable storage and transport conditions for the NRCP samples, and the erroneous interpretation of the reference point for action concept, have the potential to compromise the effectiveness of the plan. 5.4. Follow-up of non-compliant results

The acceptance procedures for incoming samples at both laboratories visited addressed the checks on completeness of accompanying documentation, the seals and general status of arriving samples. The temperature status of the NRCP samples was recorded as "frozen" or "chilled" without more detailed information on the temperature of the samples at the time of reception. In combination with absence of temperature measurement prior to arrival at the laboratory (see finding 18) and lack of data on analyte stability in matrix in the validation files (see finding 35), these arrangements do not fully meet the provisions established by EU legislation (28) to ensure analyte stability and sample integrity, and, furthermore, the samples' legal, scientific and technical validity.

citations.text: The audit team noted that, at the time of the audit, none of the testing laboratories, including the NRL, was formally designated as an official laboratory, which is not in line with the requirements of EU legislation (25).

Notwithstanding the fact that the testing laboratories are accredited, operate methods included in their scopes of accreditation and perform well in proficiency tests, the absence of their official designation, deficiencies in the validation of analytical methods, in the operation of internal quality controls and in the reporting of analytical results undermine the reliability of the results and the subsequent enforcement decisions taken. 6. OVERALL CONCLUSION The planning and implementation of official controls on residues and contaminants in live animals and animal products is largely in line with EU legal requirements. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of implementation is weakened by several factors. These include insufficient provisions on suitable storage and transport conditions for samples, erroneous interpretation of the reference point for action concept, lack of formal designation of the testing laboratories, deficiencies in the validation of analytical methods relative to the EU legislative requirements applicable at the time of validation and currently, operation of internal quality controls in the laboratories visited and the reporting of analytical results. Cumulatively, these shortcomings undermine the effectiveness of the national residue control plan. 7. At this meeting, the audit team presented the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit. citations.text: The acceptance procedures for incoming samples at both laboratories visited addressed the checks on completeness of accompanying documentation, the seals and general status of arriving samples. The temperature status of the NRCP samples was recorded as "frozen" or "chilled" without more detailed information on the temperature of the samples at the time of reception. In combination with absence of temperature measurement prior to arrival at the laboratory (see finding 18) and lack of data on analyte stability in matrix in the validation files (see finding 35), these arrangements do not fully meet the provisions established by EU legislation (28) to ensure analyte stability and sample integrity, and, furthermore, the samples' legal, scientific and technical validity.

In most of the validation files scrutinised, no information was available on the animal species from which the matrices included in the validations had originated. The absence of this basic data undermines claims that the methods in question were appropriately validated for relevant species/matrix combinations.

In all, but one, of the validation files scrutinised, stability was not addressed either in solution or in matrix. This is not in line with EU legislation (30). The audit team pointed out that, if stability data are available from scientific literature or from another laboratory, these data do not need to be determined again by the concerned laboratory, provided that identical conditions apply (30).
In all of the validation files scrutinised, ruggedness was not formally addressed/assessed while the data collected allowed this to be done. This is not in line with pertinent EU requirements (30).

In one laboratory visited, in most of the validation files scrutinised, the audit team noted that only two series, on two different days, were included for reproducibility studies, which is different from EU requirements necessitating three series (31). The GVI representative explained that it was most likely due to an ambiguous translation to Polish of the relevant part of said legislation. However, the audit team noted that the second laboratory visited had correctly included three series in all of the relevant studies.

The audit team observed a number of cases where (within-day) repeatability and (between-day) reproducibility values were either similar or identical. While single values can indeed be similar, it cannot be a systemic phenomenon due to the very nature of the repeatability and reproducibility conditions, which is reflected in EU requirements (32). The possible impact of these observations on the conclusion, that the said methods were fit for their intended use, was not commented on, or discussed in any of the validation reports seen by the audit team.

In most of the validation files scrutinised, the criteria for recovery were different from the performance criteria set by EU legislation (33). The impact of such a deviation on the intended use of the methods was neither discussed nor evaluated in the validation reports.

In all of the validation files (except for the antimicrobial substances in milk method with a commercial bioassay) which were based on the preceding EU legislation (34), the audit team checked the calculation of the decision limit (CC) since the protocol used for the calculation of the detection capability (CC) had required knowledge of (30) Part 2.1. of Chapter 2 of Annex I to Regulation (EU) 2021/808. (34) Commission Decision 2002/657/EC (was in force in the time of the validations). 7 the CC. The audit team observed that the CC calculations did not follow either of the approaches laid down in EU legislation (35). In two validation files (for screening methods) stated to be based on current legal requirements (36), the audit team checked the CC calculations and observed that the calculations did not follow any of the approaches laid down in said legislation (37).

The audit team noted that during routine use of the method for thyrostats, there was no consideration of analyte instability during freezing/thawing cycles and during storage in a freezer (38) which may undermine the validity of the results (i.e., truly non- compliant samples may not be detected).

Notwithstanding the fact that the testing laboratories are accredited, operate methods included in their scopes of accreditation and perform well in proficiency tests, the absence of their official designation, deficiencies in the validation of analytical methods, in the operation of internal quality controls and in the reporting of analytical results undermine the reliability of the results and the subsequent enforcement decisions taken. 6. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of implementation is weakened by several factors. These include insufficient provisions on suitable storage and transport conditions for samples, erroneous interpretation of the reference point for action concept, lack of formal designation of the testing laboratories, deficiencies in the validation of analytical methods relative to the EU legislative requirements applicable at the time of validation and currently, operation of internal quality controls in the laboratories visited and the reporting of analytical results. citations.text: The audit team scrutinised the implementation of internal quality controls for analytical runs including a number of non-compliant results generated in 2020-2022 by the two laboratories visited and observed the following: a. In both laboratories, largely in line with EU requirements (40), quality control samples were included, quality control charts were timely created and maintained. b. While in one laboratory there was a clear written procedure on the criteria to be used for the on-going evaluation of the quality control charts, there was no such procedure in the second laboratory. It was not clear what actions would be taken in the event of deviating results on the quality control charts. This is not fully in line with pertinent legal requirements (40). c. In both laboratories, the matrices used for in-house positive (fortified) control samples were not adequately identified in the documentation provided. d. In both laboratories, when parallel runs of positive (fortified) control samples and/or routine samples with measurable amounts of residues were carried out, there were no procedures and practice to assess whether the difference between the parallel results did not exceed the methods' within-laboratory reproducibility. Consequently, no evaluation of the possible impact of that phenomenon on the analytical and legal validity of results was made.

Notwithstanding the fact that the testing laboratories are accredited, operate methods included in their scopes of accreditation and perform well in proficiency tests, the absence of their official designation, deficiencies in the validation of analytical methods, in the operation of internal quality controls and in the reporting of analytical results undermine the reliability of the results and the subsequent enforcement decisions taken. 6. OVERALL CONCLUSION The planning and implementation of official controls on residues and contaminants in live animals and animal products is largely in line with EU legal requirements. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of implementation is weakened by several factors. recommendations.text: To ensure that sampling at BCPs is fully representative, as required by Article 3 (1) of and Annex (point 3.3 of Part A) to Implementing Decision (EU) 2020/1729, in particular that: a) sampling is based on the identification of eligible consignments at all BCPs approved for fresh meat, including new countries of origin, and not only on those received in the previous year, and b) sampling of the required proportion of eligible consignments is carried out, in order to achieve the necessary sampling frequency rates. Recommendation based on conclusion No 21 Associated findings: 12 and 19

citations.text: Planning of the BCP sampling is based solely on the number of consignments received in the previous year, and not on the number of actual eligible consignments from different countries of origin arriving in each BCP (see point 19). Additionally, although 11 consignments of bovine meat from a single country of origin arrived in a BCP in 2022, no sampling was planned in that BCP for 2023. This approach is not aligned with point 3.3 of Part A of the Annex which states "proportionate stratified sampling of consignments and meat samples per border control post and country of origin with an even distribution over the monitoring year of the consignments of imported fresh meat sampled at border control posts level."

Regarding sampling at BCPs: i. 12 BCPs are designated for products of animal origin; the majority of the meat arrives in through the following road BCPs: Hrebenne, Korczowa and Dorohusk, and Warsaw airport. ii. The selection of eligible consignments for sampling is based on the list of CN codes for fresh meat, as discussed during the drafting of the EU Decision. iii. Isolates recovered in 2021 and 2022 were subjected to AST and reported to EFSA. iv. There were no samples taken in 2023 as there was no land transport of beef or pork during this time. However, a small number of beef consignments (18) that arrived in the BCP in Warsaw airport would have been eligible for sampling. v. The competent authority confirmed that sampling is solely based on BCPs identified in the sampling plan which, in turn, is based on the previous year's data (see point 12). Therefore, any consignments arriving at a BCP from a country that did not export to Poland via that BCP in the previous year are not considered. This means that some consignments were not identified, affecting the representativeness of samples, and it is not in line with point 3.3(a) of Part A of the Annex to the EU Decision. vi. In addition, the instructions for the BCP sampling did not state that the sampling frequency is calculated based on consignments and not batches. As a result, 3 samples were correctly taken from different batches of each consignment but counted individually, which resulted in the repetition of the epidemiological unit. This affects the representativeness of samples taken and it is not in line with point 3.3(b) of Part A of the Annex to the EU Decision as regards annual sampling frequency rates of consignments. Conclusions on sampling

The design of the sampling plan precludes the sampling at certain (new) BCPs and (new) countries of origin. In addition, the sample size at BCPs is not correctly calculated. These gaps affect the representativeness of sampling at this level. 7 5.3 OFFICIAL LABORATORIES Legal requirements Article 10 of Directive 2003/99/EC, Article 3 of and Annex (points 4 to 7 of Part A) to the EU Decision, and Articles 37 to 39, 100 and 101 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. citations.text: The changes in the national legislation on the remuneration system of AVs supervising the slaughter of animals announced in the AP have been partially introduced: in slaughterhouses without automatic conveyor belt the AVs are paid per hour. (EU) 2017/625 as compromises the impartiality of staff performing official tasks. Concerning this latter system, the audit 4 team was informed that almost all the slaughterhouses in Poland use it. Very few and very small slaughterhouses do not have the automatic conveyor belt and remuneration per hour is mainly applied in cutting establishments, where the permanent presence of veterinarians is not compulsory.

During the General Follow-up Audit, MARD confirmed ongoing efforts to ensure veterinarians in slaughterhouses with automatic conveyor belts would receive hourly wages and aimed to implement this legislation within a year (i.e. October 2024). The document indicated that from 2020 to October 2023, the prosecutor's offices handled 1 928 cases concerning the violation of the animal welfare law. All these cases were initiated by the VI, and following their verification were discontinued at their initial stage. The primary reason for not proceeding with the cases was that the acts in question did not constitute a criminal offense. The audit team noted that the document lacked detailed analyses or explanations to help the DVOs understand the reasons behind the dismissals and prevent similar situations from occurring in the future.

During the meetings the audit team had with the DVOs and RVOs they noted that it is difficult to monitor the prosecutors' duties, as they are independent from any other governmental body, and explain that they usually do not receive information about the follow up of the cases they transmitted to the NPO. One of the DVOs met provided figures of the number of cases transmitted to the enforcement authorities and number of cases 8 dismissed/rejected during the investigation phase (e.g. in 2023, 180 cases were notified, 80 cases dismissed/rejected and no information on 29 cases). The DVO lodged 19 complaints for the refusal to open an investigation or closure of the case at the pre-trial stage. Examples of the penalties the enforcement authorities imposed to two operators that transported unfit bovine animals to the slaughterhouse were provided: in one case (two animals involved) the fine imposed was 700 PNL (168 Euros) and in the other case (one bovine animal involved) was 100 PNL (23.35 Euros).

According to the DVO and RVO when they identify non-compliance related to animal welfare, they do not take into account whether the same operator has repeatedly committed these breaches, nor do they maintain any records. Consequently, they lack awareness of whether an FBO has a history of repeated offenses and are unable to include this information in their notifications to the NPO.

Despite nearly all the actions from the AP being implemented and GVI's' efforts to strengthen enforcement measures for non-compliance with animal welfare rules, significant progress has not been made. Many cases are still being dismissed or rejected by enforcement authorities. According to the Polish legal system, the VI has no competence on this matter. 9 5.6 RECOMMENDATION NO 6 OF THE 2021 AUDIT "To ensure that approved establishments meet the relevant requirements of food law and that those requirements are kept under review when carrying out official controls in order to comply with Article 148(3) and (5) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Particular attention should be paid to the assessment of the HACCP procedures in poultry establishments, in order to verify that the risk associated with Salmonella contamination is adequately addressed". Findings

recommendations.text: The CA should ensure that the staff performing official controls are kept up-to-date and receive the appropriate level of knowledge in their area of competence to be able to perform their duties competently as required by Article 5 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. In this regard, particular attention should be paid to: · The assessment of the food business operators' procedures based on the HACCP principles in poultry slaughterhouses, in order to ensure they comply with Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 and are adequate to prevent and/or minimise the risk of Salmonella contamination of the meat they produce and · Controls to verify that the production of poultry meat is done in accordance with EU legislatio based on conclusion No 38 Associated findings Nos 32, 33, 34, 36 and 49

citations.text: Nevertheless, at the poultry slaughterhouses visited the audit team observed the following situations, that do not meet some of the requirements of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council and that represent a risk of contamination of the poultry meat, which had not been detected/recorded during the DVOs' controls: a) in all the slaughterhouses, after the scalding and plucking of birds the slaughter line (with the exposed carcases) continued to remain for a long time in this area (considered as dirty area by the FBOs). In one case the cutting off heads of the carcases took place in this area. This area was heavily contaminated, especially in two out of the three slaughterhouses visited and in one case it was not completely separated from the bleeding line and the hanging line of alive birds. b) in one slaughterhouse, extensive condensation was observed.

Other non-compliances, neither detected/recorded during the DVOs' controls, were also noted at the poultry slaughterhouses: a) In one slaughterhouse, several carcases considered unfit for human consumption were removed and immediately discarded by slaughterhouse staff, before the PMI so, the AVs could not check them and know the reasons for which they were rejected. This is not in line with Article 25(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 that requires all poultry carcases to undergo PMI. b) In two slaughterhouses the carcases were washed after the evisceration and before the PMI. This is not in line with EU requirements as washing prevents from assessing possible faecal contamination, and EU legislation requires that the operator must take measures to prevent the spillage of digestive tract contents during evisceration in line with Point 5, Chapter IV, Section II of Annex III of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. 10 c) In one slaughterhouse, the meat remained in the cutting area for long periods as extensive quantities of meat were processed. This could lead to temperature abuse. d) In one slaughterhouse the area of uploading of birds was also used for the cleaning of vehicles and the cleaning and storage or clean crates used for the transportation of birds. No precautionary measures were used for avoiding the contamination of clean crates during these works.

Regarding the CAs' ability to assess the adequacy of HACCP-based procedures at the poultry slaughterhouses the audit team noted improvements as, overall, all the relevant hazards were considered in the HACCP plans. However, the following aspects observed by the audit team had not been noted or recorded in the inspection reports the CAs drafted during the last year: a. Two slaughterhouses accept only Salmonella spp negative flocks and, based on that, HACCP plans consider Salmonella as a medium or low risk hazard. Therefore, preventive measures to avoid Salmonella contamination indicated in the plans were limited (e.g. PMI, washing of carcases and temperature control). However, several Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (RASFF) notifications for Salmonella spp had been issued for these slaughterhouses during the last years and the HACCP plans did not take into account the risk of receiving Salmonella positive flocks. In one of these slaughterhouses the FBO expressed some doubts about the test results indicated in the documents accompanying the flocks. For this reason, they test all flocks (neck skin samples), daily, as well as the trucks and cages transporting the animals (swab tests). Moreover, a list with farmers that were involved in Salmonella RASFF notifications is kept and birds coming from these farms are slaughtered at the end of the day. In this slaughterhouse, the number of RASFF notifications due to presence of Salmonella in meat has decreased considerably. The audit team was informed that the price of birds coming from positive Salmonella farms is 20% lower than the price from Salmonella negative ones. b. In another slaughterhouse, the Salmonella preventive measures applied at control points or critical control points, could not be validated as being effective for the control of pathogens. Such measures, for example, are the visual inspection of carcases before the air chilling (in order to detect faecal contamination) and the temperature control at the beginning and the end of the water chiller. c. In two slaughterhouses, the FBOs failed to validate or verify their HACCP plans. Despite the repeated detection of Salmonella spp in end products like chicken fillets, there were no significant modifications to the HACCP plans or the company's routine cleaning and disinfection methods.

The audit team found evidence that the HACCP training and workshop on official verification of the HACCP system for RVOs and DVOs in charge of supervising food sector establishments, as announced in the AP, took place. At a poultry slaughterhouse, the audit team met two DVOs who had participated in the HACCP training session. However, it was noted that the evaluation of HACCP documentation and records was incomplete in some areas (e.g., hazard analysis validation, monitoring procedures, and verification of the FBO's microbiological sampling). For instances, at this slaughterhouse the microbiological sampling on process hygiene criteria revealed Salmonella contamination. The DVO did not note/record that FBO had not taken corrective actions/measures for investigating the cause and no actions had been taken when the rolling window exceeded the legislative limits for Salmonella spp. A GVI representative explained that the HACCP training is not yet complete, as it consists of two parts, and only the first one has been delivered.

The implementation of most actions listed in the AP to address this recommendation has led to improvements in establishments' compliance with EU standards and in HACCP plan assessments. Nonetheless, the shortcomings noted in HACCP plans and during the production of poultry meat in some establishments indicate that the measures currently in place are either not effective enough or not delivering the expected results. 5.7 RECOMMENDATION NO 7 OF THE 2021 AUDIT "To ensure that effective corrective actions are implemented where the internal audits and/or supervision activities carried out by the competent authorities identify shortcomings, in order to comply with Articles 6(1) and 12(3) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625". 12 Findings

Despite the given explanation, the audit team found that the DVOs at the two slaughterhouses accepting only Salmonella-negative flocks (see paragraph 34a) considered their HACCP plans adequate. The risk of receiving Salmonella positive flocks, for example due to contamination during the 21-day timeframe, was not considered in the assessment of these HACCP plans.

recommendations.text: To ensure that, when the results of testing against the criteria set out in Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 are unsatisfactory (in particular, when indicating contamination with Salmonella), the measures taken by the food business operators are appropriate for the purpose of finding the cause of the unsatisfactory results and to prevent recurrence of the contamination, as required by Article 7(1) of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. Recommendation based on conclusion No 52 Associated findings Nos 50 and 51

citations.text: In all the poultry slaughterhouses visited the implementation of the measures and corrective actions provided in the HACCP plans in case of Salmonella detection could not identify the source of the contamination and prevent recurrence. It was noted that the FBO's actions and investigations were repeatedly focused on primary production (e.g. visits to farms and verification of the biosecurity measures) and did not pay attention, for example, to possible cross contamination points or production shortcomings at establishment level.

During the DVO visits, they confirm the FBOs' actions implemented to identify the source of the contamination and prevent recurrences. However, they did not assess the adequacy of these actions, as there was no comprehensive evaluation of the establishment's HACCP systems. For instance, the audit team found in two slaughterhouses where Salmonella spp was found in chicken fillets, the FBOs' investigations overlooked potential cross- contamination risks during the slaughter and cutting processes (see also paragraph 36). This issue was neither identified nor documented during the DVO's inspections. Conclusions on recommendation No 8 of the 2021 audit

Although the measures from the action plan were implemented and improvements have been observed since the 2021 audit, the actions are not effective or do not have the expected results. They often fail to identify the source of contamination or prevent its recurrence, suggesting that the measures taken by the FBOs to address this recommendation are not adequate and/or sufficient. 5.9 RECOMMENDATION NO 9 OF THE 2021 AUDIT "To ensure that in case of suspicion of non-compliance (e.g. reliability of Salmonella test results provided by some private laboratories), the competent authorities perform an inves- tigation to confirm or to eliminate the suspicion, as prescribed by Article 137(2) of Regula- tion (EU) 2017/625. In case the non-compliance is established, appropriate measures to pre- vent further occurrences of such non-compliance should be taken, as prescribed by Article 138(1) of the same Regulation". Findings

recommendations.text: To ensure that in case of suspicion of non-compliance (i.e. reliability of Salmonella test results the food business operators rely to validate or verify the correct functioning of their procedures based on HACCP principles and good hygiene practice), the competent authorities perform an investigation to confirm or to eliminate the suspicion, as prescribed by Article 137(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. In case the non-compliance is established, appropriate measures to prevent further occurrences of such non-compliance should be taken, as pre-scribed by Article 138(1) of the same Regulatio based on conclusion No 63 Associated findings Nos 54, 55, 56, 57, 58 and 59

citations.text: Although the measures implemented seem adequate for addressing the issues covered by this recommendation, there continues to be discrepancies on results obtained in the parallel testing, with the percentage of positive official samples to Salmonella several folds higher than the corresponding in FBO samples. The table 1 below reports the number of parallel samples taken from 2022 to 2024, by semester, and the Salmonella results of the official and FBOs analysis: Table 1 Year No No of Percentage No of Percentage Official/FBO Semester parallel results with of results positive of positive Testing Salmonella results tests with SE/ST results performed spp Salmonella SE/ST spp 643 154 23,95% 26 4,04% Official testing 5,13% 2022a 33 22,66% 7 1,09% FBO's testing 5,66% 459 104 20,19% 29 6,32% Official testing 6,65% 2022b 26 23,59% 5 1,09% FBO's testing 5,90% 2023a 421 85 19,00% 17 4,04% Official testing 5,60% 28 6 1,43% FBO's testing 390 92 6 1,54% Official testing 2023b 23 0 0,00% FBO's testing 2024a 413 79 5 1,20% Official testing 23 0 0,00% FBO's testing SE: Salmonella Enteritidis ST: Salmonella Typhimurium

At the poultry slaughterhouses visited the audit team confirmed that the parallel testing and collation and analysis of results continues to be in place (see table 2), although the number of samples taken in parallel has been decreasing during the last years. 3 Official samples to test for Salmonella are taken from the neck skin of poultry carcases in parallel with the own- check samples (i.e. on the same day, from carcases from the same flock), and in line with the plan specified in Row 2.1.5 of Chapter 2 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. 16 Table 2 SE: Salmonella Enteritidis ST: Salmonella Typhimurium

The discrepancy between the parallel sampling results, where test outcomes consistently favour the FBOs, raises concerns about the reliability of the FBOs' testing. In this regard, the CAs' explanation that this fact could be due to the natural variation in microorganism distribution seems insufficient, given the one-sided nature of the discrepancies and the significant differences observed. The GVI noted that a new instruction on sample collection, aimed to bring more accuracy and fairness in verifying FBOs' test results, have been introduced as of October 2024. This updated protocol mandates that both official and FBO samples are to be taken from the same neck skin of poultry carcases to ensure the samples are truly representative and comparable.

The audit team observed parallel sampling procedures at two slaughterhouses, revealing differences in practice. In one instance, the AV followed the new instruction, taking a single neck skin sample from a carcase and dividing it into two separate samples: one for official purposes and the other for the FBO use. In contrast, the other slaughterhouse adhered to the previous procedure, collecting FBO and official samples from different carcases of the same flock4. Furthermore, it was noted that disinfectant was used to clean the area before sampling at one of the slaughterhouses, compromising the quality of the sample and, consequently, the validity of the test result.

The audit team visited two approved laboratories. The visit to one laboratory was ineffective as it was not involved in Salmonella parallel testing of neck skin samples for demonstration of compliance with Reg. 2073/2005, and no neck skin samples were available or were being tested at the time of the visit. The second laboratory performs parallel testing of samples from one of the visited slaughterhouses. This laboratory has a large throughput of samples daily for microbiological analysis. Despite the 4 In its response to the draft report, the competent authority stated that During the audit in November 2024, the Office for the Safety of Food of Animal Origin, responsible for the guidelines of the CVO of 31 January 2018 for OVs on the rules of procedure for the control of sampling and performance of microbiological tests of food of animal origin and composite food produced by food enterprises subject to the supervision of the Veterinary In- spection, provided DVOs with information on the change in the method of sampling for testing as part of official verification in relation to the indicated guidelines. According to the change, samples taken as part of official verification are to be taken from the same carcasses and divided evenly between official and owner testing. How- ever, the effect of this change may be visible in 2025, after the results for the first and second half of the year have been developed. 17 microbiological section audited not being operational on the day of the audit visit, the following findings were observed: a. Sample reception was not identifying all samples in a submission, only the first one, with the rest of the labels being left to the analysts at sample preparation. Therefore, there is potential for mislabelling, especially considering the high volumes of samples tested. b. Sample reception was not taking the temperature of samples and relied on the refrigerated vehicles register of temperatures. However, the audit team observed that some clients delivered samples that arrived in vehicles without a temperature record. The temperature was not checked as there are not instruments available. c. Sample preparation was witnessed for a poultry neck skin sample that was not adequately packaged and consisted of large pieces of neck skin and fat, much larger than three 10 g pieces. The analyst preparing the sample was not aware of what constituted a neck skin sample under the microbiological criteria regulation. There were no clear acceptance criteria for neck skin samples, and there is a risk that 25 g could be taken from only one of the neck skin pieces in such large samples. d. The laboratory does not use a batch positive quality control sample. Therefore, the validity of the tested samples cannot be assured. This is particularly concerning ruling out false negative results, which could occur if the testing conditions are not optimal, such as when the laboratory is overwhelmed with a high volume of samples. The absence of a positive quality control sample can lead to an unintended mistake going unnoticed. In addition, the use of positive control organisms is an integral part of ISO 72185 standard (Point 16.2.2.3). This standard is included in the normative references of ISO 6579-1:20176, the analytical reference method for Salmonella of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. This finding was also observed in the other laboratory visited.

As of 2021, the GVI requested several checks to be performed by the NRL in some of the laboratories where discrepancies in the parallel sampling were observed. In 2023, the NRL performed an unannounced inspection in the laboratory performing parallel tests visited. The NRL' inspection report drafted after this control shows that the inspection: a. Focussed mainly on the laboratory compliance with the requirements for being approved according to the national rules. This was also the case for other NRL's reports the GVI provided to the audit team. b. Did not look for findings that could explain potential false negative Salmonella results or did not investigate the root cause that could explain the discrepant results. 5 ISO 7218, on Microbiology of food and animal feeding stuffs -- General requirements and guidance for micro- biological examinations 6 ISO 6579-1:2017 on Microbiology of the food chain. Horizontal method for the detection, enumeration and serotyping of Salmonella Detection of Salmonella spp. 18 Reasons that could impact on the reliability of the results could be related to the sample (e.g. sample traceability, sample `quality' and sample preparation steps) and the method performance (e.g. media quality, the correct time and temperature of incubation steps). If the optimal conditions are not met, Salmonella may fail to grow giving rise to false negative results. c. Did not detect, or record, any of the shortcomings the audit team observed during the visit to the laboratory (see paragraph 58).

Despite the implementation of measures aimed at addressing this recommendation, the persistence of discrepancies in the results obtained in the parallel testing shows that they are not having the desired effect and/or are not sufficiently effective. The failure to resolve this ongoing issue undermines confidence in the reliability of the results of microbiological tests on which the FBOs rely to validate and verify the correct functioning of their procedures based on HACCP principles and good hygiene practices, raising concerns about the safety assurances provided for poultry meat production. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION The audit revealed positive changes in the control system compared to the 2021 remote audit. Notably, the audit found that the actions outlined in the action plan to address the recommendations related to fees for slaughtering adult bovines, animal welfare controls at 19 slaughterhouses, and staff supervision have been implemented. As a result, the audit confirmed that these recommendations have been satisfactorily addressed. Furthermore, significant progress has been made in key areas, including staffing, prevention of conflict of interest, and information exchange between different levels of the competent authorities, addressing relevant recommendations However, the control of Salmonella in poultry meat remains a concern due to several persistent issues. Firstly, food business operators often fail to conduct thorough investigations to identify the source of contamination, which compromises their ability to prevent its recurrence. Secondly, competent authorities face challenges in assessing the adequacy of food business operators' procedures, based on HACCP principles. Perhaps most critically, the discrepancy between Salmonella test results from official and food business operators' sampling continues, with official samples showing significantly higher positive rates. This ongoing issue undermines confidence in the reliability of microbiological test results used by food business operators, which is essential for validating and verifying the effectiveness of their procedures and, therefore, for providing assurances about the safety of the poultry meat production. 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held on 25 November with VI representatives. At this meeting, the audit team presented the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit and advised of the relevant time limits for the production of the report and their response. The representatives of VI acknowledged the findings and conclusions presented by the audit team and provided some comments and explanations. 8 RECOMMENDATIONS The competent authority is invited to provide details of the actions taken and planned, including deadlines for their completion ('action plan'), aimed at addressing the recommendations set out below. With regard to those non-compliances noted in the audit report which did not result in a recommendation being made, the competent authority is, nevertheless, requested to address these. The effectiveness of the actions taken to address such non-compliances will be assessed in future audits on this topic. No. Recommendation 1. In order to comply with the requirements of Article 5(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, the CA should ensure that the procedures and/or arrangements in place provide guarantees about the impartiality of the official controls and activities and, in particular, that the remuneration system of staff performing official tasks at slaughterhouses is not based on the number of animals slaughtered. Recommendation based on conclusion No 12 20 No. Recommendation Associated findings Nos 9 and 10 2 To ensure that, when non-compliances in relation to the requirements for animal welfare are detected during the official controls, appropriate enforcement actions are taken. In this regard: a) The actions taken should prevent further occurrences of the non- compliances, as required by Art. 138(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls verify the adequacy and completeness of operators' HACCP-based procedures. Legal basis: Articles 4.3 and 29 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 Recommendation based on conclusion: 49 Associated findings: 36
recommendations.legal_basis: Articles 4.3 and 29 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 Recommendation based on conclusion: 49 Associated findings: 36

citations.text: The petfood and processing plants visited maintained HACCP-based procedures as re- quired by Article 29 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. However, the audit team noted that these procedures were deficient in several areas: (a) incomplete process flow dia- gram, (b) insufficient monitoring arrangement for critical control points or (c) missing critical control points required by EU rules on ABP and DP for processing plants im- plementing continuous processing methods. These issues were overlooked during past official controls.

Official controls at ABP plants cover HACCP-based procedures when required but they are not sufficient to reliably verify the operators' level of compliance with all of the key requirements of these procedures, resulting in incomplete identification of hazards by ABP operators.

citations.text: The audit team noted that commercial documents accompany ABP and DP during transport, as required by Article 17 of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. In most cases, they contained the necessary information. However, in one of the petfood plant visited (raw petfood), ABP commercial documents were missing for most of the category 3 materials used in the production of petfood. The audit team noted that GVI had taken action to avoid that such situation is widespread and had informed (by means of circular letters) all food business operators where ABP are generated and collected that ABP commer- cial documentation should be used in all cases. In addition, the audit team noted that all inspectors met were aware of such requirements and routinely verified the presence and completeness of commercial documentation during their inspections. 8

In relation to categorisation and handling of ABP, past inspections carried out in some of the petfood and intermediate plants visited overlooked that, contrary to the require- ments of Article 9 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, operators considered as Category 3 material the following materials: (a) material of animal origin collected from unclean sections (floor) and (b) Category 3 material containing foreign bodies. Some of these in- correctly categorised materials were recycled in the production of petfood or dispatched to processing plants for Category 3 material from which derived products may be used in feed. The audit team noted that the quantities of ABP incorrectly categorised as Cate- gory 3 were limited compared to the overall quantities of Category 3 material used by the operators.

During the review of files concerning actions taken by DVIs in cases of petfood contam- inated with Salmonella or exceeding the acceptable values for Enterobacteriaceae, the audit team noted that some of these non-compliant petfood (Category 2 material) was disposed of accompanied by commercial documentation stating these were Category 3 material, contrary to the provisions of Article 9 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. However, despite this incorrect categorisation, the audit team noted that such petfood had been processed in Category 1 and 2 processing plants, which prevented their diver- sion back into the feed chain.

In one of the petfood plant visited (canned petfood), the audit team noted that the opera- tor's procedures for dealing with ABP that were unfit for production of petfood (e.g. Category 2 material) were very succinct and did not allow for an unequivocal identifica- tion of the crates to be used for collecting such ABP. As a result, the audit team noted that containers of various colours were used, some being identified with paper labels that could easily be removed. In particular, crates for storing raw material fit for use and material unfit for production of petfood were identical, except for a paper label glued on the crate and bearing the mention `kat. 2'. On the day of the visit, the audit team noted that crates identified as holding Category 2 material were being used for the production of petfood. Previous official controls did not identify the aforementioned issues. After the visit, DVI inspectors conducted an inspection and established that the products used on the day of the visit were Category 3 material but that the operator had used crates wrongly labelled as storage for Category 2 material.

Official controls verify that operators use the correct category and types of ABP for manufacturing petfood. However, such controls are not sufficient to identify instances of incorrect categorisation and handling of ABP by some operators. This resulted in limited quantities of ABP being used for the production of feed or petfood while they are not allowed for such use under EU rules.

audits.title: assess the controls on antimicrobial Veterinary Medicinal Products

recommendations.text: To designate the competent authorities responsible for controlling that antimicrobials or groups of antimicrobials listed in the Annex to Regulation (EU) 2022/1255 are not prescribed in animals, as required by Article 137(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/6. Recommendation based on conclusions No 4. Associated findings No 1.

citations.text: According to personnel from the General Veterinary Inspectorate (GVI), the designation of the competent authority responsible for checking that antimicrobials reserved for the treatment of certain infections in humans are not prescribed for animals is contingent on having national legislation in place incorporating the requirements of the VMPR. Work is still in progress in that regard, and it is expected to be finished during the first half of 2026. This is not in line with Article 137(1).

Although the new instructions to conduct controls on the use of VMPs include the need to check whether antimicrobials in the reserved list have been prescribed, the competent authorities responsible for these types of checks have not been designated yet. Therefore, recommendation 1 of report DG(SANTE) 2023-7694 has not been addressed. 4.2 OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON THE USE OF ANTIMICROBIALS Legal requirements Articles 105(1) to (3), (5)(m) and (6), 106(1), 107(1) to (5) and (7) to (9), 108, 112 to 114, and 123. 2 Observations and findings Report DG(SANTE) 2023-7694 concluded that even though checks done in accordance with national legislation enacted before 2019 covered the trade and use of VMPs, the absence of planning and implementation of controls to verify compliance with most of the requirements under the scope of this audit, notably those on the use of antimicrobials, did not allow the competent authorities to contribute to a more prudent use of antimicrobials through the enforcement of the VMPR. The audit team noted the following:

recommendations.text: To lay down rules on penalties applicable to infringements of Regulation (EU) 2019/6, that are effective, proportionate and dissuasive, as required by its Article 135(1). Recommendation based on conclusion No 14. Associated finding No 11.

citations.text: According to personnel from GVI, they will not be able to impose efficient penalties applicable to infringements of the VMPR until national legislation is in place, incorporating the requirements of the VMPR, which is not expected to happen before the first half of 2026 (see point 1). This is not in line with Article 135(1).

Despite the number of veterinarians referred to the relevant regional veterinary chambers, the lack of national legislation still prevents GVI to impose dissuasive penalties applicable to infringements of the VMPR. Therefore, recommendation 3 of report DG(SANTE) 2023-7694 has not been addressed. 4 5 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS There has been noticeable and significant progress in designing and implementing suitable controls to check compliance with the prudent use requirements of the Veterinary Medicinal Products Regulation (VMPR). However, there continues to be: i) a lack of designation of the competent authority responsible for checking that antimicrobials reserved for the treatment of certain infections in humans are not prescribed for animals, and ii) an inability to impose dissuasive penalties applicable to infringements of the VMPR. Both issues undermine the effectiveness of the new controls to ensure compliance with the prudent use requirements of the VMPR, which in turn affects the ability of the Polish authorities to fight antimicrobial resistance. 6 CLOSING MEETING During the closing meeting, held remotely on 21 October 2024, the audit team presented the main findings and preliminary conclusions to the competent authorities, who acknowledged them. 7 RECOMMENDATIONS The competent authorities are invited to provide details of the actions taken and planned, including deadlines for their completion (`action plan'), aimed at addressing the recommendations set out below. The effectiveness of the actions taken to address such non- compliances will be assessed in future audits on this topic. No. Recommendations 1. audits.title: evaluate the system of official controls on animals and goods entering the European Union and verification of compliance of border control posts with European Union requirements

recommendations.text: To ensure that border control posts and inspection centres thereof comply with the minimum requirements for the categories of goods for which the border control post has been designated and are only listed if compliant with those requirements. Legal requirements: Article 64(3)(b) and (h) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Articles 3(1)(b) and (c), 3(3) and 8(2) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. Recommendation based on conclusion No. 28 Associated findings No. 25, 26 and 32

citations.text: The competent authorities ensured that official controls on animals and goods entering the EU are implemented in line with relevant EU legislation, competent authorities' documented procedures and arrangements in place albeit with shortcomings noted related to the frequency of physical checks on certain consignments of goods of animal origin and the follow-up of consignments of food of non-animal origin transferred to control points. The competent authorities took immediate corrective actions to address those shortcomings, thereby minimising the risk of non-compliant goods entering the EU through BCPs in Poland. 12 5.4 Compliance of border control posts and control points with minimum requirements

The audit team noted that the road BCP Koroszczyn was generally compliant with the minimum requirements for BCPs for the categories of animals, goods of animal origin and feed of non-animal origin for which it had been designated, but not for food of non-animal origin, food contact materials and plants, plant products and other objects for the following main reasons: · There were no compliant areas or rooms suitable for storage of ambient and chilled food of non-animal origin and food contact materials, which is not in line with Article 64(3)(b) and (h) of the OCR and Article 3(1)(c) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014; · There were no suitable ambient and chilled storage rooms at the inspection centre Rampa do kontroli fitosanitarnej, usytuowana bezporednio przy budynku OG w Koroszczyn used for controls on plants, plant products and other objects which is not in line with Article 64(3)(b) and (h) of the OCR and Articles 3(1)(c) and 8(2) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. A similar observation was made during an audit carried out in 2021 to evaluate the system of import controls for plant health, ref. DG(SANTE) 2021-7273 (8). The competent authority at the time submitted an action plan indicating that new facilities would be constructed and in use in early 2022. However, due to financial constraints these have not yet been constructed. The competent authority in a further update informed that they would use the storage facilities of another inspection centre and a commercial storage facility, neither of which is located in this inspection centre visited and consequently this non-compliance was not effectively addressed. The audit team found that the proposed actions were effectively implemented and noted that the competent authorities have issued further documentary procedures for the implementation of official controls on animals and goods. 5.5.2 Recommendation 2020-7004-2

audits.title: to evaluate the implementation of official controls on medicated feed

recommendations.text: To verify that veterinary prescriptions contain all information set out in the relevant legal requirements. Legal basis: Article 16(6) and point 7 of Annex V to Regulation (EU) 2019/4. Recommendation based on conclusion: 38 Associated findings: 22 and 23
recommendations.legal_basis: Article 16(6) and point 7 of Annex V to Regulation (EU) 2019/4. Recommendation based on conclusion: 38 Associated findings: 22 and 23

citations.text: At the time of the audit, there was no prescription template laid down in domestic legislation. The prescriptions seen by the audit team were often based on a former national template, adapted to cover the information required under Annex V to Regulation (EU) 2019/4. However, the audit team noted that none of these prescriptions had a dedicated section that could be filled in by veterinarians in case of use of antimicrobials in accordance with Article 107(4) (metaphylaxis) or Articles 112, 113 or 114 (cascade) of Regulation (EU) 2019/6.

The private veterinarians interviewed by the audit team routinely prescribed medicated feed for treatment of diseases in pigs. The audit team noted that in most cases, antimicrobials used in medicated feed, such as tylosin, were prescribed following a metaphylactic approach as groups of pigs (e.g. 700 to 1400 animals) containing both sick animals and animals in close contact which may already be subclinically infected, were treated with antimicrobials. The veterinarians interviewed did not specify on the prescriptions issued that these animals followed a metaphylactic treatment, contrary to the requirements of Article 16(6) and point 7 of Annex V to Regulation (EU) 2019/4. The audit team noted that none of the prescriptions for treatment of groups of pigs with antimicrobials that were reviewed during the audit contained a reference to metaphylaxis. This was overlooked during past official controls.

While inspections cover requirements for veterinary prescriptions, they overlooked that, although medicated feed was routinely prescribed for metaphylaxis, the veterinary prescriptions did not contain a statement to that effect. 5.2.3 Actions taken on non-compliances
